en: Preface to the Combined Commentary on the Benevolent Kings Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra:
Regarding the commentary on the Benevolent Kings Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, during the Anshi Rebellion, it was ravaged by the fires of war and its transmission was severed in the Central Plains.

Upon reaching the beginning of the Song dynasty, the Patriarch of Siming sought it in many ways but ultimately failed to obtain it. It had previously been transmitted to our land of Fusang; the Master...
The transmission of its characteristics has been bestowed, and its detailed study has also been heard of; could it be that this commentary shares a special affinity with our country?

Or is it that the scholars of our land are so steadfast in their faith that they have preserved it without loss? Nevertheless, as the sutra and the commentary were circulated separately, it was difficult to find them in conjunction;
moreover, errors such as those of "hai" and "shi" abounded, making the punctuation hard to distinguish. In recent times, only the commentary has survived. And yet—

The study of this has somewhat declined; might it not be for this reason? I have long wished in secret to collate and edit these various commentaries to facilitate the study of scholars, yet circumstances have hindered me, leaving my original ambition unfulfilled.

Recently, however, Juesheng arrived holding a volume titled *Combined Commentary on the Benevolent Kings Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and requested a preface from me. Upon taking it up and examining it, I found that it was produced in Min...
This was compiled through the collaboration of Master Linpai, with revisions made more precise. Alas, this is something I have long desired to do but have not yet achieved;
moreover, since it has been brought forth by a distinguished predecessor, how could I begrudge my humble words in failing to express my sincere joy? Thus I write this preface.

In the second month of the spring of the *genroku* year of the *jin-uma* cycle, the Great Cloud [Temple] on Mount Tiantai, Ryōjun, prefaces this combined edition of the *Commentary on the Benevolent Kings’ Prajñā Sūtra for the Protection of the State*.
Formerly, when the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai extensively expounded various commentaries, they were all widely circulated throughout China; however, the *Benevolent Kings*...
This single commentary fell into foreign lands for several hundred years; it was only during the Song dynasty that it returned to its native soil through the efforts of merchants.
Yet, it failed to circulate widely in the world and remained merely hidden within the Dragon Canon (Longzang).
Recently, as the national destiny has declined and calamities have occurred in succession, the Venerable Benzhao harbored deep "Qiren-like" anxieties and thus carved the *Renwang* [Sutra].

After the printing blocks for the sutra were carved and its circulation widely encouraged for recitation, Master Weilin further observed that the meaning of the scripture was profound and remote, such that it could not be understood without a commentary.
He therefore took the ancient commentary of Tiantai and synthesized it with this [text].

Although this commentary had been transmitted since the Chen and Sui dynasties for over a thousand years, it had existed in a state of being half-forgotten and half-lost, unable to manifest fully in the world, even among veteran masters and scholars of long standing.

It is rare for anyone to obtain even a single glimpse of this; yet now, these two sons have been able to put it into practice during an autumn when the four seas are boiling over and the common people are submerged in misery.
We know that this commentary shares a great karmic affinity with sentient beings of the final age, and thus dragons and devas lent their power to circulate it.
I only wish that everyone, by means of this commentary, may penetrate the sutras, and by means of the sutras...
Yet, when one penetrates the underlying principle, the spiritual power of Prajñā is such that there is nothing it cannot shatter and nothing it cannot protect;
even the state of Buddhahood and the stage of Bodhisattvah depend upon it for their realization, let alone the governance of a realm or the welfare of living beings.

Some may argue that order and chaos alternate in a cycle ordained by Heaven, and that reciting sutras while keeping one's doors shut merely perpetuates the moral failings of predecessors—what, then, is to be gained from this?

I maintain that order and chaos certainly depend upon the mandate of Heaven, yet the mandate of Heaven is fundamentally rooted in the human mind; therefore, the human mind is the source of order and chaos.

This principle is not merely a grandiose discourse of the Buddhists; if one examines the Confucian classics from afar, such as the *Great Changes* (*Yī Jīng*) and the *Great Plan* (*Hóngfàn*), it is recorded therein in full.
How can one entirely attribute everything to the mandate of Heaven while remaining devoid of the art of creating that mandate?
If one can truly savor the purport of this sutra, there will be no technique left unexhausted for the mastery of destiny.
May gentlemen who understand destiny pay close attention to this three times. At this time.
Preface to the Commentary on the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra for the Protection of the State by the Benevolent Kings*,
inscribed by the Dharma-heir Śramaṇa Yuánxián of Gǔshān in his Bǎoshàn Studio during the latter part of the fourth lunar month in the Jiǎshēn year of the Chóngzhēn era.
Composed by Chao Shuo-zhi, *Zhaoqing Lang*, *Feiqi Wei*, Recipient of the Crimson Fish Bag.
Between the Chen and Sui dynasties, Zhiyi of Tiantai received the lineage from Nāgārjuna and established a great teaching. It was transmitted nine times to Jingxi [Zhanran].
After Jingxi, it was transmitted another nine times to Fayong of Silla. Fayong transmitted it to Lisheng; Lisheng transmitted it to [Yuan]ying.
Since both Hyegyeong and Uisang were from Silla, this teaching spread to Japan and flourished abroad;
yet, during the chaos of the Central Plains, when the scriptures were destroyed, it was precisely this teaching that could not be allowed to perish, though its preservation was difficult.
Nevertheless, as the morning sun is about to rise, the dawn glow first ascends; as the True Man responds to the mandate of destiny, civilization dawns.
I have personally observed that since the beginning of the Song dynasty, this teaching has gradually crossed the sea to enter Wu and Yue;

the "Three Great Works" currently transmitted in the world are examples of this. Yet, there are still those that remained and did not arrive, as well as those that arrived but were not the authentic originals.
Regarding the *Commentary on the Benevolent Kings Sutra*, two versions arrived first, and everyone rejected them as spurious. Formerly, Fazhi...

Having received the hair of a Pratyekabuddha sent by the Japanese Zen Master Shin and having answered the twenty points of his inquiry, [Daoxuan] sought the master’s commentary on the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra*.
Shin then entrusted it to a merchant ship. Before long, a great wind and turbulent waves arose in mid-ocean;
the crew, fearing they could not appease the wrath of dragons and crocodiles, suddenly cast this commentary overboard to seek peace.
Regarding the Dharma-knowledge for seeking those of strong memorization, two monks went with a messenger to read and recite [the texts] before returning; unfortunately, the two monks died in Japan.
At the beginning of the Yuanfeng era, a maritime merchant brought three fascicles of the present-day *Renwang* (Benevolent Kings) commentary to Siming.
Thereupon, the elder monk Ruxun obtained them through karmic conditions; its text is clear, yet its meaning is subtle, and its words are concise.
However, my intention was broad; taking the Qin translation as the basis, the structure and meaning resemble a commentary on the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra*.

In truth, these are the teachings of Zhiyi recorded by Zhizhan. My sincere path is solitary and lacks companions; I study the ancients yet find them difficult to comprehend; I live in poverty and lack sufficient strength.
Failing to do even the slightest service to honor this sutra, I point to it and sigh, saying: "Its arrival has come too late for those of us in our studies."
Yet, as difficult as this is, it is better to leave it sealed away like a wild horse than to let it rot like a silkworm, unable to rest upon a desk for people to behold.
Alas! This commentary cannot even rank among the three great collections;
its brilliance and splendor remain hidden, as if far away beyond the seas. This year, at seventy-six, I have finally embraced it in a single day.
Weeping, he said, "Is it not as if [this work] will perish along with me? My resolve from the other day was mistaken.

He encountered Chao Shuo-zhi at Mount Song and said, "Why do you not write a preface for me so that it may be circulated? Shuo-zhi looked back upon himself and considered how he could possibly be worthy of this;
he had once remarked, "If a wise man were born before the Qi and Liang dynasties, Bodhidharma would not have returned to the West."

"It is coming! Exhausting the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) as the basis for *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, it takes up the source and stream of Śākyamuni’s Way and carries within its fold the essential intent of Bodhidharma.
Now it flourishes in the region of Yue; in days to come, it shall surely spread throughout the world. How could it be that only this book is impossible to conceal?
Yet, looking back, I regret that in my old age I shall not live to see its full realization; thus I have merely composed this preface to record its origins."

General Principles for the Combined Commentary on the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra*.
It was an ancient custom to place the sutra and its commentary in separate volumes; this was done for fear that fragmenting the sacred scripture might lead to its desecration.
Nevertheless, there were two reasons why they remained separated: first, as for those in separate volumes, how many people would be able to access them when they were sealed away in storage?
Now, by combining them into a single volume, even those in remote villages and secluded regions can all see them. Second... [the second reason follows].
As for these volumes, the commentaries on the sutras were not originally linked together; thus, it would have been difficult for those who had not studied them extensively to trace their threads.

Now, they have been combined into a single volume so that readers may enter the sutra by means of the topical outline (*ke*), enter the commentary by means of the sutra, and realize the underlying principle by means of the commentary.
With its headings and subheadings now orderly and its logical connections harmonious and flowing, even a student of elementary learning can trace back to the source from its stream.
In this case, because the merit is great and the fault is small, they are combined.
Regarding the various sections within the commentary (*shū*), there are some that have an introduction but no conclusion, or a conclusion but no introduction;

this is truly because many years have passed and scribes have committed omissions and errors. Now, based on what ought to be present, I have cross-referenced them from the preceding and following sections.
I shall supplement them.
Should there be any errors, omissions, or scribal mistakes—such as confusing "hai" for "shi"—within the commentaries, I have ventured to correct them;

however, I have done so only after consulting various scriptures, cross-referencing various records, and weighing them against my own critical judgment to ensure they conform to the ultimate standard of correctness. Furthermore, and...
Furthermore, I once requested various senior masters and veteran monks to verify [this work], for I did not dare to arbitrarily add or subtract anything.
Since the ancient commentaries did not accord with the sutra, their citations of the sutra merely indicated the location of a certain phrase;
now that the commentary has been harmonized with the sutra and arranged beneath it, all the superfluous characters under those phrases have been deleted to avoid redundancy.

Regarding the inclusion of several sub-sections within a single passage of scripture due to the burden of excessive detail, I have provisionally retained them for the sake of easily identifying the structural divisions; this is intended to avoid listing all the minute categories at length.
Although the topical divisions (*ko*) of this commentary are already clear, the headings (*mukō*) have never been explicitly set forth;

furthermore, as they are scattered beneath the scriptural text, they are inconvenient for consultation. Now, following the established precedent of various commentaries, I have listed the complete headings collectively in a diagram at the beginning.
Thus, the structural connections are orderly and the sequence is not confused, so that the reader may grasp the whole at a single glance.
During the Shaoding era of the Song dynasty, Dharma Master Shan Yue composed the *Shenbao Ji* (Record of the Divine Treasure) to clarify this commentary.
Since there are occasionally difficult passages or points of contention within the current commentary that are hard to understand, I have briefly cited one or two examples;
furthermore, where the record may be incomplete, I have humbly appended my own limited insights, writing them in small characters above the relevant sections.
Someone asked: "If you wish to propagate this sutra, why do you not produce your own 'hand and eye' [of insight], but instead labor over ancient commentaries?
Is this not merely picking up the dregs of those who came before? I replied: "Not so. Among those who have expounded the scriptures in the Eastern Land, Tiantai is supreme;
his refined interpretation of each sutra has been followed and upheld for a thousand ages. Moreover, it was only after this commentary was lost that its true meaning was recovered."
To attain such [mastery] is as difficult as obtaining the characters themselves; every word is like a pearl or a jade gem, none of which is not worthy of being treasured.
Although it may be said that people of today are not necessarily inferior to those of antiquity, there are certain respects in which the ancients are absolutely unattainable;

this is why people of today, despite exhausting all their skill and effort, cannot transcend the boundaries established by the ancients. How could I be one who merely prizes the past and finds fault with the present?
Ah! It is simply that those who understand the Dharma are apprehensive.

I. Explaining the Provisionality of Dharmas (II) 1. The Proper Clarification of the Provisionality of Dharmas (II) 1. Clarifying that the Fundamental Consciousness is Capable of Producing Form and Mind The fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) is capable of producing both material form (*rūpa*) and mental states (*citta*). This is because it serves as the storehouse for all seeds (*sarvabījaka*), acting as the causal basis from which the various modes of existence—both the physical and the cognitive—arise. Specifically, through its transformation (*pariṇāma*), it manifests as the objective world of form and the subjective stream of consciousness. Thus, the diversity of the phenomenal world is entirely dependent upon the generative power of this foundational awareness.

Therefore, the thesis (*siddhānta*) is that cause and effect are without marks. Question: What is the difference between the thesis (*siddhānta*) and the essence (*svabhāva*)?

The answer is: The thesis (*zong*) is like the collar and sleeves of a garment, while the substance (*ti*) is like the hair and eyes; when the collar and sleeves are shaken, the hair moves, and when the collar and eyes are raised, the substance arises—the meaning of the thesis and the substance is thus.
Furthermore, it is like the gold and silver that constitute the substance of a hairpin or bracelet, while the artisan who fashions them constitutes the thesis.
Now, the principle of true reality (*shixiang*) is the substance, and the cultivation of causes to attain the fruit is the thesis (and so forth).
Fourth, the clarification of function (*vṛtti*). As for "function," it refers to efficacy. Some say that this sutra takes the two types of protection—internal and external—as its function.

Regarding internal protection, the subsequent text states: "For the sake of all bodhisattvas, I shall explain the causes and conditions for protecting the fruit of Buddhahood and the causes and conditions for protecting the practices of the ten stages.
Regarding external protection, the subsequent text states: "I now declare for you the protection of the state."

Because these causes and conditions cause the land to attain peace, so that the seven calamities do not arise and disasters do not occur, and the myriad people live in peace and happiness—this is called "external protection.
This, however, merely attains one mundane and one true [level]; yet even the true is not fixed, as the Ten Stages (daśabhūmi) exist across the Shared, Distinct, and Perfect [teachings].
As for what constitutes the Ten Stages, they cannot be relied upon entirely; therefore, we now take the two [aspects] of the Buddhas...
Wisdom serves as the power of application: all Tathāgatas illuminate themselves through real wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*) and illuminate others through expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*).
However, this sutra contains three types of expedient and real [wisdom], both in their general and specific aspects. Although it possesses real wisdom, it is also termed "expedient";

although the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) possesses expedients, it is collectively designated as "real. This is because the Perfect Teaching constitutes the Buddha’s own practice, wherein these two wisdoms illuminate the principle.

That which discerns the capacity [of beings] is precisely that which illuminates the principle; it is like Sarvārthasiddha, who drew the bow of King Mañjuśrī to its full extent—this is called "power" (*bala*)—piercing seven iron drums and penetrating the Iron Ring Mountain (*Cakravāḍa*), reaching through the earth to the waters—this is called "function" (*kāritra*).

While these general and specific powers and functions are subtle and weak, they are like the bows and arrows of ordinary people. Why? Because they generally receive the two wisdoms of transformation and benefit for others.

Alternatively, [the other teachings] may illuminate the principle equally but not universally, or they may require sequential realization; this is not like the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao), which illuminates and realizes all-encompassingly.

Therefore, the two wisdoms of the Perfect Middle Way are taken as its function: Expedient Wisdom (quan-zhi) protects the lands of the Shared, the Further, and the Real-Reward, ensuring that the seven calamities do not arise;
Real Wisdom (shi-zhi) protects the causes and fruits of the forty-two stages of mind within the Perfect Teaching.
The Sūtra states: "Protecting the causal conditions for the practice of the ten stages. This refers generally to the ten stages practiced according to the three teachings (*yāna*). (And so forth.

Fifth, it clarifies the characteristics of the teachings: in proclaiming the True Dharma, one must recognize the partiality or universality of the teachings, as explained extensively in the *Lotus Sūtra*.
The Profound Meaning (*Xuanyi*) now briefly clarifies this: "Teaching" (*jiao*) refers to the words of the Sage addressed to those below;
"characteristics" (*xiang*) refer to the differentiation of similarities and differences. This sutra belongs to the Prajñāpāramitā division and is included within the Mahāyāna gate;

it is a "mature ghee" (*pakva-sarpis*) flavor sutra that explains the causes and conditions for protecting the fruit of Buddhahood and protecting the practices of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). Furthermore, the King asked: "How does the Mahāyāna illuminate?"

Thus, it is clear that this is not the teaching of the Tripiṭaka. Although there are eight verses discussing matters such as impermanence and arising-and-ceasing, they merely cite the past hundred Dharma masters who used the Hīnayāna to explain that the world is not solid, thereby exhorting Puming to renounce his kingdom;
these belong to the auxiliary path (*bhāvanāmārga*) and are not the primary exposition of the present sutra. This concludes the "Profound Meaning" (*xuan yi*) preceding the sutra.
Next, we enter the textual exegesis. Now, the methods of exposition in China vary; some divide the text into sections while others do not.

For instance, when the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains the *Pañcaviṃśati-sāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā*, it does not divide it into topical sections, whereas Vasubandhu’s commentary on the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* does include such divisions.
Dao’an established the distinct categories of the Prologue, the Main Body, and the Circulation, while Liu Qiu merely followed the text in his explanations.

To explain this: it is also a matter of human nature that the orchid and the chrysanthemum have different inclinations; likewise, those who seek to penetrate the profound do not concern themselves with mundane affairs.
For now, following the literal arrangement of the text, the introduction clarifies that the Sage’s preaching of the Dharma necessarily proceeds through gradual stages;

this is called the "Introductory Section" (Nidāna). The main body clearly reveals the benefits for those present at that time; this is called the "Section of the Main Discourse" (Sūtra-deśanā). Finally, the sentient beings of the末代 (final age) shall equally partake [of these benefits].
The benefits of the Dharma are termed the *parīndanā* (circulation) section. In this sutra, the eight chapters consist of the *nidāna* (introduction) section, which is the "Introductory Chapter";
the main exposition section, comprising the six chapters from "Contemplating Emptiness" onwards; and the *parīndanā* section, which is the "Chapter on Entrustment.

If one refers to the actual text, the *parīndanā* section begins with the Buddha’s address to Candraprabha at the end of the "Chapter on Receiving and Maintaining," and so forth. Now, for the first [section].
Preface to the *Buddhabhāṣita-rājā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, Chapter One: The Preface.
The title *Buddhabhāṣita-rājā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* is the general name for the entire work, while "Chapter One: The Preface" is a specific designation within that work. Regarding these terms:
"Preface" (*xu*) means "origin" (*you*) or "sequence" (*ci*). "Chapter" (*pin*) is a transliteration of the Sanskrit...
The term *varga* is translated here as "chapter" (*pin*), meaning a category. When items of similar meaning and type are grouped together, they constitute a single chapter.
Regarding the numbering, it is intended to prevent confusion. First, the meaning is presented at the beginning; second, the text is divided into two parts.

First is the sequence of testimony and faith (*saddhā-deśanā*), and second is the sequence of origination (*samutthāna*). It is also called the general introduction (*sāmānya-nidāna*) and the specific introduction (*viśeṣa-nidāna*);

it is also called the introduction of the Tathāgata, the introduction of Ānanda, and it is further termed the preface before the sūtra and the postface after the sūtra. The six matters that testify to the authenticity of the sūtra constitute the sequence of testimony and faith;
the section that initiates the main teaching constitutes the sequence of origination. All sūtras possess these [two] in common, and thus they are called the general introduction.
The sūtras each have distinct introductory titles: those spoken from the Buddha’s own mouth are called the Tathāgata’s Preface; those authenticated by Ānanda are called Ānanda’s Preface;
those existing from the time of the Buddha are called the Preface Prior to the Sūtra; and those added by the compilers are called the Preface Subsequent to the Sūtra.
For now, we shall follow the first type, from "Thus" (evam) down to "all sat down together," which constitutes the Preface of Authentication.
Introduction: At that time, following the section on the Ten Epithets, begins the Prologue of the Arousing of Resolve and the Prologue of Verified Faith.

Regarding these, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: When the Buddha was lying with his head toward the north beneath the twin śāla trees in the kingdom of Kuśinagara, about to enter parinirvāṇa, Ānanda, as yet unable to relinquish his personal affection, was submerged in an ocean of sorrow; while Aniruddha—
He spoke to Ānanda, saying: "You, who uphold the treasury of the Dharma, should not like an ordinary person sink into the ocean of sorrow.
The Buddha was about to entrust the Dharma to you; why do you now grieve and lose the task you have received? You should ask the Buddha:
after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, how shall we practice the Path, and who shall act as our teacher? Thus spoke the harsh-spoken Cchandaka.
"What is the communal dwelling? What words does the Buddha place at the beginning of the sūtras?

Having heard this, Ānanda’s distressed mind cleared slightly, and he asked the Buddha in detail about these matters while lying by the side of the Buddha’s bed. The Buddha replied: "Abide according to the four foundations of mindfulness;
the Sūtra on Liberation and the Vinaya are the Great Teacher’s chariot. Treat the bhikṣu Cunda according to the Dharma of Brahmā."
If you think that one must change the mind by teaching the *Kātyāyanāvavāda-sūtra* to attain the Way, [you are mistaken].
This is the Dharma-treasure accumulated by me over three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*. At the very beginning, it should be stated: "Thus have I heard:

at one time the Buddha was staying in such-and-such a direction, in such-and-such a country, in such-and-such a place, within a grove of trees. Within my Dharma-gate, it should be spoken thus at the outset. Why?
In the sūtras of the Buddhas of the three periods of time, these words are all present (and so forth). Furthermore, Mahākāśyapa and others asked Ānanda:
"Where did the Buddha first preach the Dharma, and what Dharma did he preach? Ānanda replied: "Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Vārāṇasī in the Deer Park of the Ṛṣis, for the sake of five bhikṣus."

When the Noble Truth of Suffering was thus taught, all those in the great assembly who heard it believed it; this is as explained in detail in the second fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (*Chidu lun*).
For this reason, there is the "Introduction of Testimony and Faith" (*samyagavadāna-nidāna*). The text consists of six parts: first, "Thus" (*evam*), which cites the essence of the Dharma heard;
second, "I heard" (*śrutam mayā*), clarifying Ānanda as the one who maintains [the teaching]; third, "at one time" (*ekasmin samaye*).

First, the section on "The Radiance of Hearing and Retention" clarifies the mutual resonance between the teaching and its response; second, the section on "The Four Buddhas Clearly Expounding the Teaching" clarifies the masters who preach the doctrine;

third, the section on "Dwelling in Rājagṛha" clarifies the location where the teaching is preached; fourth, the section on "Together with a Great Assembly of Bhikṣus" clarifies the assembly that hears the teaching together. This is the first [section].
"So it is; so it is. All the sūtras of the Buddhas of the three periods of time conclude with "So it is," for the path of all Buddhas is identical and does not contend with the world.
This is the *Lokadhātu-siddhānta-mahāśāstra*, which states that citing time and place serves to inspire faith in people; this is the teaching for persons (*pudgala*).

The two characters "ā" and "uṇ" [in the term *āyuṣmat*] are used to refute the non-Buddhists; this is the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta*. Zhaolun states: "Thus" (*evam*) is a word signifying faith and compliance.

Faith means that the principles one has heard are integrated, while compliance means that the way between teacher and disciple is established. The integration of principles is the *paramārtha-siddhānta*.
These four are all explanations based on causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*). (As detailed in the text... This is according to the classification of teachings (*yàojiào*).
The Buddha clarified that in the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) there are words, while in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) there are no words.
Ānanda transmitted the Buddha’s conventional words without alteration; because one realizes the ultimate through these conventional words, they are not otherwise.

Thus, this is the beginning of the sūtras of this treasury of teachings. The Buddha clarified that form itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is form; form and emptiness, emptiness and form, are non-dual.

Second, there is no distinction between emptiness and form; they are not different. Thus, reality is identical to phenomena. This is how it is at the beginning of the sutras of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*).
The Buddha taught that birth and death exist while nirvāṇa does not. From the existence of birth and death, one enters the non-existence of nirvāṇa.
Within this non-existence of nirvāṇa, there is neither entry nor exit—this is the Middle Way. Ānanda’s transmission of this was no different from that of the Buddha.
The beginning of this *Bie-jiao* (Distinct Teaching) Sūtra is as follows: The Buddha taught that birth-and-death is itself nirvāṇa, which is the Middle Way pervading all places;
there is nothing that is not the Buddha-dharma, and this is called the "True Aspect" (*yathābhūta-lakṣaṇa*). Ānanda’s transmission of this is no different from the Buddha’s own;
it is called "Suchness-as-such" (*tathatā-tathatā*) because it is immovable. This is the beginning of this *Yuan-jiao* (Perfect Teaching) Sūtra. This...
The Sūtra contains the meaning of the three teachings and the three truths; Ānanda transmitted it without error or mistake.
Second, to clarify Ānanda as the one who could uphold it:
"Thus have I heard."

The *Mahā-śrāvaka-vyākhyāna* states: "Because the faculty of hearing is unimpaired, the sound is within the range of audibility, and the mind intends to hear—through the convergence of these various conditions—it is said, 'I heard.
'I' refers to the aggregate [of the self], while 'hearing' refers to the specific [faculty]; this is the explanation of the aggregate subsuming the specific according to the worldly convention.
When Ānanda ascended the seat and uttered, "I have heard," the great assembly wept with grief, and one flying through the air spoke this verse; this constitutes [the introduction].
Ānanda was a human being; when he ascended the seat, the assembly doubted whether Śākyamuni had arisen again, or if Ānanda had attained Buddhahood, or if a Buddha from another direction had come.
By uttering "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*), these three doubts are immediately dispelled. This is the explanation of the remedy for these [doubts]:

Ānanda followed worldly convention in saying "I heard," yet in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), "I" is precisely non-self, and "hearing" is precisely non-hearing—yet it is not that there is no hearing.

"Having heard 'not-me' yet [claiming] 'I'—this is the explanation according to the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*). Regarding the explanation by way of the teachings (*yathāśāsana*), the *Śāstra* states:

'Ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) have three types: view, pride, and conventional designation; those in training (*śaikṣa*) have two; and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) have one. Ānanda is one who is in training;
he has no false sense of 'I,' but he subdues pride through the 'I' that follows worldly convention. This is the intention of the Tripiṭaka."
The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā* states: "To claim 'self' in any of the four propositions is to follow false views; within the Buddha’s True Dharma, there is no self.
Who could hear this and understand the intent of the Shared Teaching (*p’ungiao*)? The *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "The learned Ānanda can naturally comprehend both 'self' and 'non-self.
He knows that while 'self' and 'non-self' are two, they are non-dual, yet he distinguishes them both."

"The absence of self" is the intent of this distinct teaching (*bhedavyavahāra*). If Ānanda were to know that "self" and "non-self" are non-dual yet dual, and dual yet non-dual, he would serve as an attendant through skillful means (*upāya*) to transmit the Buddha’s wisdom; this is the interpretation according to the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-vyavahāra*).
According to the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra*, there are three Ānandas: first, Ānanda, which is translated as "Joyful," who upholds the Hīnayāna Piṭaka; second... [text continues].
Ānanda-bhadra—translated here as "Joyful Sage"—upheld the *Kṣudraka-piṭaka*. Ānanda-sāgara—translated here as "Joyful Ocean"—upheld the *Buddha-piṭaka* and the *Āgama*.
Ānanda-kośa—translated here as "Treasury"—upheld the *Bodhisattva-piṭaka*. This refers to a single individual who possessed these four virtues and transmitted these four teachings;
the meaning is clear. As for those who contemplate the mind, there are both those who hold to emptiness and those who hold to existence.
In the contemplation of the provisional and the Middle Way, the correct contemplation is that "I am emptiness" means there is no self;
"I am the provisional" means that non-self is precisely the self; and "I am the Middle" is the true self.

As for the listener Ānanda, he was born on the night the Buddha attained the Way and attended the Buddha for over twenty years. Before attending the Buddha, he likely had not heard this; thus the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says, "Ā..."

It is not that what was heard through successive transmission is not the *Sarvabuddhapravacanodāharaṇa-sūtra* (the Sūtra on Repaying Kindness). When Ānanda requested four vows, he wished for the Buddha to re-expound the Dharma he had not yet heard.

The *Garbhakośa-sūtra* (Treatise on the Womb) states: "The Buddha emerged from the golden coffin and extended his golden arm, once again manifesting to Ānanda the signs of entering and emerging from the womb. Because of this, all sūtras are said to have been "heard. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* likewise says: [it is so].
When Ānanda received his prediction, he immediately recollected the Buddha-dharma of the past so that it appeared as if present before him;
thus, all proclaimed the explanation of the causes and conditions for his renown. If one rejoices, Ānanda’s face is like the pure full moon and his eyes are like blue lotuses;
having personally received the Buddha’s instructions, it is like looking up as water is poured from one intact vessel into another, without a single drop spilling into a different jar.

To hear what has not been heard by means of this retention (*dhāraṇī*) is the joy of the noble ones dwelling on the stages of training who have attained emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, such that the six sense faculties do not leak;
this retention is for hearing what has not been heard. Ānanda, the Keeper of the Treasury, you have received and retained much, like a cloud holding rain;
this retention is for hearing what has not been heard. Ānanda, you are an ocean of those learned in the scriptures, naturally so.
To be able to discern the permanent and the impermanent, etc., and to know that the Tathāgata never speaks of the Dharma—this is called "much hearing.
The great waters of the Buddha-Dharma ocean flow into Ānanda’s mind; this refers to upholding that which is not heard and not hearing the Dharma.
This sutra contains the three teachings, such that Ānanda alone transmits and maintains them through these three virtues (and so forth).
The three types of supernormal knowledge (*vidyā*), hearing and retention, and the convergence of resonance and response intersected at one time.
"One time" means, as Sengzhao stated, the day the Dharma King inaugurated his mandate and the moment of the auspicious assembly of the great multitude; this was in this world.
Regarding the explanation of *dhātu* (the element/time), the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Kāla" refers to actual time;

when it is shown to internal disciples as "time for eating," "time for putting on robes," and so forth, it is for the sake of explaining [the practice] to people. "Samaya" is a provisional designation used to counteract the false views of non-Buddhists;
this is the explanation regarding time. In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), there is neither time nor no-time. This is explained in detail.

The meaning is fully explained in the first fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (and so forth). In terms of the classification of teachings (*yàojiào*), those from the stage of having seen the truths (*dṛṣṭasatya*) up to, but not including, the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) are called the "lower simultaneous" (*xià yīshí*).
If three people enter the primary truth (*paramārtha*) together, it is called the "middle simultaneous" (*zhōng yīshí*).

Those from the stage of entering the grounds (*bhūmi*) upward are called the "upper simultaneous" (*shàng yīshí*). Those from the first dwelling (*prathamavihāra*) upward are called the "uppermost simultaneous" (*shàngshàng yīshí*). Now, at the beginning of this sutra...

It is said that while the teaching as a whole pertains to a single period, when distinguished according to the specific capacities of those entering the Path—whether via the Separate (Bian) or Perfect (Yuan) Teachings—it comprises three periods (and so forth).
Fourth, regarding the Master who expounds the Teaching:
it is the Buddha.

The Teacher is the Buddha; "Buddha" means "Awakened. He awakens from the two ailments of body and mind—afflictions—and because his cause and effect are perfected, he is able to break the bonds of existence.

At the beginning of the kalpa there was no illness, but as the kalpa drew to a close, illnesses became many. During times of long life there is happiness, while during times of short life there is suffering.

In the eastern continent (Pūrvavideha), people are wealthy and long-lived; in the western continent (Aparagoyānī), there are many cattle and sheep; and in the northern continent (Uttarakuru), there are none.

There is no place where I am not able to move people as I do here; when the Buddha lived for eighty thousand years, the southern continent had not yet seen the fruit while they were still practicing the cause, and this remained the case even until his lifespan was one hundred years. Therefore, the Buddha appeared in this land.
This is the explanation of the Śākyas. Just as when the sun does not rise, the various lotuses in the pond—those not yet born and those already born—do not manifest at all.
When the Buddha appears, all beings are born; if he does not appear, devas and humans diminish while the evil realms increase.

When a Buddha appears in the world, there are Kṣatriyas, Brāhmaṇas, householders, the Four Heavenly Kings, and so on up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*); this is the explanation regarding human beings.

As for the three vehicles, those with the capacity of the spiritual faculties can evoke the appearance of a Buddha, whereas others cannot; even if one were to sever [the bonds of] the Peak of Existence, [only those with such faculties could do so].
"To plant [roots] so as to forever cross the stream of birth and death" is the explanation by way of remedy.

The Buddha is neither moved nor emerges from the *dharmatā*, yet he enables sentient beings to perceive movement and emergence; in the Tathāgata, however, there is truly no movement or emergence—this is the teaching of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

The Buddha is called the Awakened One (*buddha*) because he awakens to the suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya*) of the world, and awakens to the path and cessation (*mārga-nirodha*) that transcend the world. His body is one *zhang* in height.
At eighty years of age, appearing in the form of a bhikṣu, he attained Buddhahood beneath a tree through thirty-four moments of mind.
As for the "Threefold Treasury of the Fully Honored One who Awakens Himself and Awakens Others": manifesting a sixteen-foot image, he displays the exalted body (vairocana-kāya);

beneath the tree, through a single moment of corresponding realization, he severs all remaining residual habits, thereby attaining the universal Buddha-nature that awakens himself and awakens others, manifesting the exalted body.

Regarding the Buddha’s prediction received while seated upon a lotus pedestal, this distinguishes the Buddha’s self-awakening and awakening of others from the previous three phases, which were concealed;
it reveals only the inconceivable aspect like empty space, which is precisely the self-awakening and awakening of others of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).
As the *Xiangfa jueyi jing* states: "One may see a body sixteen feet tall, or see small bodies and large bodies, or see..."
Sitting upon a lotus pedestal, he expounds the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground for hundreds of thousands of Śākyamunis;

or, seeing his body as identical to empty space, leaving no trace within the Dharma-realm and free from all discrimination—this is the meaning of the Four Buddhas. Regarding the interpretation of the Fundamental and the Traces (*honjaku*):

the three Buddhas are the traces, and the one Buddha is the fundamental. (As stated above. Regarding the interpretation through the contemplation of the mind: it is the contemplation of phenomena produced through causes and conditions.

If one analyzes [phenomena] until they reach non-existence, such that these three baskets (Tripitaka) are understood through the causes and conditions of clumsy awakening and contemplation as being empty—this is the skillful awakening of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*), wherein all is awakened as empty.
If one first contemplates emptiness, then the provisional (*prajñapti*), and finally the Middle Way—this is the provisional awakening of the Distinct Teaching (*pratyeka-bhūmi-yāna*).
If one contemplates that all phenomena are simultaneously empty, provisional, and middle—this is the perfect awakening (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*) of the Perfect Teaching (*ekayāna*).
Regarding the place where the teachings of the five sciences were expounded:
[the Buddha] resided on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha.
First, the residence is explained; next, the royal city; and finally, the mountain. The Buddha, who possesses the three bodies (trikāya), has eight abodes.

The four abodes of the body are: first, the abode of life-span, which refers to the fivefold Dharma-body and so forth; second, the abode of reliance, which refers to royal cities, Mount Grdhrakūṭa, and so forth;

third, the abode of objective spheres, which refers to the realm of the three-thousandfold world system; and fourth, the abode of the four modes of conduct, which refers to walking, standing, sitting, and reclining.
Regarding the three abodes of the *saṃbhogakāya*: first is the celestial abode, which dwells among the six heavens of the desire realm; second is the Brahma abode.
Regarding those who dwell in the three types of noble abodes within the fourth dhyāna heaven: one dwells in the Dharma-body of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;

another dwells in the ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*). (And so forth. In terms of the teachings: the Buddha of the *Āgama* (Tripitaka) school attains true knowledge through the analytical gate (*vikalpa-mukha*) and dwells in the two nirvāṇas with and without remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa* and *nirupadhiśeṣa*).
The Buddha of the Shared (Shared Mahāyāna) school attains true knowledge through the essential gate (*dharmatā-mukha*) and dwells in these two nirvāṇas.
The distinct Buddha abides in the secret treasury by way of the sequential gate, while the Perfect Buddha abides in the secret treasury by way of the non-sequential gate.
Regarding the two explanations of the city, the Sanskrit original should be rendered as Rājagṛha-mahā-gara.
*Rājagṛha* means "King’s Abode" (*rāja* = king; *gṛha* = house); *mahā* means "great"; and *gara* means "city. Thus, it is the name of a kingdom.
*Gāthā* is translated here as "one who does not harm others" or "the law of non-violent killing. It is also called *Magadha*, which is translated as "Heavenly Net.
This Heavenly Net was the father of Pañcāśikha. Long ago, when this king ruled over a thousand small kingdoms, he encountered a female lion while out hunting;
she had intercourse with the king, and later, when her months were full, she came to the king's palace.
When King Shengzi (King Shen-zhi) learned that this was his son, he issued a proclamation saying, "I had no son; Heaven has granted me a son.

He raised him until he grew up. When his feet became mottled with spots, the people of the time called him Banzu (Spotted-foot). Later, when he succeeded to the throne, he took great pleasure in eating meat.
On one occasion, when his supply suddenly ran short, he took a small child who had recently died to the west of the city to provide for the royal meal.

The King greatly admired this and issued an edict that the kitchen should always follow this practice; from then on, one person was killed daily, and poison spread throughout the world until the entire nation was filled with resentment.
A thousand minor kings raised armies to attack him, but he was exiled to the Five Mountains where he was protected by rākṣasas who served as his ghost-kings.
He then made a vow with the mountain deities that he would kill the thousand kings before his wish could be fulfilled.
Using his supernatural powers, he captured all the kings; it was only King Samantaprabha who was seized last.
He intended to slaughter him as an offering to the mountain deity, but at that moment, King Samantaprabha wept with grief and lamentation, saying:

"Since birth, I have spoken only the truth, yet now my word has failed its promise. Pan-zu asked: "What proof do you seek? Samantaprabha replied: "Grant me the opportunity to go [and fulfill my vow]."
The Great Giver, Paṇḍuka, said: "I release you; go and complete your act of giving. Once it is finished, return to me.

You shall go joyfully to your own country, where you will hold a great assembly of giving. Entrust the administration to your crown prince, set your mind at ease, and with a joyful body, crawl back to your end.
Paṇḍuka asked: "The gateway of death is difficult to approach; since you have already escaped it, why do you come back again? At that time, Pabhāsa—
King Guang spoke extensively to Banzu regarding the mind of compassion and the condemnation of killing and harming, further demonstrating that all things are entirely impermanent.
Having heard and believed this, Banzu attained the realization of emptiness and equality and dwelt in the first bhūmi.

He then gathered a thousand kings, each of whom took a drop of blood and three strands of hair to offer as a sacrifice to the mountain deity; they subsequently went together with the thousand kings to Mount Wudu.

Walls were built and houses established until it became a flourishing great kingdom; as successive rulers took charge of the administration and a thousand kings resided there, it was called Rājagṛha (The Royal Residence).
Furthermore, while the commoners of the city had seven times rebuilt their houses only to have them burned down seven times, the royal residence alone was spared.
The Crown Prince declared: "From this day forward, although these may be the homes of commoners, they shall all be called Rājagṛha and must be exempt from fire."
Because the entire realm was difficult to govern, the King issued a decree that [the city] would be spared from burning; thus, the households of the common people all call it Rājagṛha (King’s House).
Furthermore, it is also said to be called Rājaśā (King’s Pardon) because King Viśvabhū released a thousand kings.
Moreover, because the four heavenly kings (Cāturmahārājika) jointly constructed this city, it is called Rājagṛha. Also, because the King of Magadha fathered a son with one head...
Because he had two faces and four hands, which were considered inauspicious, his body and head were torn apart and he was about to be abandoned in the wilderness.
A rākṣasī named Līlā rejoined his body and nourished him with her milk. When he grew up and became an adult, his strength surpassed that of all nations;
he took eighty-four thousand kings and placed them within the Five Mountains, where he established a city to rule and transform the realm with great power.
Because the King resided there, it is called Rājagṛha (the Abode of the King), and so forth. Furthermore, Magadha is named the Place Holding Ambrosia (Amṛtadhara).
It contains twelve great cities: first, the great city of Gṛjanī; second, the great city of Pūrṇabhadra; third, the great city of Ākaravatī;
fourth, the great city of Vārāṇasī; fifth, the great city of Rājagṛha; sixth, the city of Śrāvastī... [and so on].
1. The great city of Bhadrapura; 2. The great city of Vārāṇasī; 3. The great city of Kapilavastu;
4. The city of Campā; 5. The city of Vatsa; 6. The city of Kauśāmbī; 7. The city of Kuru; 8. The city of Kollagiri.

Among these twelve cities, the latter six were inhabited for short periods while the former six were inhabited for long periods. Furthermore, among the first six cities, kings resided for the most part.
He dwells for a short time in the city of Śrāvastī to repay the debt of gratitude to his *dharmakāya*, whereas he dwells in the city of Rājagṛha to repay the debt of gratitude to his *janmakāya*.
Regarding "Rāja" (the King): within the city of Rājagṛha there are six monasteries (*vihāra*):

first, the Bamboo Grove Monastery (*Veṇuvana-vihāra*), situated on level ground and built by the elder Kalandaka, located thirty *li* to the northwest of the city; second, the Gṛdhrakūṭa Hill (*Vulture Peak*).
1. The Vihāra of the Thirty-seven Leaf Cave Mountain; 2. The Vihāra of the Four Heavenly Kings Cave Mountain;
3. The Vihāra of the Nāga Deity Cave Mountain; 4. The Vihāra of Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain. Gṛdhrakūṭa is translated as "Spiritual Vulture Peak.
In the past, Śākyamuni Bodhisattva was a vulture on this mountain where he nurtured his parents; for this reason, it received its name.
It is called Gṛdhrakūṭa (Vulture Peak) because of its name; furthermore, to the south of Rājagṛha there is a Śītavana (Cemetery) forest where many vultures dwell and consume the dead.
When people are about to die, vultures soar over their homes and emit mournful cries. Because people can thus foreknow that a person is dying, it is called Gṛdhrakūṭa.
Moreover, the mountain has five peaks: the eastern one is shaped like an elephant’s head, and the southern one is like a horse’s [head].
The head facing west is that of a sheep, the north is that of a lion, and the center is that of a vulture; thus it is also named Vulture Peak (*Gṛdhrakūṭa*). Question:
For what reason does the Buddha specifically teach the Dharma at Vulture Peak within the city of Rājagṛha? Answer:
According to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-śāstra*, it is said: "Just as the city of Rājagṛha is superior to other cities, so too is Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain superior to other mountains."
Because the Buddha was at a preeminent location, this dharma-gate is revealed as preeminent;
since this Prajñā is the most supreme dharma, it is specifically taught at the royal city and Vulture Peak Mountain. "Middle" signifies that the Middle Way Prajñā is being taught.
Sixth, the explanation of the assembly of listeners. In various sūtras, the listing of the assembly does not exceed four types:

first, the "echoes and reflections," referring to Buddhas and Bodhisattvas whose great fruits are already perfected; they come as echoes and reflections so that the True Dharma may long abide in the world.
Second, the "assembly for establishing karmic connections," who, though present and hearing [the teaching], do not yet obtain benefit; however...

1. To create the causes and conditions for attaining the Way in the future; 2. To inspire the assembly of Dharma-body Bodhisattvas to mutually exhort one another to request the Tathāgata to speak, so as to benefit all sentient beings together; 3.

For the assembly of those with the capacity to receive the teaching, who have planted seeds in the distant past and whose fruit is realized in this present life, enabling them to awaken and enter [the truth] at the very moment they hear the Dharma; 4. The bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs.
The nuns, upāsakas, and upāsikās each have four meanings by which they may be understood through inference. The text is divided into two parts: first, the listing of the assembly;
second, the general summary. The first part has three sections: first, the assembly of this land; second, the assembly from other directions; third, the transformed assembly.
The first of these [the assembly of this land] has three subsections: first, the assembly of śrāvakas; second, the assembly of bodhisattvas; third, the assembly of miscellaneous classes.

The two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas) are attached to emptiness, so they are listed first; ordinary beings are attached to existence, so they are listed last; and bodhisattvas constantly practice the Middle Way, so they are listed in the middle.
Furthermore, because śrāvakas excel both in mind and form, they are listed first; because bodhisattvas excel in mind but are inferior in form, they are listed in the middle;
and because ordinary beings are inferior in both mind and form, they are listed last. Regarding the first section, there are two parts, the first of which concerns the śrāvakas.

Next, regarding the first section on the Pratyekabuddhas, there are five parts: (1) the general title, (2) the enumeration, (3) their rank and position, (4) the praise of their virtues, and (5) the summary conclusion. Now, for the first:
"Together with a great assembly of bhikṣus."

The commentator states that "together" means they shared the same treatise (*śāstra*), the same time, the same place, the same precepts, the same mind, the same views, the same path, and the same liberation.
Regarding "great" (*mahat*): it may mean "many" or "superior," as they were all *arhats*.

It is called "great" because their number reached eight hundred million; it is called "many"; and it is called "superior" because they surpassed all other heterodox paths. [This refers to] the five types of *bhikṣus*.
1. Regarding the meaning of the name: he is called a "beggar" (*bhikṣu*) because he maintains himself with purity, remaining free from the four types of wrong livelihood. 2.

He is so named because he has destroyed afflictions and views, and because he has brought about cessation through the elimination of craving (*tṛṣṇā*). 3. Regarding his title: just as the Sanskrit and Chinese names differ in their characteristics, each possesses its own specific designation.

4. He is called a *bhikṣu* because he has received the full ordination (*upasampadā*). 5. Regarding the etymology: the term *bhi* signifies "fear," and the term *kṣu* signifies "one who can terrify"; thus, he is one who can terrify the afflictions.
One who subdues the thieves of affliction is called a bhikṣu; four or more such individuals are termed a saṃgha (and so forth).
Second, the enumeration:
eight hundred million billion.
The stage of the three practices consists of both those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), all of whom are *arhats*.
Since it is said that there are both those in training and those beyond training, how can they all be called *arhats*? According to the *Abhidharmasaṃyuktavibhāṣā-śāstra*, an *arhat*...
There are two kinds: first, abiding; second, practicing. One should know that the practitioner is a person in training (*śaikṣa*), while the one who abides is a person beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "The five precepts, O worthy one, are all practiced by Arhats.

Furthermore, within this context, a single passage first clarifies virtuous conduct, namely the states of being in training and beyond training, because such a person trains toward the state of being beyond training.

Practice (*caryā*) does not carry the meaning of "heading toward" (*pratipannaka*). Among the eight types of persons, four are "heading toward" and three are "fruits"; these are called *śaikṣa* (those in training) and *aśaikṣa* (those beyond training).

The eighth, the Arhat, is called only *aśaikṣa*. The term "Arhat" translates three meanings: first, "non-arising," because the husks of ignorance have been shed and one will no longer undergo birth in the field of future existences;
thus it is said to be "non-arising. Second, "slayer of thieves," because [the nine...]* *(Note: The source text appears to be truncated at the end of the second meaning.)*

Third, because the eighteen *anusaya* (latent afflictions) are exhausted, he is called "Slayer of Thieves. Third, as one who is worthy of offerings (*arhat*), his wisdom and vows are fully perfected such that he is capable of digesting material offerings;

this is the meaning according to the *Zang* (Tripitaka) and *Tong* (Shared) teachings. If explained according to the *Yuan* (Perfect) teaching, it is not only that [the afflictions] do not arise, but even "non-arising" does not arise—this is non-arising.
Not only is he a slayer of thieves, but he also slays those who are not thieves; these are the non-thieves.

This refers to nirvāṇa; it is not only that which should be provided for the Arhats, but also that which should be provided for all sentient beings—this is "that which should be provided" (and so forth).
Fourth, the praise of virtues.
Conditioned merits, unconditioned merits, the ten knowledges of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), the eight knowledges of those in training (*śaikṣa*),

the six knowledges of those in training, the three faculties (*indriya*), the sixteen mental applications (*citta-kṣaṇa*), the contemplation of the conventional nature of phenomena as empty and unreal, the contemplation of the conventional nature of sensation as empty and unreal, the contemplation of the conventional nature of names as empty and unreal,
the three gates of emptiness, and the four truths and twelve links of dependent origination.
The text contains eight sections; the Dharma-gates therein may also be praised as being for three types of persons. First, the initial four sections praise those of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao).
Next, the three [sections on] the provisional (jia) praise those of the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao). Finally, the three [sections on] emptiness (kong) praise those of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).

Furthermore, the initial four sections praise the Dharma of the Shared Teaching, while the subsequent sections collectively praise both the Distinct and Perfect Teachings. The first [section] is divided into four parts; now, the first praises the conditioned (youwei).
Regarding "merit" (*guṇa*), it refers to conditioned qualities; regarding "virtue" (*guṇa*), it refers to unconditioned qualities in terms of the perfection of abandonment.

If one discusses them in terms of their objects, the Truth of the Path is conditioned and the Truth of Cessation is unconditioned. Because the substance given is called "merit" and its return to oneself is called "virtue," they are termed "meritorious virtues.

Following the ten knowledges of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), the text next praises the distinctions of wisdom, stating: "As for the ten knowledges: first, the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*)."
The untainted knowledge regarding phenomena bound to the desire realm; the untainted knowledge regarding causes bound to the desire realm;
the untainted knowledge regarding the cessation of phenomena bound to the desire realm; the untainted knowledge regarding the path for abandoning phenomena bound to the desire realm;

and the untainted knowledge within the category of dharma-knowledge—these are [the types of knowledge]. The two subsequent knowledges (anvaya-jñāna) pertain to the untainted [knowledge] regarding the paths of the two higher realms.

Regarding the classification of the four types of untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) within the context of wisdom according to the Four Noble Truths, as clarified above in the section on Dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*), there is only the distinction between the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).

Third is the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*): it is called the knowledge of others' minds because it knows the present mental states and mental concomitants (*citta-caitta*) bound to the realms of desire and form, as well as a small portion of the untainted mental states and mental concomitants. Fourth is conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
The knowledge of the outflows (*āsrava*) within all worlds is also called conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), as it is possessed equally by both ordinary persons and noble ones (*ārya*).

1. The knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) consists of contemplating the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self. 2. The knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*) consists of contemplating the causes of tainted phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) as cause, origin, production, and condition;

at the time of such contemplation, it is untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*). 3. The knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) consists of contemplating exhaustion, cessation, excellence, and renunciation; at the time of such contemplation, it is untainted knowledge.
1. Knowledge of the outflows (*āsrava-jñāna*); 2. Knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*); 3. Knowledge of the right track (*pratipad-jñāna*); 4. Knowledge of the vehicle (*yāna-jñāna*); 5.

Knowledge of the time for cultivation (*kāla-jñāna*); 6. Untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*); 7. Knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*)—having seen suffering, having abandoned its origin, having realized cessation, and having cultivated the path;

8. Conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*)—as stated in the *Abhidharma-śāstra*: "I have seen suffering, abandoned its origin, exhausted it, realized it, and cultivated the path"; 9. Knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*)—having seen suffering, there is no further [arising].
This refers to the "equality of vision" (*darśana-samatā*). In various sūtras, it is sometimes called the "eleventh wisdom.

The *Prajñāpāramitā* is the wisdom of suchness (*yathābhūta-jñāna*), which knows the general and specific characteristics of all phenomena as they truly are; knowing them with correct and unimpeded realization is what constitutes suchness.

This wisdom exists solely within the mind of a Buddha, as the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) have no share in it; therefore, they are said to possess only ten types of wisdom. Those in training (*śaikṣa*) possess eight types of wisdom.

This refers to the Anāgāmin who, while in the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), possesses only eight [knowledges] because they lack the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).

Regarding the six knowledges of those still in training (*śaikṣa*): this means that within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), there are only the four truths along with the six knowledges of dharma (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent inference (*anvayajñāna*), and so forth.
As for the "three faculties" (*trīṇi indriyāṇi*): next, one praises the virtues of the three faculties; according to the sequence of cultivation, one should first distinguish these three.

Following the discussion of the faculties (*indriya*), the ten knowledges (*jñāna*) are now distinguished; here, first the fruits are explained, followed by the causes. First, regarding the faculty of "desiring to know what is not yet known" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*):
it is the combination of the nine untainted (*anāsrava*) faculties. For a practitioner on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), this is termed the faculty of "desiring to know what is not yet known.

The nine faculties refer to the five beginning with faith (*śraddhā*) and the four beginning with joy (*prīti*), pleasure (*sukha*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), and the mental faculty (*manas*). Second, regarding the faculty of "knowing" (*ājñendriya*).

Within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) for those who have attained the stage of faith-understanding through vision (*śraddhādhimuktidṛṣṭiprāpta*), these nine faculties (*indriya*) are designated as the faculty of knowing (*ājñendriya*), as previously explained.

Once the three types of knowledge (*trividhajñāna*) have been realized, if one reaches the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*), these nine faculties are designated as the faculty of having known (*ājñātāvīndriya*), and so forth.

Regarding the practitioner of the sixteen moments of mind (*ṣoḍaśacittakṣaṇa*), next comes the praise of the sixteen gates of contemplation (*ṣoḍaśākāra-vipaśyanā-mukha*), because they proceed from the movements of the mind.

The term "mental formations" (*citta-saṃskāra*) does not mean that the mind itself is the formation; rather, it refers to what follows the sequence of cultivation and should logically precede the ten knowledges (*daśajñāna*).

Furthermore, it is explained first because it represents the fruit. Moreover, the sixteen aspects (*ṣoḍaśākāra*) are established by departing from the four truths; "formation" (*saṃskāra*) takes the sense of proceeding toward [the goal].

Because practicing these sixteen contemplations enables one to proceed toward the principle of the four realities, they are called "formations. [This applies to] the four [aspects] following "suffering."
The first four aspects of the [Truth of] Suffering are: 1) impermanence, 2) suffering, 3) emptiness, and 4) non-self. The next four aspects of the [Truth of] Origin are:
1) origin, 2) cause, 3) condition, and 4) arising-and-ceasing. The next four aspects of the [Truth of] Cessation are: 1) exhaustion, 2) cessation, 3) wondrousness, and 4) the path.

The final four aspects of the [Truth of] the Path are: 1) path, 2) rightness, 3) track, and 4) vehicle. Furthermore, there are the sixteen aspects such as the patience regarding phenomena (*dharmakṣānti*). This is based on...

Generally speaking, if the forty stages prior to the [Buddha] ground are taken as forty grounds, and the ten levels of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) and Sublime Enlightenment (*pratyak-saṃbodhi*) are taken as sixteen,
this is according to the specific explanation (and so forth).

Next, regarding the contemplation of the provisional nature of dharmas (*dharmaprajñapti*) and the next [contemplation] of the three types of provisional designations (*trividha-prajñapti*): The "provisionality of dharmas" refers to the dharma of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
The "provisionality of sensation" (*vedanā-prajñapti*) refers to the four [remaining] aggregates. Taking these two names is called the "provisionality of names" (*nāma-prajñapti*).

They are real in their own right yet lack intrinsic substance; they exist only by depending on others, and thus are termed "provisional. Furthermore, the aggregate of form is the "dharma," while sensation and the others are the "names"—this constitutes the first [point].
Within all the world, there are only name (*nāma*) and form (*rūpa*); yet here, three distinctions are specifically mentioned (and so forth).

Regarding "the empty and the real": first is the empty, second is the real. They receive their designations by way of mutual contrast. The factors of the aggregates (*skandha-dharma*) are empty, yet ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) call them real.
When wisdom seeks to understand them, they cannot be found; being only real [in appearance] yet empty [in substance], they are called "empty and real. This is the general meaning.
Furthermore, if one explains the distinct meanings, within each of the three provisionalities (*prajñapti*) there are three contemplations (*vipaśyanā*).

Provisionality itself is emptiness, which is the contemplation of emptiness; emptiness itself is provisionality, which is the contemplation of reality. A single form or a single fragrance is none other than *prajñā*, which is the contemplation of provisionality. The single character "contemplation" (*guan*) is the contemplation of the Middle Way.

Because emptiness and provisionality constitute the path of skillful means (*upāya-mārga*), they do not establish specific names for their contemplations; rather, by entering through them, one attains [the Middle Way].
The Middle Way alone is rightly called the contemplation of sensation (*vedanā*) and the categories of names (*nāman*) and so forth; this can be understood thus.

To speak in its perfect sense, the three dharmas are emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the provisional (*prajñapti*), and the middle (*madhyama*); they are both simultaneously illuminated and simultaneously extinguished.

(And so forth. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "All dharmas are not real; ordinary beings, through false recollections, conceptualizations, and discriminations, falsely claim there is a person, like a dog [approaching...]"
A man once scolded his own reflection in a well; seeing no dog there but only its reflected image, he conceived a malicious intent and threw himself into the well and died.
Sentient beings are just like this: the harmony of the four great elements is designated as a "body. Arising from causes and conditions, it performs actions, speaks words, and so forth.
Within this, ordinary people falsely give rise to the notion of a "person"; these phenomena are merely provisional, yet they give rise to attachment and aversion.

The fool delights in falling into the three evil realms; this is the conventional designation of "reception. Furthermore, all phenomena arise solely from the combination of names and have no further name beyond them.
For example, because the head, feet, belly, and spine combine, they are conventionally designated as a "body.
Because hair, eyes, ears, nose, mouth, skin, and bones combine, they are conventionally designated as a "head. Because the various hairs combine, they are conventionally designated [as such].
Because hair is a composite of parts, it is conventionally designated as "hair"; because various particles of mud and dust are combined, they are conventionally designated as "parts";

and because those parts are further combined, they are called "particles. This is what is meant by "conventional designation" (*prajñapti*). Because of these conventional designations, all phenomena are empty.

Regarding the "three emptinesses" and so forth, this next section praises the virtues of samādhi; it is because of the causal conditions of the three types of conventional designations [that all things are empty].

Obtaining the three gates of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is called the sequential explanation of cause and effect. Because phenomena (*dharma*) are provisional, they are empty; because sensation (*vedanā*) is provisional, it is signless (*animitta*);

because names (*nāman*) are provisional, they are wishless (*apraṇihita*). Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "By means of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, one enters the gate to *nirvāṇa*.
There are three such gates, namely: emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. Regarding the gate of emptiness, one contemplates all...

In phenomena there is neither self nor what belongs to a self; all dharmas exist through the combination of causes and conditions, and therein is no agent and no experiencer—this is called the Gate of Emptiness.
As for the Gate of Signlessness: although the body is empty, it possesses signs; because people are attached to these signs, they cultivate signlessness.
As it is said: one contemplates the bowing and rising, the bending and stretching, the standing, staying, going, and coming.
When observing speech, one finds no reality within it; because the wind depends upon consciousness, there is that which acts, yet this is the mark of the cessation of consciousness.
Since there is nothing here from moment to moment, these men and women have the notion of a self.

Because they lack wisdom, they falsely perceive a chain of bones connected together, covered by skin and flesh, with mechanisms moving like a wooden man. This is the gate of signlessness (*animitta-mukha*); it is non-existent.
That which creates the gate has no marks, nor does it have this name; thus it is "unconditioned" (*anabhisaṃskāra*).

Among all these meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), if these three concentrations are absent, they are not called *samādhi*, because through such regression one falls back into the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). As it is said: "One who can maintain pure precepts is called a bhikṣu;
one who can contemplate emptiness is called a practitioner of emptiness; and one whose single mind is always diligent and energetic is called a true [monk]."

When a practitioner of the Way practices these three, they can reach Nirvana and attain the three gates of liberation (etc.). Regarding the Four Noble Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination:
next, one praises these two truths and conditions. They are similar in that both are for Śrāvakas to sever the afflictions of views and thought; thus, they are called "similar.
They are distinct because their capacities—sharp or dull—differ, and because their breadth, brevity, and numerical counts differ; thus, they are called "distinct. First, the Four Noble Truths:

For those of dull faculties who contemplate the Great Sūtras, there are four types of Four Noble Truths—those of arising and ceasing according to the *Sūtra* and *Vinaya* teachings—which are not discussed here.

This present sūtra possesses the three teachings and thus contains three types of Four Noble Truths, namely: the unarisen (*anutpāda*), the immeasurable (*apramāṇa*), and the effortless (*anabhisaṃskāra*).

The four dharmas beginning with suffering are called "truths" (*satya*) because they are examined as real and not false. If suffering and its origin (*samudaya*) are outflows (*āsrava*), [they are the truths of the *Sūtra* teaching].
The cessation and the path are untainted (*anāsrava*); this is the Tripitaka [teaching]. If all four truths are untainted, this is the Shared [teaching].
If all four are both tainted and untainted, this is the Distinct [teaching]. If all four are neither tainted nor untainted, this is the Perfect [teaching].
Regarding the sharpness or dullness of the twelve links of dependent origination, there are also four types as observed in the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra.
Within each of these four types, there are three further distinctions: first, the twelve links of dependent origination across three lifetimes; second, those across two lifetimes;
and third, those within a single lifetime. These are explained in detail elsewhere (and so forth).
Fifth, the summary:
it can be known that all immeasurable merits are fully accomplished.
Second, the assembly of pratyekabuddhas is listed.

Furthermore, there were eight hundred million billion great seers, pratyekabuddhas who had fully accomplished the Four Noble Truths and the twelve links of dependent origination, which are neither annihilated nor eternal.
The text has four parts: first, the introduction; second, the enumeration; third, the designation of the stage; fourth, the praise of virtues; and fifth, the conclusion. The first part is clear.
Regarding "the Great Sage Pratyekabuddhas" (the second part), there are three distinctions: first, the Solitary Realizers (*pratyekabuddha*).

For example, in the past, there was a king who entered a garden for recreation. At dawn, he saw that the flowers, fruits, and groves were exceedingly delightful. At that time, the king... [text continues].

Having finished eating, he immediately lay down to rest. While the king’s court ladies were all vying with one another to pluck and destroy the trees of the grove, the king awoke and realized that all phenomena are impermanent.
Using this external event as an analogy for the internal truth, he became a Great Seer (Maharṣi) Pratyekabuddha. There are two types of Pratyekabuddhas:

those who appear in the world during the time of a Buddha and hear the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination to sever [wrong] views; and those who appear when no Buddha is in the world and awaken through the conditions of the twelve links of dependent origination.

Regarding the three types of afflictions of thought (*kleśa*), the "lesser *pratyekabuddha*" refers to a person who has attained the stage of *srotāpanna* and is born among humans at a time when no Buddha exists and the Buddha-dharma has already ceased.
Having undergone seven births among humans and likewise seven births in the heavens, they do not undergo an eighth birth;
through self-awakening, they achieve the Way and thus become a lesser *pratyekabuddha*. The phrase "neither annihilated nor eternal" is a triple praise of their virtues.

Because the two past causes draw forth consciousness and the other factors, it is not annihilation; because consciousness and the others cease, and because the two causes do not arise again, it is not permanence.
Furthermore, because there is continuity across the three periods of time, it is not annihilation; because they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it is not permanence.

Moreover, in the forward order (*anuloma*), birth and death are without limit, thus it is not annihilation; in the reverse order (*pratiloma*), ignorance is consumed and exhausted, thus it is not permanence. [The four truths and the ten...]

The second [section] establishes the four conditions (*pratyaya*) based on the lower [level]. Question: Previously, when listing the *śrāvakas*, they were also said to take the Truths as conditions (*satya-pratyaya*);

now, in praising the *pratyekabuddhas*, this is again clarified. Yet, when listing the *bodhisattvas* later, they are still called "arhats. Why is this? Answer: Regarding a single object, the realizations attained differ;
it is like three animals crossing a river or three birds escaping a net—the river is the same, but the animals differ, and the net is the same, yet the birds differ.

Because the birds differ, the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "By observing with inferior wisdom, one attains the enlightenment of the śrāvaka; by observing with middling wisdom, one attains the enlightenment of the pratyekabuddha;
by observing with superior wisdom, one attains the enlightenment of the bodhisattva; and by observing with the most superior wisdom, one attains the enlightenment of the Buddhas.

This is because while the principle is one, the perspectives differ; therefore, the truths (*satya*) and the conditions (*pratyaya*) are explained interchangeably. [As stated]... Question: Regarding the pratyekabuddha—
Question: Since there are no Buddhas in the world [during certain periods], how can they now be listed among the assembly of those who heard the Dharma together? Answer:

Even when Pratyekabuddhas appear while a Buddha is in the world, they are simply subsumed within the category of Śrāvakas.
