As for "being able to sever the bonds of the afflictions of the mind and so forth within the three realms," this clarifies the removal of hindrances; previously, the afflictions of form were severed.

This refers to severing the afflictions of the mind; furthermore, while the former severed the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), this severs the delusions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-kleśa*), which is why it is called "mind.

Thus, the phrase "manifesting one body" below clarifies that the previous stage of "patience through faith" (*śraddhā-kṣānti*) clarified the manifestation of transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*), hence it was said "manifesting a hundred, a thousand, or ten thousand bodies.
Now, at the stage of "patience through conformity" (*anulomikī-kṣānti*), the true body (*dharmakāya*) is clarified, hence it is said "manifesting one body" before the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Regarding the transformation of sentient beings through lands, it is asked: "How does a single body manifest in many lands? The answer is:
"By means of the inconceivable power of supernatural transformations (*ṛddhi-vikurvaṇa*), causing the multitude to see them.
Fourth, the elucidation of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Furthermore, for a Bodhisattva who has attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), there is what is called the distant, immovable contemplative wisdom;

because this also severs the habitual tendencies and afflictions of mind and form within the three realms, it manifests unspeakably, unspeakably many meritorious powers and spiritual transformations (*abhijñā*).

The third section [of the introduction] now begins with the first part: the designation of the name and stage. This means that when one seeks the two dharmas of form and mind through the perspectives of self, other, both, or no cause, they are found to be unobtainable;

the wisdom attained therein is called "patience regarding non-arising" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). What is referred to as "the distant, immovable contemplative wisdom" (*dūra-anācalita-vipaśyanā-prajñā*) is the assignment of this stage.
"Distant" refers to the seventh stage, the Far-Reaching (*dūraṃgamā*), which reaches the ultimate limit of the state of effortful mental application (*sābhoga-manasikāra*).
Therefore, "immovability" refers to the eighth stage, the Immovable (Acalā), because it cannot be moved by the afflictions associated with signs;

"contemplative wisdom" refers to the ninth stage, the Good Wisdom (Sādhumatī), because through the four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid), one transforms sentient beings and is also able to sever the habitual tendencies of the afflictions regarding mind and form within the three realms.
Second, regarding the clarification of the removal of obstacles: previously, two layers were severed at each stage; now, both are severed simultaneously.
This is because it is the correct practice; therefore, the following three sections clarify the scope of the transformation through guidance (saṃgraha-vinaya).

(And so forth. Fifth, the exposition of the patience of quiescent extinction (śānti-kṣānti) consists of four parts: first, the designation of its name and stage; second, the discernment of the removal of hindrances;
third, the differentiation according to the truths (satya); and fourth, the scope of the transformation through guidance. Now, for the first [part]:
Furthermore, regarding the patience of quiescence (*śānti-kṣānti*), both Buddhas and Bodhisattvas employ this patience to enter the Vajra-samādhi.

Practicing within the stage of "lower patience" (*mṛdu-kṣānti*) is termed the Bodhisattva’s practice of "upper patience" (*adhimātra-kṣānti*); practicing within this is termed *sarvajñatā* (omniscience).

Section on the Names (3): First, regarding the designation of the names—while the preceding four patiences have not yet exhausted the source of phenomena, this present patience pacifies all mind and form and extinguishes conceptualization and habitual tendencies;
it is therefore named "Patience of Cessation" (*kṣānti-nirodha*). [As stated in the text... Second, the passage beginning with "The Buddha and the Bodhisattvas" clarifies the function of realization.
"Vajra" is a metaphor, and "samādhi" is meditative concentration. There are those who hold that afflictions are like a vajra, and...

That which is stubborn and rigid cannot be severed immediately; it is not that the power of a Buddha’s wisdom is incapable of severing it, for as stated in the sutras, that which can be broken by a tortoise shell or a ram's horn is precisely this meaning.
There are those who, with wisdom like a vajra, can shatter afflictions without being harmed by them; likewise, a great sutra states that a precious vajra flask cannot be shattered.
"Sound" is its meaning. Now, the Buddha and the Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage (daśabhūmi) equally employ the patience of quiescence (*śānti-kṣānti*) to enter the Vajra-samādhi (and so forth).

Within the practice of the lower patience (*mṛdu-kṣānti*), the three lower [levels] correspond to the stages; the lower patience is the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmamegha*), and the upper patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*) is the Buddha.
*Sarvajñā* is translated here as "all-knowledge" (*sarvajña*). Furthermore, the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*) constitutes the causal stage.
Because it is subsumed [under the stage of patience], it is called "lower patience" (*kṣānti*); because it is subsumed under the fruit of the path of liberation, it is called "upper patience.

Furthermore, when the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmamegha*) and the Buddha both enter the Vajra-samādhi, the preceding mind is called the Bodhisattva and the subsequent mind is called the Buddha; there is no interval between them.

Therefore, there are only the "upper" and "lower," as the former four patiences belong solely to the causal stage (*hetu-bhūmi*) and thus possess three grades. [Question: Regarding the various sūtras...
If there is Equal Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi), why is it not established here? If one relies on other sūtras, there should indeed be three grades:
the inferior grade of the Ten Stages (daśabhūmi), the middling grade of Equal Enlightenment, and the superior grade of Sublime Enlightenment (pravarābhisambodhi).

However, because this *Prajñāpāramitā* follows the general [teaching] and differs from the distinct teaching (viśeṣa-śāsana), it discusses only the Dharma Cloud Stage (dharmameghā-bhūmi) as being equivalent to the Buddha Stage (buddhabhūmi). As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "A Bodhisattva of the tenth stage..."

One should know that the "Suchness" (tathatā) of the Buddha is not yet [fully realized]; the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* also states that Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages have not yet fully understood the nature (dharmatā).
These points all represent the intent of the Shared Teaching (*pāṭha-sādhāraṇa-śāsana*). (And so forth.)
Second, the explanation of the removal of hindrances:

by collectively contemplating the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), one severs the habitual tendencies of the mind within the three realms; the exhaustion of ignorance (*avidyā*) is the mark of the vajra-exhaustion, and its signlessness (*animitta*) is sarvajñā (omniscience).

The text has three parts. First, it clarifies that while the object of contemplation is the same—contemplating the True Truth (*satyadharma*)—there is a difference in clarity and obscurity, as the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage hear and see the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), whereas the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, see the Buddha-nature with their eyes.

Furthermore, Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage are called "Superior Beings" (*uttarapuruṣa*), while Buddhas are called "Unsurpassed Beings" (*anuttarapuruṣa*). Moreover, Bodhisattvas are like those of the tenth stage...

"The Buddha’s moon of the fourth night is equal to the moon of the fifteenth night," and so forth. Regarding the "one who has severed the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the mind within the three realms":

this is the second section, which correctly explains the removal of hindrances. Previously, within the stage of *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena), one simultaneously severed the coarse habitual tendencies of both mind and form;

now, within this present patience, one eternally severs the subtle habitual tendencies of the mental factors (*caitta*). The passage beginning with "the characteristic of the exhaustion of ignorance" clarifies the distinction between the two paths below.
That the characteristic of the exhaustion of ignorance is the diamond-like [samādhi] refers to the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*).
Regarding the term "characteristic of exhaustion," it carries the sense of not yet being exhausted; for example, smoke is the characteristic of fire but is not yet fire.

Likewise, the diamond-like samādhi is the characteristic of the exhaustion of ignorance, yet ignorance is not yet exhausted. Question: If ignorance is not yet exhausted, it should be an affliction (*kleśa*); why is this?
Therefore, the preceding passage states that the Buddha and the Bodhisattva enter this samādhi together, answering that the nature of ignorance is itself clarity (*vidyā*).
Just as a lamp is extinguished at the very moment it is lit, so too does a single thought-moment of ignorance transform into clarity;
this subtle clarity is the great clarity of the Bodhisattva, which is the Buddha. When all characteristics are exhausted and become signless, this is *sarvajñā* (omniscience).
Prior to this path of liberation, during the stage of the diamond-like samādhi, one merely exhausts the coarse and subtle characteristics of form and mind;

thus, it cannot be called "all-knowledge" (*sarvajñatā*). Now, at the stage of Buddhahood, not only are these characteristics exhausted, but even the signless (*animitta*) is exhausted; therefore, it is rightly named all-knowledge.
This may be described as the simultaneous merging of object and contemplation, where both the objective realm and the subjective wisdom are quiescent.
Third, the distinction is clarified by way of the truths (*satya*).
Transcending both the worldly truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), it is the eleventh stage, the awakening of *sarvajñā* (omniscience),

which is neither existent nor non-existent, profoundly serene and pure, eternally abiding and unchanging, identical with the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and equal to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
The three stages of worthiness (*tri-śaikṣa*) mostly abide in conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), while the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) mostly abide in ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

Ultimate truth is non-existence, whereas conventional truth is existence. Because it transcends conventional truth, it is not existence; because it transcends ultimate truth, it is not non-existence. This state of being neither existent nor non-existent is *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).
Question: What is the difference between *sarvajña* (the omniscient one) and *sarvajñā*? Answer: There are two explanations. One says: [text continues].
The same two [texts] state that "identical" means there is no distinction between this and that, while "different" refers to *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge) and *sarvākārajñā* (knowledge of all modes).

Now, regarding the explanation of the five patiences (*kṣānti*), since within the patience of quiescent extinction (*śānta-nirvāṇa-kṣānti*) there are already only two categories, there should not be a further distinction between *sarvajñā* and *sarvākārajñā*. Yet, it is further stated that they do exist.
The meaning of the *Guhyavidyā-saṃbodhi* (Secret Wisdom Enlightenment) exists within the patience of cessation (*nirodha-kṣānti*), which is divided into superior, middling, and inferior levels.
The inferior level corresponds to the "all-knowledge" (*sarvajñatā*) among the ten stages (*bhūmi*). The superior level corresponds to the "knowledge of all modes" (*sarvākārajñatā*).
If one follows the sūtras, it transcends the two truths and constitutes the eleventh stage, *sarvajña*. This is according to the previous explanation, and so forth.
The fourth section clarifies the scope of gathering and transforming sentient beings; it has two parts: first, the brief exposition, and second, the extensive exposition. Now, for the first:

through great compassion that is without objective conditions, one teaches and transforms all sentient beings, riding the vehicle of *sarvajñā* (omniscience) to come and transform those within the three realms.
All sentient beings dwell within the triple world, yet the Buddha rescues and delivers them through great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). As the *Lotus Sūtra* says:
"The children were playing and entered this house," and the prose section states: "The elder was startled and entered the burning house. The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says:
"The illness of a bodhisattva arises from great compassion. All these passages convey this same meaning. Great compassion is that which enables transformation.
The mind and sentient beings are the objects to be transformed; omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) is the essence that performs the transformation. Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) is threefold:

first, compassion directed toward sentient beings (*sattvālambana-karuṇā*), which even non-Buddhists possess; second, compassion directed toward phenomena (*dharmālambana-karuṇā*), which even those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) possess; and third, unconditioned compassion (*anālambana-karuṇā*), which belongs exclusively to the Buddha alone.
The second [section] is the extensive explanation based on the fundamental tenets.
Good son, the afflictions (*kleśa*) of all sentient beings do not transcend the treasury of the triple world (*tridhātu*).

The twenty-two faculties (*indriya*) of the retributive fruits of all sentient beings do not transcend the triple world. Furthermore, the transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) and the dharma body (*dharmakāya*) of all Buddhas likewise do not transcend the triple world.

"If there are no sentient beings outside the triple world, what would the Buddha transform? Therefore, I say that outside the triple world there exists a separate realm of sentient beings, a treasury.
This is taught in the *Mahāvaipulya-mahāsannipāta-sūtra* of the non-Buddhists, not spoken by the seven Buddhas.
Great King, I have always said that all sentient beings who sever the afflictions of the triple world and exhaust its karmic retribution are called the Buddha’s own nature."
Purity is named the nature of *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge).

The text has three parts: first, regarding the correct principle, there are the "three realms," which are the three of desire, form, and formlessness; "treasury" (*garbha*) refers to its capacity to contain the six destinies and four modes of birth;
"fruit" refers to the fruit of retribution consisting of segmented existence; and "retribution" refers to the retributions of suffering, pleasure, and so forth.
Regarding the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*): the six faculties beginning with the eye constitute six; the five faculties of suffering, pleasure, grief, joy, and equanimity constitute eleven;
the three faculties of female, male, and life-continuum constitute eighteen; and the five faculties of faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom constitute twenty-three.

When combined with the faculty of "I-shall-come-to-know-the-unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), the faculty of "knowing" (*ājñendriya*), and the faculty of "having known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*), they form the twenty-two faculties. Of these, twenty-one do not transcend the realm of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).
Having understood that the faculties do not transcend the three realms, one realizes that even the three bodies of the Buddhas of the three realms do not transcend them;
this is because the Dharma-body is itself the response-body and the transformation-body. As the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "This body of mine is now the Dharma-body.
And as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states: "He is always on Vulture Peak and in all other dwelling places. And as the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-dhyāna-sūtra* states: "Śākya..."
The name Kāśyapa-muni is Vairocana, who pervades all places; as the *Avataṃsaka* says, he is also named Śākya and also named Śāna, and so forth.
Since one knows that the three bodies are in fact one body, one must also know that what is outside the triple world is precisely within the triple world.

There are no sentient beings outside the triple world. The following two sections clarify the hearing and preaching of the Dharma. Regarding "preaching," it says: there are sentient beings outside the realm.
Question: Is it the case that those who can be transformed are born outside [this realm], as this non-Buddhist (tīrthika) teaching claims, rather than as the Buddha’s teaching?
Answer: The sacred teachings differ, and there are divergent views regarding existence and non-existence. This sutra states that there are no sentient beings outside the realms;

other sutras, however, maintain that there are. For instance, the *Lotus Sūtra* speaks of manifesting as a Buddha in other lands, establishing a transformation body at a distance of three hundred *yojanas*.
The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* states that in the region above, beyond as many world-systems as there are grains of sand in forty-two Ganges Rivers, there is a Buddha named Gandhottamakūṭa.
If there were no people outside those realms, how could it be possible for there to be so many Buddha-lands further upward within the triple world?
Therefore, we know that there must indeed be [beings there]. As for this sūtra stating they do not exist and other sūtras stating they do, how should these be reconciled?

Answer: This sutra states that there are no sentient beings with segmented existence (*prādeśika-sattva*), whereas other sutras state that there are sentient beings with transformational existence (*pariṇāmi-sattva*).
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says that śrāvakas are born in the Silver World outside this realm and are without afflictions.
This statement of "no afflictions" is simply a way of saying "no sentient beings"; yet, since the ignorance (*avidyā*) of the śrāvaka has not been severed, how could they truly be non-existent?
This text precisely follows the intent of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) in its partial discussion of sentient beings afflicted by defilements within the realms.

The non-Buddhist Vaiśeṣika school asserts six categories (ṣaṭpadārtha), among which "Great Existence" (mahāsattā) is one; that scripture states that beyond these three realms there exist separate worlds.
To claim that there are sentient beings existing separately outside the three realms would be identical to the views of those non-Buddhists.
To speak according to the true principle: if one says that there are sentient beings outside the realms (*dhātu*), it is the same as the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*);
if one says there are none, it is the same as the followers of the Two Vehicles (*dvayāyāna*). Those who see [the truth] as the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do, see neither existence nor non-existence.
Neither existence nor non-existence means neither like nor different. Neither like nor different means not seeing the triple world as the triple world.
Such matters as these are what the Buddha has now clearly and fully explained in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

Great King, I have always said—this is the third citation of the past to prove the present—that one who has completely severed the afflictions of the three realms and exhausted their karmic retribution is called a Buddha.
How could there be sentient beings existing apart from the three realms? That which is intrinsically pure is named *sarvajñā* (omniscience).
Nature is precisely the Buddha-nature as the direct cause; all sentient beings, Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas equally possess this.
How could there be any other sentient beings to be converted apart from the triple world?
Third, the summary:
the fundamental karma of sentient beings is the complete fulfillment of the fourteen patiences within the five patiences that were originally cultivated by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

The second section [of the text] has two parts. First, a general summary: the original karma of sentient beings within the five stages of patience (*pañca-kṣānti*) is precisely their afflictions (*kleśa*).

Even when Buddhas and Bodhisattvas had not yet attained the Way, they likewise possessed afflictions; because of these afflictions, they cultivated various merits and wisdom, and have now attained Buddhahood.
Since the original afflictions of the Buddhas were no different from those of present-day sentient beings, they are called "original" [afflictions] within the context of the five patiences.
Regarding the "perfection of the fourteen patiences": there are two ways of explaining them, the extensive and the concise.

The concise consists of five patiences, while the extensive consists of fourteen—namely, the three stages of the ordinary person (the *śaikṣa*), the ten stages (*bhūmi*), and the stage of Buddhahood, which together constitute the fourteen. Thus concludes the preceding response to the question, which has also fulfilled the benefit of others.
(The *Shenbao ji* states: "The commentary explains the five patiences (*pañca-kṣānti*) by correlating them with the six categories of spiritual nature (*ṣaḍ-gotra*).

Because the text on the afflictions to be severed and their characteristics is so interwoven, it is quite difficult to clarify. One should first set forth the distinct characteristics before one can achieve a synthesis.

As for these distinct characteristics, according to the standard interpretation, the path of realization (*darśana-mārga*) at the first stage (*bhūmi*) of the Separate Teaching (*pratyeka-śāsana*) is identical to that of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), wherein ignorance (*avidyā*) has already been destroyed.")

He is able to manifest as a Buddha throughout a hundred worlds; yet, the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) produced by this sutra are divided into four—namely, the first three and the final one—when contrasted with the standard ten stages.
Thus, the first two [stages] therein still correspond to the two patiences (*kṣānti*) of faith and compliance, while only the latter three begin to shatter ignorance.
If this is so, then his realization of the Way in the first stage and his manifestation of the fruit of perfect division differ in only one respect.

Furthermore, regarding the afflictions to be abandoned, the two types of patience (kṣānti) through which one conforms to the truth bring about the cessation of the coarse heavy burdens (dausthulya) of the form and mind within the three realms;

this differs from the conventional approach—this is the second point of distinction. One must understand that while the path of realization (darśana-mārga) necessarily accords with what was previously explained as being identical and perfected according to both scriptural authority and logical proof, we here adopt the perspective of the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga). Thus, there is no contradiction in the fact that the ten stages (bhūmi) possess distinct grades. Therefore...

Regarding the meaning of destroying delusions, there are those who progress and those who do not; thus, the stage of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) is established with its divisions of superior, middling, and inferior, as in the present text.
Because their faculties are either sharp or dull: for those with sharp faculties, they destroy ignorance at the first three grades;

for the next, middling ones, they begin to destroy it at the middle three grades; and for the next, inferior ones, they destroy it only at the final three grades. Since it is granted that destruction begins at the outset, there is no impediment to realization.

Their stage is the same as that of the *yuan* (those with dull faculties); since they have not yet severed [delusions], they still abide in faith and compliance. This is also a mutual illustration through abbreviation.

As for the latter three stages of severance, it is only then that their position is fixed; this is because those of inferior faculties receive the "reception" (*shoujie*) and their stage is thus determined.

Although the delusions to be destroyed are divided into the distinctions of matter and mind, or coarse and subtle, for those who are sharp, these are simply ignorance (*avidyā*), while for those who are dull, they are view-delusions and thought-delusions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *vitarka-kleśa*).

Furthermore, why be so stubbornly insistent? How much more so regarding *siddhānta* (established tenets) applied to sentient beings, where there is originally no fixed dharma and various paths are taught;
do not allow yourself to be deluded by names and appearances. Those with the resolve to study should apply their minds fully to this; if it were otherwise, one might simply set it aside.
(○ Since this sutra is interpreted through the lens of the comprehensive approach, the Great Master explained the five patiences using the three teachings of the Shared, Distinct, and Complete;
however, regarding points where these differ from the conventional understanding, the Great Master did not provide a comprehensive reconciliation, leaving readers with no small amount of difficulty.
Now, the Record-Master’s reconciliatory commentary is complete in both text and meaning and can be said to be of great benefit to students; therefore, it is recorded here in its entirety).
The second response to the subsequent question, including the section on self-benefit, is in two parts: first the question, then the answer. This is the first [the question].
He addressed the Buddha, saying: "How does a bodhisattva purify their fundamental practice while transforming sentient beings?"
To highlight the preceding question, this section is restated: the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are the fundamental activity (*mūlakarma*) of a bodhisattva.
Because a bodhisattva is unstained by saṃsāra and bodhi, it is called "fundamental activity of purity. By means of pure dharmas, they teach and transform sentient beings;

this differs from ordinary people and those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), who employ dharmas mixed with afflictions (*kleśa*) to transform sentient beings. Question: [How do they] transform sentient beings while being mixed with afflictions?
What fault is there? The answer is: since one is already bound oneself, how can one transform others? If it concerns ordinary persons, then when the teacher falls, the disciple follows in falling;
if it concerns those of the Two Vehicles, they slander the Buddha and ruin the Dharma, giving rise to resentment toward all sentient beings—how could this accomplish any benefit?
Regarding the second part, the text of the answer first provides a brief explanation and then an extensive one;

here is the former. The Buddha said: "Because from the first stage up to the final stage, one knows and sees all that is within one's own sphere of practice as well as the sphere of practice of the Buddhas."
The text has three parts. First, it clarifies the basis for pure karma, which refers to the stages from the Stage of Joy up to the Cloud of Dharma.

Question: Why are only ten stages mentioned? Answer: The stages prior to the ten [bodhisattva] stages are the three levels of the Worthy (Śaikṣa); they are "worthy" but not yet "sages," and thus are not called the fundamental purity of karma.

The Single Stage of Sublime Awakening (*ekakṣaṇa-abhisambodhi*) already possesses the perfected fruit. Therefore, among the causes, the ten stages are cited as the answer, representing the sphere of one's own practice.
The lower section briefly distinguishes two types of spheres of activity: first, the sphere of one's own practice, which is the realm of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*);

second, the sphere of the Buddha’s practice, which is the realm of the stage of wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). This is because prior to the ten stages, one practices only within the sphere of one's own conduct; thereafter, at the diamond-like mind (*vajracitta*), one traverses both spheres. As the text below states:
"Attaining the samādhi of the exhaustion of principle, one shares the same sphere of practice as the Buddha. Furthermore, the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* says: "O Son of the Buddha..."
At that time, the Bodhisattva dwells in the gate of great tranquility, even transcending the ten stages to sit together with the Buddha.

Regarding the phrase "because of all-knowing vision," there are three explanations for establishing purity: it is only through the five eyes of the Buddha that one can see all phenomena, and it is only through the three wisdoms of the Buddha that one can know all phenomena.
The second part, the extensive response, consists of three sections: first, the heading; second, the explanation; and third, the conclusion. Regarding the first:
"fundamental karma" (*mūlakarman*) is easily understood.
The second explanation (the ten stages as ten): first is the Stage of Excellent Awakening (*Sudurjaya-bhūmi*).

If a bodhisattva dwells in the lands of a hundred buddhas and acts as a Cāturmahārājika king of Jambudvīpa, he cultivates a hundred dharma-gates with a mind of equality regarding the two truths to transform all sentient beings.
Section Five: Now, first, the explanation of the breadth and narrowness of the lands. Regarding the phrase "dwelling in the lands of a hundred buddhas," there are three types of lands:

first, the land of preaching the Dharma, where a billion suns and moons transform those of the Hīnayāna; second, the land of supernatural powers, where ten billion suns and moons transform those of the Madhyamāyāna;
third, the land of wisdom, where immeasurable worlds transform Bodhisattvas. What is mentioned here as "a hundred buddha-lands" refers to the first.

This refers to the land where he preached the Dharma. Having become one of the Four Heavenly Kings of Jambudvīpa, he was assigned a position among them as the Southern Heavenly King Virūḍhaka, because Jambudvīpa is superior to other regions as it is here that Buddhas appear.
Furthermore, according to the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, he successively became the Four Heavenly Kings; specifically, as a Bodhisattva on the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), he acted as [the first king].

Regarding the Iron-Wheel-Turning King of Jambudvīpa, it is not said that the four heavenly kings wear necklaces; rather, those who have practiced for one, two, or three kalpas and possess the ten levels of faith (daśa-śraddhā) are divided into three grades:
those with superior-grade goodness become Iron-Wheel-Turning Kings who transform a single world-system; those with middle-grade goodness become minor kings (kṣatriya-samanta-rāja);

and those with inferior-grade goodness become kings among men. Those with the ten abodes (daśa-vihāra) become Copper-Wheel-Turning Kings, and those with the ten practices (daśa-caryā) [become Silver-Wheel-Turning Kings].

The ten stages of the silver wheel-turning king correspond to the first stage and above of the gold wheel-turning king; the ten stages of the lapis lazuli wheel-turning king correspond to the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra*;
and the first stage corresponds to the iron wheel-turning king—this is the intent of the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*).

According to the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda Sūtra* and this present sūtra, practicing the ten wholesome paths constitutes the iron wheel-turning king—this is the intent of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). Those who cultivate the hundred dharma-gates are those who manifest the three dharma-gates; that is to say, from oneself...
Regarding "beneficial conduct" (*hitakriyā*), because each of the ten wholesome paths is further clarified as being itself tenfold, they are called the "one hundred dharma-gates.

Regarding the "mind of equality regarding the two truths," this refers to the distinct practices within the four explanations of the stages (*bhūmi*). Because it is both conventional and ultimate, it is called "equality.
Regarding "transforming all sentient beings," this refers to the universal practice within the five explanations of the stages; every stage employs this to transform beings.
The textual passages for the nine stages following "For the practice" can be understood by analogy with this.
Second, the explanation of the stage of "Leaving behind and Attaining":
If a bodhisattva dwells in the lands of a thousand Buddhas and acts as a king of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, they cultivate a thousand dharma-gates of the ten paths of wholesome action.
He transforms all sentient beings.
Regarding the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven—here translated as the "Thirty-three Heavens"—the *Dìjīng* (Sutra on the Stages) states that in the second stage, one wears a golden light king-ornament;
this is the same as in this sutra. As for the "thousand dharma-gates," each of the ten wholesome actions mentioned previously is practiced individually.
[This refers to] the hundred virtues (and so forth).
Third, the explanation of the Radiant Ground (*prabhākari-bhūmi*):
If a bodhisattva dwells within a hundred thousand Buddha-fields as a King of the *Yāma* Heaven and cultivates a hundred thousand Dharma-gates and the four *dhyānas*.
The *Dìjīng* (Sutra on the Stages) renders this as "the crown-ornament of the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven," which is the same as here.
Fourth, the explanation of the *Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*.

If a bodhisattva dwells in ten billion buddha-fields as the King of the Tuṣita Heaven, they cultivate ten billion dharma-gates and practice the *mārgavarga* (stages of the path) to transform all sentient beings.

In the *Dìjīng* (Sutra on the Stages), it is stated that [the bodhisattva] acts as the King of the Yama Heaven; the description of the necklaces is the same here, and the *mārgavarga* is composed as [describing] the King of the Tuṣita Heaven.
These are the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.
Fifth, the explanation of the Difficult-to-Conquer Stage (*Sudurjayā-bhūmi*):
If a bodhisattva dwells in a thousand-billion buddha-fields as the King of the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (*Nirmāṇarati*) and cultivates a thousand-billion dharma-gates.
The Truths consist of the Four Truths, the Eight Truths, and the transformation of all sentient beings.
The Two Truths are the ultimate and the conventional; the Four Truths are suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path;

and the Eight Truths are the four conditioned and the four unconditioned. Furthermore, suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self, together with permanence, bliss, self, and purity, constitute the eight.
The *Yedi jing* (Yedijing) renders it as the King of Tuṣita Heaven; here it is rendered as the King of Nirmāṇarati Heaven.
Sixth, the Manifestation Stage (*Abhimukhī-bhūmi*):
If a bodhisattva dwells within ten trillion buddha-fields, acting as the King of Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven and practicing ten trillion dharmas.
The gate of the wisdom of the twelve links of dependent origination transforms all sentient beings.
The *Dì jīng* (Sūtra on the Grounds) refers to the King of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven wearing a necklace; here it is made the same as that of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.
Seven: the Far-Reaching Ground (*Dūraṃgamā-bhūmi*).
If a bodhisattva dwells in a hundred trillion buddha-fields as a king of the first dhyāna, cultivating a hundred trillion gateways to the Dharma through skillful means,
wisdom, and the power of vows, thereby transforming all sentient beings.

The *Dìjīng* (Earth Sūtra) states that the *Tāzhìhuàtiānwáng Sīngluòjīng* (Sūtra on the Garland of the King of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven) says: "The Brahmā King constantly transforms sentient beings by means of two kinds of wisdom.
This is the eighth [section], the Explanation of the Stage of Equal Contemplation (*Samatā-bhūmi*).
If a bodhisattva dwells in as many buddha-lands as there are atoms in ten million particles, acting as a Brahma King of the Second Dhyāna,
they cultivate as many dharma-gates as there are atoms in ten million particles, illuminating both skillful means and supernormal wisdom to transform all sentient beings.
The *Dìjīng* (Earth Sūtra) states that the Brahmā Heavenly King rules over a thousand worlds; his "necklace" is called the "Brahmā Lion Necklace.
The light of this necklace illuminates both the ultimate and the conventional truths simultaneously without contradiction, which is termed "expedient wisdom" (*upāya-jñāna*).
Within the state of meditative absorption, he is able to manifest supernormal powers, which is termed "supernormal power wisdom" (*abhijñā-jñāna*).
9. Explaining the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (*Sādhumatī-bhūmi*).

If a bodhisattva dwells in as many buddha-fields as there are atoms in ten million billion *asaṃkhyeya* [worlds], acting as a Great Brahmā King of the Third Dhyāna, cultivating as many dharma-gates as there are atoms in ten million billion *asaṃkhyeya* [worlds] and the four types of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*) to transform sentient beings.
"All sentient beings.

In the *Dì jīng* (Sūtra on the Stages), this is called the Brahmā King who rules over two thousand worlds; in the *Yíngluò jīng* (Sūtra of the Necklace), it is called the Śuddhāvāsakāyika Heaven King.
The tenth is the *dharmameghā-bhūmi*.
If a bodhisattva dwells in unspeakably unspeakable Buddha-lands as the Great Pure Heaven King (Mahāśuddhadeva-rāja), the lord of the third dhyāna and the triple world,
practicing the unspeakably unspeakable Dharma-gates and attaining the Samādhi of the Exhaustion of Principle, they share the sphere of action of the Buddhas,
reach the source of the triple world, and transform all sentient beings according to the realm of the Buddhas.

The *Dìjīng* (Earth Sūtra) states that the Great Maheśvara Heavenly King rules over the three thousandfold world system; the *Yíngluòjīng* (Sūtra on the Necklace) states that the Great Śuddhāvāsa Heavenly King is the Great Maheśvara;
and the *Dàjìngzhùjīng* (Great Pure Abode Sūtra) states that the Great Pure Heaven—all these are identical.

When study and practice are complete, it is called the Samādhi of the Exhaustion of Principles; there is but one practice, which is the practice of the Tathāgata, namely, the Mahāparinirvāṇa of the Bodhisattva.
It may also be called "the same sphere of activity as the Buddha. Ignorance is the root of the three realms; when this delusion is exhausted, the source of the three realms is likewise exhausted.
This concludes the third section.
Therefore, the fundamental practice of transformation of all bodhisattvas is as pure as that of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions;
by cultivating this practice, they attain the fruit of sarvajñā (omniscience), become kings of the three realms, and transform all immeasurable sentient beings.
The explanation has two parts: first, the summary of the karma of the Bodhisattvas; second, from "If in the ten directions... onwards, the summary of the karma of the Tathāgatas.
This also constitutes the direct answer and explanation regarding the stage of wondrous enlightenment (*miao-jue-di*). Thus, the direct answers to the two questions are concluded.

now, before the Buddha, he extols him with verses, saying:

The Teacher is fully endowed with wisdom; he is fully endowed with the Dharma-body of the three vajras;
he is fully endowed with the four minds and the tranquility of liberation; he is fully endowed with the five turnings of the wheel of Dharma to transform others (and so forth).

Regarding "swiftly responding to capacities through eloquence and the eight tones," the *Brahmayu Sūtra* states: first, the most excellent voice; second, the easily understood voice; third, the harmonious...
1. Harmonious voice; 2. Soft and gentle voice; 3. Unerring voice; 4. Not feminine voice; 5. Reverent voice; 6. Profound and far-reaching voice. "Hóng" (洪) means great.

At this point, the assembly below offers three exclamations of praise regarding the Sangha Jewel. In the preceding text, although the general assembly includes devas, they do not possess the dharma of renunciation (*pravrajyā*);
the mention of "renunciation" here is spoken in reference to the mind, as it is practiced in common by those of the Three Vehicles.

Because of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), it is said that one accomplishes the assembly of *bhikṣus* while practicing the bodhisattva path; furthermore, leaving the household life as a human being constitutes becoming part of the assembly of *bhikṣus*, whereas leaving the household life as a celestial being constitutes practicing the bodhisattva path.
Second, a specific praise of the five patiences (*kṣānti*).

Regarding the meritorious qualities of these five patiences, this sublime Dharma-gate can be correctly understood by fourteen virtuous persons (*satpuruṣa*) who practice within the stages of the three worthies (*triyāna*) and ten sages (*daśārya*);
only the Buddha alone can exhaustively fathom its source.

The three stages of worthiness and the ten stages of sagehood are names for the causal positions; practicing patience therein, the Buddha dwells on the ground of fruition, exhausting the source and reaching the ultimate principle, which is called "being able to exhaust the source.
Furthermore, the reason all fourteen are called "Righteous Persons" (Saddharmasatva) is that they correspond to the forty-one stages:

the ten grounds constitute the ten abodes, while the practices, directions, and Equal Enlightenment together form the four [remaining] stages, totaling fourteen. These are the Great Beings of the Perfect Teaching.

The fourteen types of noble beings all, through the threefold contemplation of a single mind, clearly realize all dharmas; this is called practicing the various deeds of Vairocana within the stage of patience.
Because they bring rest to all activities, it is called "being able to exhaust the source" (and so forth).
The threefold exaltation of the single essence of the Triple Gem:
within this are subsumed the immeasurable merits of the Three Treasuries of the Buddha, the Sangha, and the Dharma.
The Buddha is the Buddha-gem, the Sangha is the Sangha-gem, and the Dharma is the Dharma-gem; they are as encompassing as the ocean and as accumulated as a vast storehouse.
Because they are contained therein, immeasurable merits are subsumed within them.

Second, regarding the separate verses on the fourteen types of patience (*kṣānti*), there are five sections: first, nine lines of verse for the patience of subduing (*vinaya-kṣānti*); second, twenty lines of verse for the patience of faith (*adhimukti-kṣānti*);
third, eight lines of verse for the patience of conformity (*anuloma-kṣānti*); fourth, forty lines of verse for the patience of non-arising (*anutpāda-kṣānti*); and fifth, eight [lines].
The first section of the verse on the patience of tranquil extinction (*śānti-kṣānti*) consists of two parts:

the first two lines of verse praise the skillful means of the patience of subduing (*vinaya-kṣānti*) (namely, the ten stages of faith), while the subsequent seven lines praise the merits of the patience of subduing (namely, the three stages of worthiness). Within the first part, there are two further sections: first, clarifying the departure from faults;
second, clarifying the inclusion of stages. This is the first [section].
When a Bodhisattva of the Ten Good Deeds resolves upon the Great Mind, they forever part from the ocean of suffering in the three realms of existence.
An ancient said: "A Bodhisattva of the Ten Faiths, by resolving upon the Great Mind and seeking to escape the three realms, has not yet actually emerged from them;

however, because they are already able to remain far removed from the sufferings of the evil paths and so forth, it is said that they have 'forever parted' from them. This is not the case, however, according to the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao).

The ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) belong to the outer ordinary beings (*bāhyapṛthagjana*); since they have not yet been able to leave [suffering] even momentarily, how could they be able to depart from it permanently?

In the Perfect Teaching (*yāna*), the delusions of the triple world are severed during the ten stages of faith; upon reaching the beginning of the ten abidings (*daśa-vihāra*), one immediately severs the delusions of ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth beyond the triple world.

Because they sever only the four abidings (*catuḥ-vāsabhūmi*) of the triple world, they are equal to the Arhats; they permanently depart from the sea of suffering and are born together with those of the Two Vehicles (*dviyāna*).

Furthermore, there are other lands where if Arhats or Pratyekabuddhas encounter another Buddha in those lands who preaches the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* for them, they immediately become Bodhisattvas and advance to sever ignorance.
Even if Bodhisattvas of the ten stages of faith have not yet heard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, they are nonetheless able to gradually sever ignorance on their own.
How can it be said that simply because one is not reborn in the evil realms, one has forever parted from suffering?

Hǎi asked: "To what stage in the Separate Teaching (biejiao) are these ten levels of faith (shixin) similar? He answered: "If we speak in terms of comparison, they correspond to the stages prior to the Grounds (diquan) in the Separate Teaching:

the Ten Abidings (shizhu) practice the contemplation of entering emptiness from the conventional (cong jia ru kong guan); the Ten Practices (shixing) practice the contemplation of entering the conventional from emptiness (cong kong ru jia guan);

and the Ten Transferences (shihuixiang) practice the contemplation of the Middle Way (zhongdao zhengguan). In the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao), the Ten Faiths are already able to encompass all [stages] perfectly."

Regarding the cultivation of the three contemplations, one cannot discuss them as being identical; rather, they are distinct. If one asks with which stage the [distinct] teaching aligns, it is equal to the tenth stage of the Ten Dedications (*daśaniryāṇa*).

Answering by way of refutation: although the two teachings of the *Āgama* (Tripitaka) and *Vaipulya* (Shared) differ in their skillfulness, they both perceive only emptiness and do not perceive non-emptiness;
thus, they do not yet recognize the Middle Way. In contrast, the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) of the Perfect Teaching fully cultivate all three contemplations.
The three contemplations cannot be compared with the two preceding teachings; rather, they are discussed as being superior to them.

In the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), during the stage of the ten faiths (*shixin*), the Buddha of the *zang* and *tong* teachings and the two vehicles (*ersheng*) all sever both the delusions of views (*jian*) and the delusions of thought (*si*). Thus, they are equal to the Buddha-stage of the *zang* and *tong* teachings.

What is called the "great mind" refers to the greatness of the vow, the greatness of saving sentient beings, the greatness of preaching the Dharma, and the greatness of compassion, joy, pity, and equanimity.
Furthermore, it distinguishes between the various categories of suffering— the three sufferings, the eight sufferings, and the eighty-four thousand types of suffering—
which revolve incessantly like a wheel and rise and fall, emerge and submerge like the ocean (and so forth).
Second, the clarification of the inclusion of stages:

wholesome deeds of medium and inferior grades result in the status of a minor king (a *kṣullaka-rāja*), while those of superior grade result in the status of an Iron Wheel-turning King (*cakra-vartin*).

When practicing the ten wholesome paths of action, one must necessarily possess three mental states; the middle and lower of these three constitute the state of a minor king among the assembly of petty rulers.

For the most part, one who practices the ten wholesome paths of action with a superior mind, like a minor king among the *kṣullaka-rāja* (scattered-kinglets), becomes an Iron-Wheel-Turning King (*ayaścakravartin*) ruling over Jambudvīpa;

his iron wheel-treasure is one *krośa* in width (and so forth). Whether it be a superior, middle, or inferior Iron-Wheel-Turning King, or a minor king among the *kṣullaka-rāja*, or an inferior human king (and so forth).
Regarding the second verse, which describes the merits of the upper, middle, and lower levels of the "Patience of Subjugation" (伏忍), the text is divided into two parts:
first, two lines specifically praising each of the three levels as the three types of Universal Monarchs (轉輪王); second, five lines praising the three levels collectively. This is the first part.

Those of the lineage of practice (śikṣāgotra) rule over two worlds as copper-wheel-turning kings; those of the lineage of nature (prakṛtigotra) rule over three worlds as silver-wheel-turning kings; and those of the lineage of the path-seed (mārgagotraka), possessing firm virtue, become wheel-turning kings with the seven treasures and golden light who rule over the four worlds.
A Bodhisattva of the tenth stage who belongs to the lineage of practice becomes a copper-wheel-turning king who rules over two worlds; as for that copper wheel:
The precious wheel of the Silver-Wheel King, who belongs to the lineage of the nature-disposition (*gotra*) Bodhisattva at the stage of the ten practices, is two *krośas* in width;

he rules over three continents. The precious wheel of the Golden-Wheel King, who belongs to the lineage of the path-disposition (*gotra*) Bodhisattva at the stage of the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*), is three *krośas* in width;
he rules over four continents. The precious wheel of the Golden-Wheel King [at the next stage] is four *krośas* in width.
The seven treasures are the woman-treasure, the jewel-treasure, the wheel-treasure, the military-commander treasure, the treasury-minister treasure, the elephant-treasure, and the horse-treasure.
Regarding the second section, the general praise of the three categories of texts, there are two parts: first, the listing of the thirty minds; second, the formal praise of their merits. Now...

First: The thirty persons of the Noble Womb (āryagarbha) of the Patience of Submission (kṣānti-avaivartika), consisting of the ten stages of faith (śraddhā), the ten stages of cessation (sthiti), and the ten stages of firm resolve (adhyāśaya).

They are called the "Noble Womb" because they serve as the womb for the ten [stages of] the Sages; thus, these thirty persons provide the general enumeration of the numbers, while the following sections on the ten abodes (vihāra) and so forth provide the specific details.

In the various editions of the sutra, the character for "faith" (信) appears; some say that "faith" refers to the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), "stopping" (*zhi*) to the ten abidings (*daśa-vihāra*), and "firmness" (*jian*) to the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*).

This, however, seems to contradict the meaning and principles of the sutra text. Others say that "faith" refers to the ten abidings, "stopping" to the ten practices, and "firmness" to the ten stages of dedication (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*).
This interpretation accords with the meaning but contradicts the literal text. Now, I maintain that these are merely provisional designations based on similarities in their transmission.
The scribe’s error should be read as the character "dwelling" (住).
Second, it is the formal praise of its merit:
all Buddhas of the three worlds practice therein without exception; from this "patience of subduing" (伏忍) arise the roots of all bodhisattva practices.

For this reason, it is difficult to give rise to the mind of faith; yet once one has attained the mind of faith, one will certainly not regress and will enter the first stage of the path of non-arising.
To practice within awakening for the sake of teaching and transforming sentient beings is called the Bodhisattva’s initial arousal of the mind.
Section Four: First, praising the Patience of Subduing (*kṣānti*) as that which can give birth to all Buddhas.

Taking the patience of subduing as the initial gateway for entering the Path and the pivotal point of Bodhi—since no one emerges without passing through the door—all Buddhas of the three periods of time are born from this.
Second, praising the patience of subduing as that which can give birth to the great ocean of Bodhisattvas; it is the fundamental source.
It is said that among all streams, the source of every stream must begin with a single drop; likewise, the practice of a Bodhisattva originates in the patience of subduing [the passions].
The establishment of this patience of subduing depends upon faith. If one can give rise to faith and enter the perfect stage of the Ten Abodes, one will immediately sever ignorance (*avidyā*).

This ignorance is vast and pervasive, such that it cannot be severed except by the wisdom of the threefold contemplation within a single mind. It is precisely this wisdom that is capable of severing it.

Because it arises from the Ten Faiths, the Buddha praised them, saying that the mind of faith is difficult to attain. If one attains this mind of faith, the following three sections clarify its efficacy:
if one attains the perfect mind of faith, one will certainly not regress and will immediately enter the path of the First Ground (*bhūmi*).
Within this scriptural passage, two teachings are contained; if we consider the Distinct Teaching (*bhedavyavasthāna*), one gradually progresses from the Ten Faiths.

"Retreating and then ascending to the Stage of Joy": if it is a Bodhisattva of the ten levels of faith (*śraddhā*) in the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), they do not regress and immediately ascend to the first dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*).

Since the first dwelling of the Perfect Teaching is equivalent to the first stage (*bhūmi*) of the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*), the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and the subsequent scriptural passages also treat the ten dwellings as the ten stages.
As for "certainly not regressing," this means that those in the ten levels of faith of the Perfect Teaching are necessarily non-regressive.

Regarding the falling away of ordinary beings, those of the two vehicles, and those within the three realms, the *Mūlakarman-saṃbandha-vaipulya-sūtra* explains that during the sixth stage (*bhūmi*) among the ten stages,

when right observation manifests and one encounters the protection of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), one emerges into the seventh stage and is forever non-retrogressive.
Those prior to the seventh stage are termed "stages of retrogression," as was the case with the eighty thousand [monks] at the Buddha’s first assembly.

Question: Why does this sutra not mention those who regress—such as the Devaputra Śuddharaśmiprabha, the Prince Dharmamati, Śāriputra, and others—who, while seeking to enter the seventh stage (*bhūmi*), encountered adverse conditions and fell back among ordinary beings into unwholesome and evil states, forming great false views?
Answer: The minds of people are like faces; each is different. The Great Sage [taught] in accordance with [their capacities].
Because of their capacities, there are also distinctions. Some say that bodhisattvas on the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) who possess the nature of the lineage (*gotra*) may still fall back into hell;

furthermore, those who fall back during the first *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa* are precisely those entering the stage of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). There are also those who fall back even at the first [stage] of the *sragdharā* (the Garland Sutra).
The first [text] speaks of the ten abodes (*daśavihāra*), naming the seventh "Abiding in Non-retrogression. Prior to the seventh abode, one is indeed subject to falling back.

Regarding the meaning of "retrogression," there are distinctions according to the teachings: retrogression during the first *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa* refers to the Tripiṭaka (Āgama) teaching; retrogression during the ten stages of practice (*daśa-caryā*) refers to the Shared (Sādhāraṇa) teaching; retrogression during the ten stages of transference (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*) refers to the Distinct (Pratyekabuddha) teaching;

and retrogression during the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) refers to the Perfect (Ekayāna) teaching. What is now stated—that one does not regress from the stage of faith and enters the ground of the first abode (*prathama-vihāra*)—is precisely the meaning of the Perfect teaching.

Regarding the subsequent four lines on "teaching and transforming sentient beings": 1. To teach and transform sentient beings is the Bodhisattva’s great compassion. 2. To teach and transform sentient beings is the Bodhisattva’s great vow. 3. To teach and transform sentient beings is the Bodhisattva’s great skillful means. 4. To teach and transform sentient beings is the Bodhisattva’s great power.
The first phrase clarifies the practice of benefiting others: it teaches that one must transform sentient beings so that they always achieve awakening and never regress.
The second phrase concludes by praising the initial resolve (*cittotpāda*). As the *Mahāyāna-sūtrālaṃkāra* states: "The initial resolve and the ultimate [resolve] are not two different things;
between these two resolves, the former is more difficult. And as the *Prajñāpāramitā* says: "One who can give rise to a single thought of pure faith regarding the Unborn..."
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "To practice the five pāramitās for immeasurable kalpas is not as good as hearing of the Buddha’s lifespan and giving rise to faith and so forth.
All such meanings are contained herein. The verse on the Patience of Submission (*kṣānti*) is concluded.

The second verse concerns the merit of faith and patience; the text is divided into two parts: first, the verses on the three grades, and second, the concluding praise. Regarding the first part, there are three sections:
the first four lines of verse describe the "lower patience" (*mṛdu-kṣānti*) of the first stage (*bhūmi*); the next two lines describe the "middle patience" (*madhya-kṣānti*) of the second stage;
and the final two lines describe the "upper patience" (*adhimātra-kṣānti*) of the third stage. This is the first [section].

The Bodhisattva Good Awakening (Sujāta) and the Twin Kings of the Four Heavens illuminate the equal path of the two truths; through skillful means they transform sentient beings and travel among a hundred lands, beginning their ascent upon the signless path of the One Vehicle.
Entering into the principle of *prajñā* is called "abiding" (*vihāra*); the arising of virtuous conduct from this abiding is called a "ground" (*bhūmi*).
In the first ground, the mind is fully endowed with virtuous conduct, remaining unmoved within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

The text has two parts. First, one and a half lines praise the sovereign power of acting as a king: the conventional is like an illusion and exists; the ultimate is like an illusion and does not exist.

Although the mind is not real, it is not non-existent with respect to illusions; since it is perfectly manifest within illusion, it is said that it "shines upon both the ultimate and the conventional.
Because it is empty, it is called "equality. Second, starting from "Having first ascended to the One Vehicle," the next two and a half lines clarify the merit of entering the stages (*bhūmi*).
Abiding in the principle of the Truths by means of the three wisdoms within a single mind is called "abiding," which is the source from which all virtues arise;

this is termed the "Ground" (*bhūmi*) in the Separate Teaching (Biaojiao), specifically the first Ground, the Joyful (*pramuditā*), and the "Abode" (*vihāra*) in the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), specifically the first Abode, the Joyful.

Within this single mind, one cultivates the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*), and all myriad virtues and myriad practices are simultaneously contained therein. As the *Huashou jing* states: "All merits..."
That "virtue resides entirely within the initial aspiration for enlightenment" is precisely its meaning. Regarding "remaining unmoved within the primary truth":

in the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*), because Bodhisattvas at the stage of the Ten Dedications (*daśapariṇāmanā*) have not yet realized the Middle Way through their cultivation of correct contemplation (*samyag-darśana*), they are subject to movement; only upon reaching the first ground (*bhūmi*) and attaining realization do they become unmoved.
In the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), even while cultivating the threefold contemplation within a single mind during the Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), there is still [movement].
It is only upon attaining the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) that one becomes truly immovable.
The second verse concerns the middle grade of the patience of faith (*śraddhā-kṣānti*).

The Bodhisattva who has attained detachment and penetration manifests the form of a King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven within a thousand lands across the six realms of existence; he is without conditions and without marks (*animitta*). Third.
The Truths are non-existent, non-arising, and non-dual illumination.

Those who have attained liberation are free from the defilement of violating the precepts and have thoroughly mastered the three contemplations. In the Separate Teaching, these correspond to the second stage (*bhūmi*), while in the Perfect Teaching, they correspond to the second abode (*vihāra*) of the Bodhisattva.
The terms "Bodhisattva" (開士), "Great Being" (大士), and "Righteous Being" (正士) all share the same meaning: one who opens the path of the Dharma of emptiness.

The Trāyastriṃśa Bright King manifests his form through the transformation of clarity; there is no object for equality, and the wisdom of clarity is such that in the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) there is no dharma to be taken as an object, and in the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) there is no dharma to be characterized.
This absence of objects and absence of characteristics is precisely the Middle Way, the primary ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
Since there is neither non-existence nor non-non-existence—neither non-existence as an object nor non-existence as a characteristic—and since both of these are absent, how could there be arising?
Therefore it is said: "Since non-arising is already true, how could there be illumination within non-arising? And: "How can there be non-dual illumination?
For illumination has nothing to illuminate; this is because of non-duality.
These three verses concern the superior grade of the stage of patient acceptance (*kṣānti*).
The Celestial King Minghui Kongzhao Yan manifests forms throughout the myriad nations to guide all sentient beings toward the patient mind (*kṣānti*) that is non-dual.
From within the Two Truths, he emerges from existence and enters non-existence, manifesting transformations.

Specifically, on the third stage, he realizes the two kinds of emptiness—of persons and phenomena—and achieves the perfection of patience; thus he is named Kongzhao (Empty Illumination). Generally, this refers to the third [stage].
Abiding is emptiness, which is provisionality, which is the Middle; this is called "empty illumination. Responding to forms is "manifest transformation";
the mind of patience is "clear wisdom. Because the three truths are one truth and the three minds are one mind, it is said there is no duality.
Because being is emptiness, it is called "exiting existence and entering non-existence"; because emptiness is existence, it is called "the arising of transformations."
Second, the summary of faith and patience:

Those on the three paths of the person of good awakening and detachment from illumination are able to extinguish the afflictions of form within the triple world; they further contemplate the dharma-nature of the physical forms of body and speech within the triple world as the supreme, leaving nothing unilluminated.

That which can extinguish the afflictions of form within the triple world is that form itself is emptiness; returning to contemplate the forms of body and speech within the triple world, one sees that emptiness is form.

This dharma-nature is supreme, leaving nothing unilluminated, and there is nothing that is not the Middle Way. There is a variant text that reads "only illuminating," but this is not the intended meaning of the scripture.
The third verse concerning *anulomikī-kṣānti* (conformable patience) consists of two parts: the first six lines present the actual verse, and the final two lines provide a summary.
The first part has three sections: the first two lines praise the inferior grade, the next two lines praise the middling grade, and the final two lines praise the superior grade.
This is the first [section].

The Tushita Heavenly King, Flame-Wisdom-Miraculous-Light-Great-Vigor, travels through billions of lands; his true wisdom is quiescent in its conditions, his skillful means reach the path of non-arising, and he illuminates emptiness while understanding existence.
Regarding "Flame-Wisdom-Miraculous-Light" and so forth: this refers to Bodhisattvas of the fourth stage in the Separate Teaching who have attained the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*).

The accomplishment of the Perfect Teaching refers to the Bodhisattvas at the stage of the Four Abodes; their diligent application to the three contemplations is the realization of quiescence, which is real wisdom (prajñā), while their illumination of both emptiness and existence is expedient wisdom (upāya).
Next is the verse on the middle grade.

With supreme wisdom, one personally realizes the three truths and clearly transforms the realm of the King of the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (*Nirmāṇarati*). Within the hundred billion lands, one contemplates the truth of emptiness as non-dual in appearance, manifesting transformations throughout the six realms of existence while entering the Avīci Hell.

Bodhisattvas of the fifth stage in the Separate Teaching enter profound meditative concentration to attain supreme wisdom; in the Perfect Teaching, this corresponds to the bodhisattva of the fifth dwelling.
"Sāya" (Svayaṃ): By contemplating emptiness within emptiness as non-dual, movement itself is stillness; transformation within the six realms is itself stillness, and stillness itself is movement.
Three verses on the superior grade.
The Dharma-manifesting Bodhisattva Sovereign King is non-dual and non-illuminating; having realized the principle of emptiness, the three truths manifest before him.
The light of his great wisdom illuminates thousands of billions of lands, teaching all beings.

Because Bodhisattvas of the sixth stage of the Separate Teaching attain the perfection of Prajñā, it is said that "the Dharma manifests," etc.; [this applies to] the sixth [stage] of the Perfect Teaching.
Abiding in the middle, being without duality and without illumination, etc., is stillness; the universal radiance of the light of wisdom is movement.
This is the second summary:
the manifestation of the supreme flame-like Dharma within the signless samādhi can sprinkle away the deluded mind and afflictions of the three realms; empty wisdom is tranquil and without conditions.
The contemplation of returning to the contemplation of the mind results in the immeasurable retribution of emptiness.
"Flame" refers to the fourth stage (*bhūmi*); "excellence" refers to the fifth stage; and "manifestation of dharmas" refers to the sixth stage.

These three Bodhisattvas attain the contemplation of the Middle Way, wherein the two marks of existence and non-existence do not arise. They wash away the defilements of ignorance with the water of right contemplation. Emptiness.
"Wisdom and so forth" refers to the emptiness of both matter and mind; "returning to observation and so forth" refers to the conventional designation of both matter and mind.

Regarding the fourth verse on the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), the text is divided into three parts: first, five lines of verse describe the lower patience (*mṛdu-kṣānti*) of the seventh stage; next, three lines of verse describe the middle patience (*madhya-kṣānti*) of the eighth stage;
and finally, two lines of verse describe the upper patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*) of the ninth stage. Within the first part, there are two sections, the first of which is as follows:
Explaining the two stages of severing delusions through the aspects of practice; here begins the first.
Having reached the distant realization of non-arising, the King of the First Dhyāna constantly teaches sentient beings across ten trillion lands until they are all delivered.

At this stage, the retributive body has but one more birth remaining as he enters the "Flow of the Dharma" stage (*dharmasrotas-bhūmi*) of Equal Enlightenment. He then enters the "Vajra-like Patience" (*vajropama-kṣānti*) which is objectless, whereby his retributive form within the three realms is forever [extinguished].
The third meaning of non-reception and contemplation is the twofold illumination of the twenty-one types of practice in emptiness and quiescence.
It reaches far into the Great Chapter on Non-arising (*Anutpāda-mahāparivarta*). While the meaning of "deeply entering" and "reaching far" is similar [to the previous stage], it is not the same;
for in the sixth stage there is still interruption in realization, whereas here one reaches the source of the Dharma, and thus it is called "deeply entering. Deep.
"Entering" refers to the Ground of Far-Going (*dūraṃgamā*), as it is proximate to the eighth ground; thus it is further called "Far-Going," meaning that one has reached far.
Regarding the phrase "constantly ten thousand *koṭis*," etc., this clarifies the function of transformation (*nirmāṇa-karma*); since it cites a general number, it says "ten thousand *koṭis*.

The passage "not yet crossing over" and below clarifies the reduction of birth (*janmanirvartana*). "Not yet crossing over the reward-body" means the body of segmented birth (*paricchinna-janman*). Having exhausted this...

Because the body immediately enters into transformation, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that a Bodhisattva of the seventh stage has not yet discarded the physical body, nor has he transcended his final birth among twenty lifetimes.
Because he contemplates both truths simultaneously, it is called "equal contemplation" (*samadarśana*).

Furthermore, because the two dharmas of form and mind have no marks of distinction, it is called "equal contemplation. In the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavyavasthāna*), the seventh stage still possesses [these distinctions].

Through effortful application, one enters the eighth stage; within the state of non-effortful mind, the Middle Way flows naturally toward the ocean of *sarvajñā*—this is the intended meaning of "connecting the distinct [stages].
Upon first entering the objectless *vajra-kṣānti*, one no longer receives a segmented body (*bhavāgra-śarīra*) within the triple world.
This is a preliminary explanation of the merits from the eighth stage upward, because one will certainly be able to attain such excellence.
Because the divine [realization] is attained before long, it is mentioned first; this is like how, when teaching the śrāvakas, one first praises their future fruition.
Regarding the Middle Way, the Supreme Truth (paramārtha-satya), in contrast to the conventional (saṃvṛti-satya), it is the third [truth];

since the middle encompasses all middles, it is said to be "non-dual. The illumination [of these stages] consists of three grades—lower, middle, and upper—for each stage from the first to the seventh bhūmi.
Seventh, throughout twenty-one lifetimes, one contemplates the emptiness and quiescence of all phenomena; this constitutes the practice.
Second, the clarification of the limits for severing delusions.
The habitual tendencies of craving within the three realms are thoroughly understood through the samādhi that accords with the Path by the solitary sage who has attained correct realization.
Bodhisattvas of the sixth stage sever the active manifestations [of these tendencies], while the severing of their habitual tendencies is as described in the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra*:
"This Stage of Far-Going (*dūraṃgamā*) is not called 'possessing afflictions,' because no afflictions whatsoever manifest; yet there remains a yearning for the wisdom of the Tathāgata."

Because these have not yet been fully perfected, they are not called "possessing afflictions"; this sutra is also like this. Because those who love the Buddha and possess wisdom have not yet severed their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), it is therefore called "conforming to the path.

Regarding the truth of concentration (*samādhi-satya*), which refers to thorough reality: although the afflictions were severed in the previous six stages, the habitual tendencies of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsanā*) had not yet been severed;
now, in this seventh stage, the heavy residues of the afflictions (*kleśa-dausthulya*) have long since been completely exhausted.
Therefore, one can clearly discern that the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of ignorance have not yet been severed. "Craving" refers to deluded craving;

because of this deluded craving, one undergoes the body of birth and death. As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "From delusion comes craving, and thus my illness arises. Now, within the seventh stage, this has been permanently severed.
The second verse concerns the medium stage of patience regarding non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

It describes how the Bodhisattva, through equal contemplation, transforms the two dhyāna-kings into the Dharma-body, emitting immeasurable light that enters a hundred *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* worlds to transform all beings.

This light perfectly illuminates the events of all kalpas throughout the three periods of time, while reflecting back toward the source of joy in emptiness and non-exhaustion, abiding eternally within the third truth.
"Quiescent" refers to the Bodhisattva of the Eighth Stage (*bhūmi*). This phrase designates the name and indicates the rank. Regarding "transforming birth into the Dharma-body":

at the Seventh Stage, the *paricchinna-bhava* (segmented) *vipāka-kāya* (retribution body) has already been relinquished; by transforming that segmented state, one attains the *nirmāṇa-kāya* (transformation) *dharma-kāya*. Therefore, it is said to "transform birth."
Because one realizes the principle of the dharma-nature to accomplish this body, it is called the Dharma-body. "Entering a hundred lands of Ganges-sands" below clarifies its superior function:

that which precedes the Path is the past; that which is within the Path is the present; and that which follows the Path is the future. "Reflecting back" means illuminating the events prior to the seventh stage;
"delighting in emptiness" means taking conditions in the present as the object; and "the inexhaustible source" refers to the future.

Regarding the illumination of future events: although one attains non-dual illumination in the seventh stage, because this is first realized and not yet clearly tranquil, it is now, upon reaching the eighth stage, that the mind becomes even more refined and matured; therefore, it is eternally tranquil.
The three verses concern the supreme patience regarding non-arising.

The Bodhisattva Prajñāprabha, King of the Third Dhyāna, is able to manifest [the teachings] of a thousand Ganges-sands of Buddhas simultaneously; he constantly abides in the practice of unconditioned emptiness and quiescence, and realizes the treasury of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in a single thought-moment.
This refers to the Bodhisattva Śubhavyūha of the Ninth Ground; "constantly abiding in the unconditioned" and so forth means that movement and stillness are practiced simultaneously.

Regarding the fifth verse on the patience of cessation (*kṣānti-nirodha*), the text is divided into two parts: the first five lines of the verse describe the lower grade, and the final line describes the [higher grade].
The first of the superior grades:
The Bodhisattva King of the Four Dhyānas, having conferred empowerment, transforms sentient beings across lands as numerous as the sands of ten million Ganges Rivers;

he has just entered the Vajra stage of "All-Comprehending," having forever transcended twenty-nine births within the patience of quiescent extinction (*śānti-kṣānti*), and through the middle and lower levels of patience, he contemplates the single revolution of the eternal *samyak-saṃbodhi*.

The three grades of those who have received the empowerment of profound and equal wisdom eliminate the remaining residual habits; because they have exhausted the ignorance that conditions ignorance and the manifestations of the habit-energies of ignorance, their afflictions and the principles of the two truths are thoroughly investigated and all are brought to an end.

Regarding the term "consecration" (*abhiṣeka*): it is so named because it is above the twelve types of Dharma masters; thus, it is called the "Crown. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, fascicle twenty-seven, states:

"For example, when the crown prince of a wheel-turning king (*cakravartin*) has perfected the royal marks, the waters of the four great oceans are taken and poured upon his head, whereupon he is called the 'Great Consecrated King.
It is the same for a Bodhisattva: when receiving the office of a Buddha, all Buddhas [perform this rite]."
The "Water of Wisdom" is poured upon the crown of this Bodhisattva; this is called the Dharma-King of Empowerment (*abhiṣeka*).

This is what is meant by the Bodhisattva entering the stage of the office of wisdom, namely the Stage of the Dharma-Cloud (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*). [This Bodhisattva] acts as the Heavenly King of the Fourth Dhyāna;

according to some texts, he is the King of the Fifth Dhyāna, which refers to including both the Desire Realm and the four *dhyānas*. Regarding the phrase "beginning to enter the Vajra," it is for this reason.
Through meditative concentration, one shatters ignorance and realizes everything; from the initial stage of *pramuditā* (Joy) to the final *dharmameghā* (Cloud of Dharma), there are thirty births.
Here, only twenty-nine births are mentioned because the thirtieth birth is this present body currently undergoing experience, while the preceding twenty-nine have already passed;
thus it is said that one has "forever transcended" them. This refers to the contemplation of the lower patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*).

The "cause-limit" (*hetu-paryanta*) refers to the stage of one turning toward wondrous enlightenment; the "fruit-limit" (*phala-paryanta*) refers to the stage of attaining that very turning of the mind.

Although this has not yet been attained, it is as if it were already attained. "Equal" refers to the Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage; "wisdom" refers to the Bodhisattvas of the ninth stage, the Light of Wisdom;
and "consecration" (*abhiṣeka*) refers to the Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage. These three classes of Great Beings together eliminate the remaining habitual tendencies and ignorance.
