The causal condition of ignorance (*avidyā*) and its habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are called "old afflictions" (*paurāṇa-kleśa*); the four abiding guest-dusts (*ātma-āgantuka-rajas*) are the "new afflictions.

The two truths are the principles of the ultimate and the conventional; their exhaustive realization is the Middle Way. When these three contemplations are attained, both the manifest activities and the habitual tendencies of the truths are completely exhausted.
The two verses on the Stage of Wondrous Enlightenment (which is the Supreme Patience of Quiescence):
Perfect wisdom is signless; the King of the Three Realms has exhausted the thirty births and attained Great Enlightenment. Great quiescence is unconditioned;
Vajragarbha, with all retributions exhausted, possesses infinite compassion. The Ultimate Truth is eternally secure; he has reached the source and exhausted the nature of things—wondrous!
Wisdom abides;
because one attains the perfection of all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) and exhausts the characteristics of ignorance, it is called "perfect wisdom without characteristics" (*animitta*).
Only upon attaining this absence of characteristics does one become the sovereign of the triple world. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* also says: "This triple world is entirely..."
I have an analogy for this: "At that time, the master of the house was standing outside the gate," and so forth.

A Bodhisattva of the tenth stage who undergoes a thirtieth birth has not yet reached the end; however, because a Bodhisattva of wondrous enlightenment (miao-jue) does not undergo this birth, it is called the "end.
Since the preceding thirty births are not yet exhausted, one is not called a Greatly Awakened One (Mahabuddha); because birth in the Buddha-ground is exhausted, one is called "Great."
One perceives that Nirvāṇa is called "Great Quiescence," "Without Remainder," and "Unconditioned," which the four Māras cannot destroy, being like a diamond treasury (*vajragarbha*).
In the preceding thirty births, there was simultaneously the exhaustion of causes and the arising of results; now, with the great fruit perfected, there is no further rebirth.
Therefore, it is said that when retribution is exhausted, one reaches the end of the future limit (*anāgata-koṭi*) to uproot the suffering of sentient beings; thus, compassion is inexhaustible.
Furthermore, because the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is itself *nirvāṇa*, it is eternally peaceful and secure—that is, eternal, blissful, self, and pure.
It exhausts the source of ignorance and eliminates the nature of afflictions; thus, it differs from the nihilistic views of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) and the emptiness realized by Śrāvakas.

Although there is neither attainment nor accomplishment, wondrous wisdom constantly illumines [all things]. The above concludes the verses on the five patiences (*kṣānti*), following the prose and verse commentary.

The five levels of patience (*kṣānti*) are explained reciprocally, yet the emergence and disappearance of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and wondrous enlightenment differ; this is because the Great Sage adapts his phrasing to the capacities of beings to reveal the underlying meaning.
Third, the eight lines that conclude by praising the five patiences consist of three parts: first, a praise of the fruit of the Pure Land; next, a praise of... [text fragment].
Regarding the praise of the fruit of benefit following the fruit of the Dharma-body, this is the first [section].

The three stages of worthiness and the ten stages of sagehood abide in the fruit of retribution; only the Buddha alone dwells in the Pure Land. All sentient beings temporarily abide in the fruit of retribution, while those who have ascended to the Vajra-ground originally dwell in the Pure Land.

To clarify their superiority, one first sets forth their inferiority: the three types of worthies refer to the thirty minds prior to the stages (the ten abidings, ten practices, and ten transferences), while the ten sages refer to the bodhisattvas of the ten stages.

These forty minds are all born together in the land of the fruit-retribution of the Flower Treasury World (*Huāzàng*). This is not the fruit-retribution of the *zhàng* (Treasure) or *tōng* (Penetrating) teachings.
If one speaks of the *zhàng* teaching alone, it is merely the realm where ordinary beings and sages dwell; if one discusses the *tōng* teaching alone, they are born only [in that specific realm].

There are others who speak of a "transformed city" (nirmāṇa-pura); here, when it says "retribution," this refers to those of the Separate and Perfect Teachings who attain birth in the Unobstructed Land within the Unobstructed Realm.
Question: Are the three stages of worthiness and the ten stages of sagehood herein of the Separate Teaching or the Perfect Teaching?

Answer: They are precisely of the Perfect Teaching. Question: Since the Perfect Teaching should logically entail birth in the Constant Quiescent Light (śānta-prabhāsvara), why is it that [these practitioners] are born [there]?

Huazang replies: Within the Huazang [world-realm], the distinct (Vyāvṛtta) and the perfect (Pūrṇa) teachings arise together; because causes cannot give rise to effects, they cannot be born in the Land of Tranquil Light (Śāntaprabhāsa).
Therefore, within the Huazang land, there is the arising together of the ten stages (bhūmi) of the distinct teaching and the forty minds (citta) of the perfect teaching.
As for the ultimate fruit of wondrous enlightenment, Vairocana alone is born in the Land of Tranquility.
Question: Since there are also pure lands within the first three of the four lands, why is it that only the Land of Tranquil Light (*śāntaprabhā*) is specifically named the Pure Land?

Answer: In the Land of Common Residence for Ordinary Beings and Sages, sages are few while ordinary beings are many; thus, it is defiled rather than pure. In the Land of Traceless Transformation (*nirmāṇa-śeṣa*), one has merely eliminated the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhava-kleśa*) but has not yet severed ignorance (*avidyā*);
this is a purity of partial truth (*ekadeśa-satya*) and not true purity. [The Pure Land] refers to the Flower Treasury World (*puṣpa-garbha-loka*).
Because there are still residual expedient means (*upāya*) present, it is not yet purely the Land of Tranquil Light; since this [Land] lacks such things, it receives the name "Pure Land.

Regarding the claim that all sentient beings dwell temporarily in the land of retribution: although sentient beings have no beginning, they do have an end and thus receive retribution only for a time, whereas the Buddha has neither beginning nor end and therefore dwells in the Pure Land.
Now, it is said that when the Buddha attains Wondrous Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), he manifests in response...

This is said because, within the Land of Quiescent Light (*śāntaprabhāsa*), in order to transform sentient beings, one temporarily manifests a lifespan of varying duration and thereby undergoes the retribution [of that life].
Second, the praise of the fruit of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
The virtues of the Tathāgata’s three karmas are infinite; I, Candraprabha, now pay homage to the Triple Gem.
The pure land is the *niśraya-vipāka* (retributive support), while the clarification of the Dharma-body is the *mukhya-vipāka* (primary retribution).
The preceding line is a formal praise, and the subsequent line is a prostration to the Triple Gem as a single essence.
Third, the praise of transforming other realms (which refers to the fruit of benefit mentioned in the preceding heading):
The Dharma King, supreme among men, like a tree that provides shade for the great assembly, possesses immeasurable light; his mouth constantly preaches the Dharma, which is never without meaning;

his mind is in a state of tranquil extinction, yet he illuminates all without conditions; this Lion among Men speaks for the sake of the multitude, and the great assembly rejoices as they scatter [flowers].
The hundreds of millions of lands of Jinhua shook in six ways, and all living beings received wondrous retributions.
The Honored One spoke joyfully of the fourteen kings; therefore, I now briefly praise the Buddha.

In the text, the first line presents a simile praising the benefit of the physical form; the next line provides a doctrinal explanation (dharmadeśanā) praising the Buddha’s vocal activity as the benefit of sound.
Non-Buddhists lack this meaning entirely; the Two Vehicles possess it only partially; Bodhisattvas possess it but not yet perfectly; only the Buddha possesses both the words and the meaning.

"Mind and wisdom" refers to contemplation (*vipaśyanā*); "tranquil extinction" (*śamatha*) refers to the object of that contemplation. The union of contemplation and its object is called "objectless" (*anālambana*).
Furthermore, external forms have nothing to be perceived, and the internal mind has nothing to be illuminated. Next, one line clarifies the great assembly’s offerings;
next, one line clarifies the earthquake; and next, one line concludes by praising the Buddha: when among humans he is the Honored One of Men, and when among devas he is the Honored One of Devas.
Moreover, the Great Sūtra states: "The King of Men is the King of Devas. The fourteen kings are the three [kings].
The "Virtuous Ones" refer to the ten types of noble ones (*ārya*) and so forth; they are praised briefly here because a detailed exposition might cause the assembly to find it difficult to receive.
Furthermore, the Buddha’s virtues are immeasurable and cannot be fully extolled, which is why he is praised only briefly.
Commentary on the *Buddha-bhāṣita-rājñī-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, Scroll Middle;
Commentary on the *Buddha-bhāṣita-rājñī-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, Scroll Lower.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin Dynasty.
Commentary by the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai during the Chen and Sui Dynasties;
compiled by the junior monk Daopai of Minjian Prefecture. Part Three:
Distinguishing the Benefits Received by the Great Assembly.
At that time, when the great assembly heard King Candraprabha extol the immeasurable treasury of merit of the fourteen kings and attain the great benefit of the Dharma,
ten *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* numbers of celestial kings, ten *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* numbers of Brahmā kings, ten *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* numbers of ghost-king spirits,
and even those from the three lower realms attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), as did the eight classes of beings and the *asura* kings.

Manifesting in the form of a ghost, they receive the Way in the heavens; after three births, some enter the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), while others do so after four, five, or even ten births.
Having attained the nature of a noble one (*ārya*), they obtain all manner of immeasurable rewards.

The text is divided into three parts: first, the benefits for the One Vehicle and the three realms of existence; second, the benefits for the eight classes of beings; and third, the varying speed with which they attain the Way. Regarding the first:

it is said that those who attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) include those above the third stage in the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*), above the first stage in the Distinct Teaching (*pratyeka-bhūmi-yāna*), and above the first dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*) in the Perfect Teaching (*ekayāna*).
Question: How can those in the evil realms attain the patience of non-arising? Answer: As stated in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*: [text follows].
It is said that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature and will certainly attain Buddhahood; having now encountered the Buddha as a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), they have attained the Way.
Furthermore, regarding the relative laxity or urgency of the precepts and the vehicle (*śīla-yāna*), this has already been explained in detail previously.

Because the Mahāyāna is urgent while the three grades of precepts are lax, one may encounter the Buddha and hear the Dharma even with a body born in the evil realms—namely, among the eight classes of non-human beings (*aṣṭa-graha*) belonging to the lower two categories.

This section concerns the benefits obtained. Regarding those who enter the stage of the correct position (*samyaktva-niyāma*) after three lifetimes: the difference between the lower three [vehicles] and the attainment of the Way lies in the remoteness or proximity of their realization, which arises from whether their faculties are sharp or dull and their awakening is shallow or deep.

There are two meanings for "the correct position": first, the emptiness of persons, which is attained at the stage of the ten understandings (*daśa-vyākhyāna*) in the Separate Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-yāna*) and the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) in the Perfect Teaching (*ekayāna*);

second, the emptiness of phenomena, which is attained at the first ground (*bhūmi*) in the Separate Teaching and the first dwelling (*vihāra*) in the Perfect Teaching. This occurs after having heard the Dharma.

One attains the state of certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*) within one lifetime up to ten lifetimes; for example, as in the *Lotus Sūtra*, there is the passage concerning the reduction of births (*kṣīṇa-janman*), and so forth.
This concludes the Moonlight Verse Praise.
The third major section: The Tathāgata’s Confirmation in Text. Part Two: First, praise of the speaker; second, praise of that which is spoken.
The first section has two parts: first, the actual praise; second, the description of the praise. Now, for the first:
The Buddha addressed the great assembly who had attained the fruits of the Path, saying:

"Good sons, this King Candraprabha, during ten thousand kalpas in the past, under the Dharma of King Nāgaprabha, was a Bodhisattva of the fourth stage (*caturthabhūmi*), while I was a Bodhisattva of the eighth stage (*aṣṭamabhūmi*)."
Saṃgharakṣita now utters a great lion’s roar before me.

This section has two parts: first, he addresses the assembly; second, he informs those who have truly attained the fruits of the Path that they do so through expedient practice, for they do not know the true origin and manifestation of Candraprabha.
Therefore, he says to them: "Good sons, beneath this Candraprabha... [The following two points are then set forth.]
In the past, at Longguang Temple, he was the fourth-stage Bodhisattva Yanhui, while I was the eighth-stage Bodhisattva Denguan.
Now that I have attained Buddhahood, Yueguang has become the Bodhisattva Fayun. How do we know this is so?
Because the Lion’s Roar is called the "Definitive Teaching," and none but those of the tenth stage can endure it. Furthermore, [it is stated thus] in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*.
It praises the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages, saying they are able to roar the lion’s roar and their fame is heard throughout the ten directions.
Second, the descriptive praise:
"Just so, just so! As you have understood it, you have attained the true meaning; this teaching is inconceivable and immeasurable."
"Only Buddhas and Buddhas know this matter.
First, he praises the teaching spoken by King Adhimukta as being in accord with the principles it expounds; because the teaching and its underlying principles correspond, he repeats "Thus" (*evam*).
From the ninth stage downward, this cannot be conceived by mind or discussed by speech. Next, he clarifies the understanding.

The *Prajñāpāramitā* states: "Only Buddhas and Buddhas know this matter. There are those who interpret this as "it is not [known] by Buddhas," but rather that "only when you understand this do you become equal to the stage of a Buddha. It is not as if Bodhisattvas do not pose such questions.
The second section, the praise of the Dharma taught, has three parts: first, the actual praise; second, the exhortation to practice;
and third, the offerings of the great assembly. The first part [the actual praise] has three sub-sections: first, explaining that it is inconceivable; second, explaining that it is immeasurable;

and third, explaining that only a Buddha knows it. The first of these [inconceivable] has three further divisions: first, a brief exposition; second, a hypothetical inquiry; and third, a detailed explanation.
First: Good son, that which he has taught— the fourteen *prajñāpāramitās*, the thirty *kṣāntis* of the stages of the earth (bhūmi) categorized as superior,
middling, and inferior, the treasury of all practices, the treasury of all Buddhas, and the inconceivable— is [as follows].
Section Four: One, Designating the Number—referring to the fourteen types of *prajñā*. Three, Matching the Stages below—referring to the three grades of patience (*kṣānti*).

The three grades of patience refer to the three categories of the Patience of Subjugation (*vinaya-kṣānti*): the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*), the ten stages of cessation (*samatha*), and the ten stages of firm resolve (*adhyāśaya-citta*).

Regarding the thirty types of patience from the first stage (*bhūmi*) through the tenth stage: from the initial stage up to the tenth stage, each possesses the three grades of superior, intermediate, and inferior; thus, the ten stages constitute thirty [types of patience].
"Patience" refers to the "repository of all practices," which is subsumed under the three repositories. The "repository of all practices" refers to the thirteen patiences (*kṣānti*).
The "repository of all Buddhas" refers to the supreme tranquility (*śānti*). Because these two encompass all merits, they are called "repositories.
"Inconceivable" refers to the fourth summary of the inconceivable.
Second, the provisional inquiry into the two treasuries.
Why is this? It is precisely because one inquires into the two treasuries of the Buddha of Practice.
The third section, the extensive explanation of the text based on its meaning, has three parts: first, clarifying the inconceivability with respect to the Buddha;
second, explaining the inconceivability by combining the two baskets; and third, concluding the inconceivability of both baskets.
This is the first part.

All Buddhas are born within this, cease within this, and manifest transformations within this; yet they are without birth, cessation, or transformation, being without self and without other, supreme and non-dual.
They are neither transformed nor untransformed, neither non-existent nor possessing marks, and are without coming or going, for they are like empty space.

The text has two parts: first, clarifying that there is no arising or ceasing with respect to the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body); second, a further explanation in response to objections. Regarding the first part, there are two sections:

first, the establishment; second, the refutation. Regarding the first [the establishment]: the *dharmakāya* is without marks, yet for the sake of sentient beings, it takes form in the royal palace and undergoes extinction at the twin śāla trees, manifesting birth and death to transform living beings.
Yet, as for its lack of birth and death, the following two [sections] refute [any limitation], showing that its function is all-pervasive. Its...

Because its essence is utterly quiescent, there is no arising or ceasing; because there is no transformation, there is neither self nor other. Below, the difficulties are addressed through a repeated explanation, first by means of the Dharma and then by means of a simile.

Regarding the former: since both "self" and "other" have perished, there is neither self nor other; since both object and wisdom are severed, there is no duality. Because it is the supreme Middle Way, it is the foremost.
Thus, movement itself is quiescence, and therefore it is not a transformation; quiescence itself is movement, and therefore it is not a transformation.

"Neither non-transformation nor the absence of signlessness" explains away hidden doubts. Fearing that people, upon hearing that there is no birth-and-death or transformation, might conclude that there are no supramundane dharmas of signlessness, he clarifies their doubt by saying: "It is not that signlessness does not exist, nor that coming and going do not exist;
rather, because one seeks coming and going and they cannot be found, one says 'no coming and going. It is just like this.
"Space" is the second metaphorical illustration.

Second, the combined explanation of the two *piṭakas* clarifying the inconceivable; this section has two parts: first, the explanation, and second, the conclusion. Within the explanation, there are two parts:
first, distinguishing the inconceivable through the contrast between person and dharma; second, distinguishing the inconceivable through the contrast between object and wisdom.

Regarding the first of the two [sections] on the initial and subsequent [analyses], there are two parts: first, clarifying the emptiness of persons; second, clarifying the emptiness of phenomena. Now, for the first:
all sentient beings are without arising or ceasing, without bondage or liberation, neither cause nor effect, yet not without cause or effect;
because they are devoid of afflictions, self, person, cognition, views, the experiencer, and what belongs to the self, they are empty of the practice of all suffering.

The text has two parts: first, the emptiness of sentient beings is distinguished by means of three meanings; second, the emptiness of self and person is distinguished by means of various names. This is the first part. Regarding the "three meanings":
first, there is neither arising nor ceasing; second, there is neither bondage nor liberation; third, there is neither cause-and-effect nor non-cause-and-effect.

Because the meaning of "sentient being" is unobtainable, one is free from suffering and thus there is no arising or ceasing; because one is free from the origin [of suffering], there is no bondage or liberation.

There is neither bondage nor liberation; being free from accumulation, it is not a cause, and being free from suffering, it is not a fruit. Although it is neither cause nor fruit, cause and fruit are nonetheless manifest;

therefore, it is said that it is not the case that there is no cause and fruit. Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "Form is empty; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty.
Since the five aggregates are empty, by what means would one undergo birth? Thus, there is no birth. Since there is no birth, how could there be [suffering]?
Regarding "because of cessation, there is neither cessation, nor bondage, nor liberation," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Taishō 1509), fascicle 51, states:
"The five aggregates are neither bound nor liberated. If they are ultimately empty and there is no agent, who is bound and who is liberated?
Because the dharmas of ordinary persons are false and unobtainable, they are not bound; because the [dharmas of] noble ones are ultimately unobtainable, they are not liberated," and so forth.
Because the Bodhisattva dwelling in this path is not dragged down by the various afflictions (*kleśa*) into the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), it is said that he is "not bound.
Because he does not destroy the afflictions by means of the various outflow-free dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*), it is said that he is "not liberated. This is as explained in detail there.
The Vaiśeṣikas reckon the self (*ātman*) to be the agent, which they call the cause; the Sāṃkhyas reckon the self to be the experiencer, which they call the fruit. Now, as for my [view]...

Since they are empty, they are not truly cause and effect. Because the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is non-existent while the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) exists, it is said that they are "not non-cause-and-effect.

Regarding the afflictions, self, and person: the latter two [sections] distinguish the emptiness of self and person through the various names for the self and the aggregates. This section has two parts: first, the explicit clarification of the emptiness of self;
second, the clarification of the emptiness of what belongs to the self (*ātmīya*). Now, for the first part, there are five sections: 1. Self; 2. Persons; 3. Knowledge.
Regarding the four views, the five aggregates of grasping, and "what belongs to me" (*mamakāra*): next, it clarifies that what belongs to me is empty.

All painful feelings (*duḥkhavedanā*) are called the suffering of suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*); pleasant feelings (*sukhavedanā*) are called the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*); and neutral feelings (*upekṣāvedanā*) are called the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāraduḥkhatā*).
Since these three are all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) and are equally phenomena belonging to me, it is said that all painful feelings are empty of the nature of conditioned formations.
Therefore, secondly, it clarifies the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*):

all phenomena are a collection of illusory and transformative five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), neither joining nor dispersing; as phenomena are identical to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), they are quiescent and empty.
The "assemblage of all dharmas" refers to the conventional designation (*prajñapti*) formed by the collective arising of causes and conditions;

this is the conventionality of names. The "illusory five aggregates" means that the five aggregates lack substantial reality; this is the conventionality of dharmas. "Neither combining nor dispersing" refers to the conventionality of sensation (*vedanā*).

Because they arise together through causes and conditions, there is no dispersal; because causes and conditions are themselves empty, there is no combination. That "dharmas are identical to the dharma-nature" [is as follows]:...
All phenomena are identical in their nature to True Suchness (*tathatā*), because they are fundamentally quiescent and empty.

Second, the inconceivable is distinguished through the mutual relation of object and wisdom. This section has two parts: first, distinguishing the emptiness of the object; second, explaining the emptiness of wisdom.
Now, the first part.

The realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) is empty, empty, signless, non-turning, non-inverted, not conforming to illusion, devoid of the Three Jewels, devoid of sages, and devoid of the six realms of existence, because it is like space.
This passage has two parts: first the teaching, then the metaphor. Within the teaching, the statement that "the realm of phenomena is empty" clarifies universal emptiness, meaning the first...
There is not a single dharma that is not empty. Regarding "emptiness is signlessness," the following two sections clarify the specific emptinesses.
First, it clarifies the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*): "Emptiness" refers to the samādhi of emptiness; "signlessness" refers to the samādhi of signlessness.

"Non-turning" means that the defiled dharmas of suffering and its origin cannot be transformed into the pure dharmas of the outflows-free (*anāsrava*). Furthermore, within the gate of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), there is no sign.
Because they do not meet, they are called empty; because the markless mark cannot be moved, they are called non-turning; because they are free from delusion, they are without inversion;
because they are free from attachment, they are called non-conforming; and because one knows all phenomena are empty, they are called illusory transformations.

Regarding the absence of the Three Jewels, the two pairs manifest the emptiness of both persons and phenomena. Regarding the absence of sages and the six realms, the three clarify the emptiness of persons. As it says:
"Space" is used as a double metaphor. Second, it explains the emptiness of wisdom (*jñāna*).
Prajñā is without knowing and without seeing; it does not function, does not take objects, has no cause, is not received, and is not attained—it is the universal reflection of all things.

Therefore, the characteristics of practicing the Way are like the characteristics of empty space. Since the characteristics of dharmas are thus, how could there be a mind that attains or a mind that does not attain?

[The text] has three parts: the Dharma, the analogy, and the application; here begins the first. Because one knows there is nothing, it is said "no knowledge"; because one sees there is nothing, it is said "no seeing."

Because one does not engage in the dharma of arising and ceasing, one is untainted by ignorance and conditions; furthermore, because one contemplates that both conditions and [the object] are quiescent, it is said "one does not engage" and "one does not condition.
Because one does not arise from causes, it is said "not from causes. Because there is no dharma that can be received, it is said "non-reception.
As for the statement "not obtaining any marks of appearance," how could this mean being without mind, lacking knowledge, or failing to see due to a lack of causes? It is simply because...

This is because, through principle-contemplation (*li-guan*), [the mind] is found to be unattainable. This is the first section on the characteristics of the path. Next, the second section provides an analogy.

Regarding the third section, which states that the characteristics of phenomena (*fa-xiang*) are thus: since both mind and object are empty, how could there be a mind? Since both mind and object are provisional (*jia*), how could there be no mind?
There are two bonds.
Therefore, the merit of prajñā cannot be practiced by acting among sentient beings; it cannot be practiced by acting among the dharmas of the five aggregates;
it cannot be practiced by acting within objects; and it cannot be practiced by acting within liberation.
The text for the four preceding meanings constitutes four "inabilities": the inability [to find a self] among sentient beings, which concludes with the emptiness of persons;

the inability [to find a self] among phenomena, which concludes with the emptiness of dharmas; the inability [to find a self] among objects, which concludes with the emptiness of objects; and the inability [to find a self] among understandings, which concludes with the emptiness of wisdom.
The third pair concerns the inconceivability of the two baskets (*piṭaka*).
Therefore, the *Prajñāpāramitā* is inconceivable; furthermore, because all bodhisattvas practice therein, they too are inconceivable.
Moreover, the transformation manifested by all Tathāgatas within the illusory and non-abiding dharmas is also inconceivable.
The Discussion. Part One: A General Conclusion Based on Wisdom, beginning with "And all... Part Two: A Specific Conclusion Regarding Persons, beginning with "All Tathāgatas...
Part One: Clarifying that Bodhisattvas practice non-practice, which is inconceivable. Part Two: Clarifying... [text ends]
The Buddhas manifest through non-manifestation in an inconceivable manner.
Second, the explanation of the aforementioned "immeasurable":
"Good son, this treasury of merit, even if it were as infinite as the sands of the Ganges, [is opened by] the twelfth consecration."
The Licchavi Vimalakīrti said: "Of these merits, that which the King has described is like a single drop of water in the great ocean;
that which the Bodhisattva of the Tenth Ground has described is like a single drop in the ocean; that which Candraprabha has described is like the great ocean itself;

and furthermore, that which the King has described is like a single drop in the ocean, while that which the Bodhisattva of the Tenth Ground has described is like the great ocean. [The Licchavi asked: "With what intention did the King speak thus?"
The Bodhisattva Śūra replied to the king: "How can the Ground of Original Non-existence (Mūlābhāva-bhūmi) be known?
Thirdly, the explanation above states that only a Buddha can know it.
I shall now briefly describe its partial meaning and merits; it brings great benefit to all sentient beings and is for the sake of those in the past."

The merits of King Candraprabha’s portion of meaning have been described and approved by the countless Tathāgatas of the past and present, and praised beyond measure by the three classes of worthies and ten stages of sages;
because the immeasurable virtues of Candraprabha are exhausted even by this brief summary, they are called "a portion of the meaning."

The second section, the exhortation to practice, consists of three parts: first, the formal praise and exhortation to practice; second, the inquiry; and third, the detailed explanation. This is the first part.

"Good son, these fourteen dharma-gates have been practiced by all sentient beings of the three periods of time, by all those of the three vehicles, and by all Buddhas; future Buddhas shall likewise do so. If all Buddhas..."
It is impossible that a bodhisattva could attain *sarvajñā* by means other than this gateway.
The preceding section clarifies the self-cultivation of both ordinary beings and sages; the section beginning with "If all [beings]" below is a formal exhortation to practice.
Second, the inquiry:
"For what reason?
Third, the detailed explanation.
Because there is no divergent path for all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, therefore, O sons of good family, if there be anyone who hears these Dharma-gates of patience—

namely, the patience of faith, the patience of tranquility, the patience of firmness, the patience of excellent awakening, the patience of penetrating detachment, the patience of clear wisdom, the patience of flaming wisdom,

the patience of supreme wisdom, the patience of the manifestation of dharmas, the patience of far-reaching penetration, the patience of equal awakening, and the patience of the light of wisdom— [they shall attain liberation].

Those who have received the empowerment and attained the patience of perfect enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi-kṣānti) have transcended hundreds and thousands of kalpas, as numerous as the sands of immeasurable Ganges Rivers,
and having passed through the hardships of birth after birth, they enter this Dharma-gate and attain their fruition in the present body.
Section on the Text: Part One, Subsection One, Marking the Correct Path. The previous section was titled "The Gate" because it is unimpeded;

the current section is titled "The Path" because it is able to lead through. Therefore, regarding all that follows, the correct path of the two vehicles below should be studied by relying upon the fourteen patiences (*kṣānti*).
This person transcends the three lower levels. Raising up the fruit to praise its excellence, there are two benefits: first, the departure from suffering; second, [the attainment of bliss].
They attained bliss.
At the time of the third great assembly offering,
ten billion Bodhisattvas named Gaganagañjāsāgara within the multitude, each rejoicing in the joy of the Dharma, [individually...]
Flowers scattered into the void transformed into immeasurable flower pedestals, upon which immeasurable multitudes spoke of the fourteen right practices (*caturdaśa-samyak-pratipatti*).
The kings of the eighteen Brahma heavens and the six desire heavens also scattered precious flowers;

each sat upon a flower pedestal in the void and spoke of the fourteen right practices, upholding, reciting, and explaining their principles and meanings. Immeasurable spirits and deities manifested their forms.
The practice of the *prajñāpāramitā* is presented in three sections:
first, the merit of the Bodhisattva’s offerings; next, the offerings of the devas; and finally, the practice of the ghosts and spirits.

This proceeds from the superior to the inferior. Thus far, the first and second questions have been answered, concluding the discussion on practices for one's own benefit and for the benefit of others.
The second major section: The response concerning the characteristics of the sentient beings to be converted. This section consists of three parts: first, restating the previous question;
second, the formal response; and third, the benefits obtained.
Herein begins the first part. The Buddha said to the Great King: "As you previously asked, what are the characteristics of the sentient beings who can be converted?"
Reiterating the previous question: what kind of sentient beings can be transformed?
Part Two: The Direct Answer, which has two sections—the brief and the extensive. Now, the first:
if one perceives illusory transformation-bodies as being illusory transformations themselves, this is the true practice of a Bodhisattva in transforming sentient beings.

Since both the transformer and the transformed are born of causes and conditions, both are illusory transformations. One who can act in this way is truly practicing the transformation of sentient beings;
as the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* says: "It is like an illusory person preaching the Dharma for illusory people."

The second part, the extensive answer, has two sections: first, clarifying that the objects of transformation are like an illusion; second, clarifying that the transformers are like an illusion. The first section has two parts: first, the explanation; second, the conclusion.

Within the first part, there are six sections corresponding to the six provisional designations (*prajñapti*). First is the explanation of the provisional designation of phenomena (*dharma-prajñapti*), which has two sub-sections:

first, the direct clarification of the provisional designation of phenomena; second, the clarification of the differences between the objects of ordinary beings and sages. The first of these [sub-sections] further has two parts. One.
It clarifies that the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) is capable of producing both form and mind.
At the very first moment of a sentient being’s consciousness, this consciousness differs from wood or stone; it gives rise to innate goodness and innate evil.

Evil serves as the basis for immeasurable evil consciousnesses, while goodness serves as the basis for immeasurable good consciousnesses. From the first moment of gold-like adamancy (*vajra*) until the final moment, within this [process], [the fundamental consciousness persists].
The birth of unspeakably unspeakable numbers of consciousnesses constitutes the form and mind of sentient beings.

This fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna) is the正因佛性 (direct cause of Buddha-nature); it differs from wood or stone, being neither existent nor non-existent, neither knowing nor forgetting, and possesses a nature like the moisture of water, the heat of fire, or the gold-essence within yellow stone—existing only in accordance with objective conditions.

Differences arise such that encountering a favorable environment produces goodness, while encountering an unfavorable environment produces evil, even leading to the formation of bodies in the hells and so forth.
From the very first moment until the diamond-like samādhi (*vajropama-samādhi*), throughout this interval, there arise unspeakable numbers of wholesome and unwholesome mental and physical states.
As a great sūtra says: "The medicinal herbs of the Snowy Mountains are of but one flavor; yet according to where they flow, they take on various kinds."
The name "seed" refers to its true and authentic flavor, which remains steadfast and cannot be overwhelmed by the groves of yam fruits.
One asks: Do all sentient beings have a fundamental limit (*pūrvakoṭi*)? If one says they do, why does the *Madhyama Āgama* state that the fundamental limit of sentient beings cannot be found?
The answer is briefly twofold: first, it cannot be spoken of within the realm of ultimate principle (*tattva*).
Regarding the afflictions and the body, there are two preceding and succeeding points of discussion, which include the passage stating that "a single moment of consciousness arises.
Second, it clarifies how form and mind constitute the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and so forth; this section has two parts, the first of which establishes the five aggregates.

The fundamental substance of sentient beings consists of the coverings of form (*rūpa-āvaraṇa*), mind (*citta-āvaraṇa*), perception (*saṃjñā-āvaraṇa*), feeling (*vedanā-āvaraṇa*), and formations (*saṃskāra-āvaraṇa*). "Covering" (*āvaraṇa*) functions as an obscuration or concealment;
"body" (*kāya*) is named for its accumulation [of elements].

The first point of red and white [semen and blood] is called the covering of form; because of the power of karmic formations, consciousness (*vijñāna*) takes refuge therein, which is called the covering of consciousness.

This refers to opening the mind regarding the four hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*); "hindrance" means that which covers over, which is the meaning of "aggregate" (*skandha*). The aggregates are so called because they cover over;
the hindrances are likewise. As for the body being called an "accumulation," it is because this body is composed of thirty-six constituent substances.
Second, explaining the establishment of the twelve bases (*āyatana*).

Great King, this single dharma of form gives rise to immeasurable forms: that which is apprehended by the eye is "form," that which is apprehended by the ear is "sound," that which is apprehended by the nose is "odor," that which is apprehended by the tongue is "taste," and that which is apprehended by the body is "tangible. That which is firm and stable is called "earth," and that which is moistening is called "water."

Heat is called fire; lightness and movement are called wind; that which serves as the basis for the arising of the five consciousnesses is called a faculty (*indriya*). In this way, within a single form and a single mind, there are inconceivable forms and minds.
The text has three parts. First, it clarifies how a single form gives rise to immeasurable forms—namely, how the five sense objects and the four great elements give rise to the five consciousnesses.

Regarding the term "bases" (*āyatana*), there are two explanations for how they constitute the five sense-faculties (*indriya*): because they are derived from the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and can give rise to the five consciousnesses, they are called faculties.
Thus, one form and the following three [categories] summarize that one form gives rise to the five objects and the five faculties;
the four great elements do not clarify the form within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*). When the mind moves, it generates thought within the twelve spheres (*dvādaśāyatana*).
Among the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), those that can give rise to the six consciousnesses and the space element (*ākāśadhātu*) are omitted from the explanation.
Second, it clarifies the differences between the objects of ordinary beings and noble ones (*ārya*).
Great King, because the six consciousnesses of ordinary worldlings are coarse, they perceive immeasurable conventional forms such as blue, yellow, square, and round;
because the six consciousnesses of noble ones are pure, they perceive real dharmas, namely all real form-dharmas such as visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility.
The text has two parts: first, it clarifies that ordinary realms are all provisional; second, it clarifies that the realms of the sages are real. The first part is readily understandable.
Regarding the six consciousnesses of the sages, the following section clarifies that although the provisional names of the sage-realms are one, their perceptions differ from those of ordinary beings.

While ordinary beings falsely perceive and cling to impermanent form (*anitya-rūpa*), sages extinguish this impermanent form and attain permanent form (*nitya-rūpa*); this is the intended meaning of the *Bie* (Distinct) and *Yuan* (Perfect) teachings.
The second clarifies the conventional designation of "sentient beings.

"Sentient beings" is a name in the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Whether they exist or do not exist, the mere arising of the mental recollection of "sentient beings" is called conventional truth.
Because conventional truth is provisional, deceptive, and illusory, it exists; thus, even within the six realms of existence, illusory sentient beings perceive illusions.

The transformation of illusions—seeing illusions as Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, devas, and so forth, including our own form and mind—is called the "Illusion Truth" (māyā-satya). This passage consists of four sections:
first, it relates to the two truths; second, it clarifies existence and non-existence; third, it relates to the six realms of existence; and fourth, it relates to the four castes. Now...

First, the preceding section clarifies that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are merely provisional designations of phenomena (*dharma-prajñapti*); that there is a "sentient being" is a provisional designation of a person (*pudgala-prajñapti*).

From the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), they exist; from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), they do not. Regarding "existence or non-existence," the following two sections clarify existence and non-existence:
externalists take substantial reality as existence and vacuity as non-existence; this is the root of the sixty-two views (*dvāṣaṣṭi-dṛṣṭi*). It is merely the arising of sentient beings...

The first section, "Giving rise to recollection," explains that there is a reason for this: ordinary people falsely conceptualize that there is a recipient [of sensation], whereas the noble ones see sensation as being like a magical illusion;

this is all based on contrasting the noble with the ordinary. The second section, "Extending even to the six realms," thirdly clarifies the conventional nature of sensation by means of the six realms.
The fourth section, "Seeing magical illusions as magical illusions," concerns what is seen by those of the four castes. As for the term "seeing" mentioned therein:

"Illuminating the true as an illusory transformation" refers to a person transformed from the unreal into the real; "the illusory is true" refers to the person of the Distinct Teaching (*bhedavyavahāra*). This clarifies the provisional nature of the recipient (*pratigrahaka*) in terms of both the transformer (*nirmātṛ*) and the transformed.

Third, the explanation of the provisional nature of names has two parts: first, clarifying that there was no name prior to the Buddha; second, clarifying that the Buddha established the name for them.

First: In the reality of illusion, before a Buddha appeared in the world, there were no names and no meanings. It was called an illusory dharma, a magical transformation, devoid of names and lacking essence or characteristics.
There were no names for the three realms, no names for the retributions of good and evil, and no names for the six paths of existence.
Section One: Threefold Exposition. First, clarifying that there is no referent for names, which explains that before the Buddha appeared in the world, there were no Great Sages to speak them;

thus, names are provisional. Furthermore, illusory phenomena and transformations—this second point clarifies that there is no essence corresponding to names. Zhaoming states: "Names lack the power to apprehend things, and things lack the reality to correspond to names.
Regarding the absence of the three realms and six paths—this third point clarifies that there is no existence within the three realms and six destinies.
Furthermore, secondly, it clarifies that the Buddha establishes names for beings.
Great King, for this reason, each Buddha appears in the world for the sake of sentient beings, teaching them regarding the three realms and the six paths of existence.
Names are called "immeasurable names," such as the dharmas of space, the four great elements, mental dharmas, and material dharmas.

The text has two parts: first, the Buddha establishes names which are complete with knowledge and are conventional designations; this is what is meant by "immeasurable. Second, it concludes that names are not singular.
Fourth is the continuity of manifestation.

The conventionally designated phenomenon of continuity is neither identical nor different; it is not continuous as an identity, nor is it continuous as a difference. Because it is neither identical nor different, it is called the Truth of Continuity.
Section on the Text: Part One, Establishing the Thesis (1); Part Two, Explanation (2). Regarding "neither continuous" (亦不續): it is not continuous because [the cause] is one;
it is also not continuous because [the effect] is distinct. As for "neither one nor different" (非一非異), the following three points conclude the argument accordingly.
This is like a sprout and its stem, which cannot be said to be either one or different.
Fifth is the conventional designation of mutual dependence (*apekṣā-prajñapti*).
All phenomena that are conventionally designated through mutual dependence are called "dependent" and are also called "indeterminate dependence," such as the five colors and so forth.
Regarding existence, non-existence, and all such phenomena, all dharmas are provisionally established through conditions and constitute sentient beings.
Within this passage, there are two meanings regarding all things being mutually dependent. First, regarding "mutual avoidance" (*parihāra*), the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states:
"If a phenomenon is established through dependence, that phenomenon itself becomes dependent. Phenomena such as the five colors are examples of mutual relativity;
their relativity is like the eye seeing form or the ear hearing sound. As for the relativity of long and short, this refers to mutual dependence through comparison (*apekṣā*).
Furthermore, all phenomena are conventionally established through conditions; the five aggregates and other such phenomena serve as conditions to conventionally establish sentient beings.
Sixth is the explanation of conventional establishment through causal production:
simultaneous cause and effect, sequential cause and effect, and the good and evil of the three periods of time.
For example, the five fruits and three causes are simultaneous cause and effect; the two past causes and the five present fruits are asynchronous cause and effect.
Furthermore, the condition of seeing is a simultaneous observing cause, while the observed object is an asynchronous cause.
Moreover, the beams and rafters forming a house are simultaneous, whereas the twelve periods of time constituting a day are asynchronous. Finally, the lamp and its light are simultaneous.
Darkness and light exist at different times.
These two fetters are merely provisional designations.
All illusory transformations are the sentient beings of the illusory truth.
This first clarifies that the emanated is like an illusion.
Second, it clarifies that the emanator is like an illusion:
"Great King, if a bodhisattva perceives all sentient beings as illusory transformations as described above—merely false deceptions like those in space—"
The Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes and the Buddhas, with their five eyes, see that all things are like illusions; thus they truly perceive how Bodhisattvas transform sentient beings.
Because Bodhisattvas see that sentient beings are unreal—just as one with a diseased eye sees flowers in the sky—sentient beings do not realize this.
Therefore, it was proclaimed that all these were the power and function of the Bodhisattva.
During this third period, the assembly attained benefits:
at that time, immeasurable sons of heaven and the great multitude attained the patience of subduing [the afflictions], and attained the patience of emptiness and non-arising.
This includes the unspeakable virtues from the first bhūmi through the tenth bhūmi.
The text has two parts: first, it clarifies the attainment of patience, referring to the stages prior to the bhūmis as well as the bhūmis themselves; second, it clarifies the virtues of the bhūmis.

In the *Buddhabhāṣita-rāṣṭrapāla-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, Chapter Four, "The Two Truths" (*Dvayasatya-varga*), Part One, within the section on "Internal Protection," there are three distinct divisions. Now, this "Two Truths" chapter is the third, clarifying the basis upon which the two types of protection rely.

As for the "Two Truths," they constitute the great mainstay of the Buddha’s teaching: the truth of reality (*satya*) and the truth of illusion (*māyā*). There is a distinction between them, and one enters [the path] through them.

The seven types—such as the universal entry into the universal and distinct teachings, and the universal entry into the distinct and universal teachings—are explained in detail in the *Fahua Xuanyi* (Treatise on the Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra), and so forth.

However, because the vision of ordinary beings is shallow, it is called "conventional" (*sāṃvṛti*); because the vision of sages is deep, it is called "real" (*bhūta*). Because they are examined and verified, they are called "truths" (*satya*).
Furthermore, the preceding "Chapter on Contemplating Emptiness" clarifies that both true wisdom (*tattvajñāna*) and expedient wisdom (*upāyajñāna*) are empty, yet they protect all [beings].

Since those who have not yet attained realization must necessarily practice transformation, and such transformation must have its basis—namely, the Two Truths—it is for this reason that they are clarified here.
The text of this chapter consists of two parts: first, the question and answer; second, the exhortation to uphold [the teaching]. The first part has three sections:

first, clarifying the non-duality of the Two Truths; second, clarifying the non-duality of preaching the Dharma; third, clarifying the non-duality of the Dharma-gates. The first of these has two sub-sections: first, the question; second, the answer.
Answer: First, at that time King Prasenajit said: "Is there conventional truth within ultimate truth? If one says there is not, then wisdom should not be twofold;
if one says there is, then wisdom should not be single. What is the meaning of this duality and unity?"
The inquiry consists of three parts. First, the dual introduction: from "At that time" (*tadā*) onwards, as one is about to formulate an objection, two questions are raised.

Second, "If one says they do not exist," and so forth, which constitutes the dual refutation. Someone says: "If one says they do not exist, then the wisdom of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) should not be twofold—namely, the two truths of the ultimate (*paramārtha-satya*) and the conventional (*saṃvṛti-satya*). If one says they do exist, then the wisdom of the noble ones (*ārya*) should not be singular."
This is precisely the primary meaning (*paramārtha*). Now, it is said: if one says "existence" exists, one should not say that both existence and non-existence are empty;
if one says "non-existence," one should not differentiate between the two views of existence and non-existence. The meaning of "one" and "two" concludes the three pairs below.
II. The Text of the Response, Part One: III. The Direct Response, II. Citing Scriptural Evidence, III. Explaining the Accomplishment. Now, for the first [the Direct Response]:
The Buddha addressed the Great King: "Regarding the one meaning and the two meanings you previously asked of the seven Buddhas of the past, you now do not listen and I now do not speak.
This absence of listening and speaking is itself the one meaning and the two meanings; therefore, listen attentively, listen attentively, and well!"
Reflecting upon this, practice according to the Dharma.
The text has three parts: first, praising the past causes of Candraprabha so that you may understand;

second, the formal response stating that both hearing and speaking are empty—thus they are non-dual—and yet hearing and speaking remain distinct—thus they are not one; therefore, listen attentively; third, the admonition.
This section encourages the cultivation of the three types of wisdom.
Second is the citation of scriptural evidence. The eight and a half lines of the verse are divided into three parts: the first three lines correctly extend the two truths;
the next three lines explain the meaning, which is the actual response to the question; and the final two and a half lines provide the conclusion.
The first of the superior meanings is as follows:
the seven Buddhas’ verses are thus.
The supreme ultimate truth is signless; it is not produced by self, nor produced by another, nor by causes and conditions; it is fundamentally self-existent, yet without self or other production.

The nature of phenomena is fundamentally without nature; it is the emptiness of the ultimate truth. Just as all existing things are fundamentally composed of dharmas gathered through the three provisional designations, they exist provisionally;
yet there is no true reality in non-existence, for cessation is the supreme emptiness. Such is the meaning of existence and non-existence regarding the dependent origination of all phenomena.

The prose section has three parts. First, one line clarifies the Two Truths of the Separate Teaching (*bhedavyavahāra*). The first half clarifies the True Truth (*paramārtha-satya*), which is emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and existence (*bhāva*);

the second half clarifies the Conventional Truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), which is emptiness and the possession of greatness. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "By whom was the twelvefold dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) created? The Buddha replied:
"It was not created by a Buddha, nor by a Bodhisattva, nor even by any of the holy ones (*ārya*). Therefore, it is said to be "without self" and "without [creator]."
The first line, "The nature of phenomena is fundamentally without nature," clarifies the Two Truths of the Shared Teaching (*samānyayāna*):

the first half clarifies the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*), and the second half clarifies the Conventional Truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Regarding the "three provisional designations," these are names given to phenomena based on reception.

The three lines beginning with "There is no non-existence" clarify the Two Truths of the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya-yāna*): there is no distinction between the conventional, which is one, and the ultimate, which is one. There is no separate conventional; it is one. There is no separate ultimate; it is one.

Because there is no [intrinsic nature], it is said that there is no truth of non-existence. The first two lines clarify the ultimate (paramārtha), the next line clarifies the conventional (saṃvṛti), and the final line provides a summary.
Second, the direct response to the objection clarifies neither identity nor difference.

Existence and non-existence are fundamentally two, like the two horns of an ox. When one illuminates and understands them, one sees that there is no duality; the two truths are eternally not identical.
Through the understanding-mind, one sees non-duality, and though one seeks duality, it cannot be found. This does not mean that the two truths are one rather than two—how could they be?
In understanding, there is always oneness; in the truths, there is always duality. To penetrate this non-duality is to truly enter the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
The textual explanation has three parts. First, one line clarifies the correspondence between wisdom (*jñāna*) and principle (*tattva*) to dispel the notions of identity and difference:
the first half clarifies non-duality, while the second half clarifies neither-identity-nor-difference (and so forth). Next, two lines clarify that the mind of understanding is non-dual;

through the correspondence of wisdom and principle, attachment is dispelled: the first half clarifies that when the mind of understanding seeks duality, it is unobtainable, while the second half clarifies the dispelling of clinging.
What is called "understanding" is seeing that both truths are empty; one then becomes attached to this emptiness. Since even duality cannot be found, how can non-duality be found?

In understanding, one always remains at the level of one [truth] below and three [aspects] above. This is the praise of entering the true meaning through the mutual correspondence of principle and wisdom.
The third [section] concludes the preceding meaning:
In conventional truth, illusory transformations arise like flowers in the sky, like shadows, or like a third hand; because they lack causes and conditions, they are deceptive.

There is the seeing of illusions, and sentient beings who see these illusions are called "illusory truths. When the illusionist sees the illusory phenomena, they are realized as being entirely non-existent.
The names of the Buddhas are thus, and the contemplation of the Bodhisattvas is likewise.

The first line clarifies existence and non-existence according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) through three metaphors: first, the example of flowers in the sky; second, the example of a reflection;
and third, the example of the three hands. Although these have no reality, they are not non-existent. As for the illusionist seeing the illusion, the following two [lines] explain this.

The first line clarifies that the holy vision perceives both existence and non-existence, which is termed "the contemplation of all Buddhas. The second half of the line clarifies the correct contemplation of the three fetters.
Third, the explanation of the text has two parts: first, clarifying two meanings; second, clarifying one meaning. This is the first [part].
Great King, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva constantly illuminates the two truths within a single reality to transform sentient beings:
he illuminates the conventional truth to transform ordinary people, and he illuminates the ultimate truth to transform those of the two vehicles.
Second, clarifying the single meaning; the text is divided into three parts. First, clarifying the single meaning through the mutual correspondence of subject and object:
The Buddha and sentient beings are one and not two. Why? Because sentient beings are empty, one can establish that awakening is empty;
because awakening is empty, one can establish that sentient beings are empty.
There are three [parts]: first, the heading; second, the inquiry; and third, the explanation. "Why is this? is the inquiry.

"Because sentient beings are empty" is the explanation, which establishes that emptiness of awakening (bodhi) is possible because of the emptiness of sentient beings; this explains the capacity of the Buddha to transform others.

Furthermore, "because awakening is empty" establishes that the emptiness of sentient beings is possible; this explains those who are transformed. Moreover, the emptiness of sentient beings refers to the emptiness of persons (pudgala-śūnyatā).
The emptiness of bodhi is the emptiness of dharmas.
These two—object and wisdom—are explained as having a single meaning in their mutual correspondence.
Because all dharmas are empty, even "emptiness" is empty. Why? Because Prajñā is signless, and the two truths are like space. Prajñā...
If emptiness is devoid of both self-characteristics and other-characteristics from ignorance up to omniscience (*sarvajñā*),
then when the five eyes are perfected, one sees nothing seen; one does not accept practice, nor non-practice,
nor neither practice nor non-practice, and so on, up to not accepting any phenomena whatsoever.

The text is divided into three parts: the heading, the inquiry, and the explanation. First, regarding the heading: "all dharmas" refers to both the object and the wisdom; because both are empty, it is called "emptiness of emptiness.
The phrase "Why is this so? constitutes the second part, the inquiry. In the explanation that follows, beginning with "Prajñā is signless," there are two sections.
The first is the direct explanation, the meaning of which is easily understood. The second begins with "Prajñā is empty of ignorance," and so forth.
To resolve this difficulty through a further explanation: since the characteristics of all things being empty are manifest and can be known, what distinction is there in the emptiness of Prajñā?
Therefore, the present explanation states that [the distinction] is clarified by tracing the path from ignorance (*avidyā*) up to the fruit of Buddhahood.

The text has two parts: first, the characteristics of emptiness are explained through the stages of delusion and awakening, which is easy to understand; second, [it is explained] at the time of the accomplishment of the five eyes (*pañca-cakṣus*).
The lower section, which clarifies the characteristics of emptiness based on the fruit of Buddhahood, consists of two parts. First, it explains that while there is no seeing, there is seeing;

the four eyes—fleshly, divine, and so forth—exist within the Buddha and are called the Buddha’s five eyes. Furthermore, it explains that even though there is no practice, there is practice, thereby departing from the five fallacies.
Third, the single meaning is clarified through the contrast between defilement and purity.
When a bodhisattva has not yet attained buddhahood, they take *bodhi* (enlightenment) to be affliction; when a bodhisattva has attained buddhahood, they take affliction to be *bodhi*.
Why is this? Because in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), they are non-dual. Thus, for all Buddhas and Tathāgatas...
Because all phenomena are as they are (*tathatā*).

In this passage, there are three parts: first, the thesis; second, the inquiry; and third, the explanation. First, the thesis: "is visible. Second, the inquiry: "Why is this so? Third, the explanation:
from "In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), they are non-dual" onwards. Although saṃsāra and bodhi are like light and darkness—appearing as two—they are empty.
It is non-dual. Second, the clarification of the non-duality of the teaching of the Dharma consists of two parts: first, the question, and second, the answer. Now, for the first:
he addressed the Buddha, saying, "How is it that the Tathāgatas of the ten directions and all bodhisattvas do not depart from words and letters yet practice [the Dharma]?"

Regarding the characteristics of all phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*): the intent of the question is this— if the emptiness and suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena are devoid of words and letters, for what reason do the noble ones employ them to teach and transform others?
The second part, the response, has two sections: first, explaining the teaching of emptiness; second, explaining the cultivation of emptiness. Now, for the first:

"Great King, the Wheel of Dharma consists of: the *Sūtra* (Dharma-discourse), the *Geya* (Repetition), the *Vyākaraṇa* (Prophecy), the *Gāthā* (Verses), the *Udāna* (Spontaneous Utterance), the *Nītiśastra* (Precepts), the *Avadāna* (Parables), the *Dharmatā* (Nature of Phenomena), the *Itivṛttaka* (Past Occurrences), the *Vaipulya* (Extensive Teachings), and the *Adbhutadharma* (Marvels)..."
In the past, there were those who engaged in doctrinal debates regarding names, phrases, syllables, sounds, fruits, letters, and recorded sentences;
if one grasps all such things as mere letters, one does not practice emptiness.
Section Three: Clarifying the Names of the Dharma-Wheel. There are generally two kinds of dharma-wheels: first, practice; second, the teaching.
The *sūtra* is the *sūtra-piṭaka*. The *geya* is the *geya-piṭaka*. The *vyākaraṇa* is the *vyākaraṇa-piṭaka*.
The *gāthā* is the *gāthā-piṭaka*, which does not consist of recited verses. The *udāna* is that which is spoken spontaneously without being questioned.
The *Sūtra on Precepts* (*Śīlasūtra*) is the *Nidāna-sūtra*; the *Avadāna* (Parables) is the *Apadāna-sūtra*;
the *Dharmadhātu* (Dharma Realm) is the *Itivṛttaka-sūtra*. As the *Mahāsūtra* states, the *Precepts* and *Vastu* (Past Events) are the *Vastusaṃgrahaṇī* (or *Jātaka-sūtra*);
the *Vaipulya* (Extensive) is the *Vaipulya-sūtra*; and the *Adbhuta* (Marvelous) is the *Adbhuta-dharma-sūtra*.
The *Dharmapada* is the Sūtra; the *Upadeśa* is the Treatise (*Śāstra*). These twelve are all empty, which is precisely Suchness (*tathatā*).
This is called the emptiness of names, phrases, and sentences. The following two sections clarify the emptiness of the teaching:

by taking the sounds of this land as the Buddha-work, and because the nature of written characters is detached [from inherent existence], they are all Suchness. "If one grasps at written characters" introduces the third section, clarifying non-practice.
To view emptiness as empty is not the King’s contemplation.
Second, the explanation of the cultivation of emptiness has three parts; first, the analysis of its practice:
"Great King, suchness is the letter that cultivates the mother of the wisdom of all Buddhas, the fundamental wisdom-mother of the nature of all sentient beings."

This is the very essence of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge). Before the Buddhas have attained Buddhahood, they take the future Buddha as the mother of wisdom; that which is not yet attained constitutes its nature, while that which has already been attained is *sarvajñā*.

The text has two parts: first, it clarifies the causal stage, wherein wisdom arises from the teaching, and thus the teaching is the mother of wisdom; furthermore, emptiness is like written characters.
Because letters are like space, they are called "suchness" (*tathatā*). Because this suchness can give rise to the Buddha-wisdom, it is called the "mother of wisdom.

Regarding the phrase "all sentient beings": the following two points clarify the state of fruition. When [the potential] resides within the bodies of sentient beings, it is called the "Buddha-nature";

when it resides within the body of a Buddha, it is named "omniscience" (*sarvajñatā*). Since one has not yet attained Buddhahood, one must necessarily attain it; because one will certainly be able to attain it, [it is so designated].
The name "Mother" refers to the stage before one has attained the Way, which is called Buddha-nature; once the Way has been attained, it is called All-Knowledge (sarvajñā).
Second, a further explanation in response to an objection.
The Prajñā of the three vehicles is neither born nor extinguished; its self-nature is eternally abiding, for all sentient beings take this as their awakened nature.

If a bodhisattva is without reception and without words—transcending words yet not being non-words—and practices non-practice as practice, then one who practices with words attains the true nature of Prajñā, the Prajñāpāramitā.

This refers to what was previously stated: "the mother of Buddha-wisdom" and "the fundamental wisdom-mother of nature. Fearing that others might find this difficult to understand, the text now provides a further explanation in two parts:
first, the explanation of the nature of principle (li-xing); second, the explanation of the nature of practice (xing-xing).

Regarding principle, it is the mother of suchness-wisdom (*tathatā-jñāna*). First, the explanation of the nature of principle: this refers to the aforementioned "fundamental wisdom-mother. If a bodhisattva lacks... [the following is] the explanation of the nature of practice.
Suchness is the mother of wisdom; if a bodhisattva studies without words and practices without practice, they immediately attain true wisdom, which is prajñā.
Thus, the three fetters are perfected through cultivation.
Great King, if a bodhisattva protects the Buddha, protects the transformation of sentient beings, and protects the practices of the ten stages, it is as follows.
Third, the Dharma-gate of Non-duality: first the question, then the answer; now, the former.
He addressed the Buddha, saying: "The faculties of the immeasurable classes of beings are also immeasurable, and their practices are also immeasurable.
Are the dharma-gates one, two, or immeasurable?
In this inquiry, there are three parts: first, the question regarding the faculties; second, the question regarding the practices; and third, [the question regarding] whether the dharma-gates are...

This is the Dharma-gate of the Three Questions Following One Inquiry. Furthermore, the intent of the question is as follows: since the faculties, natures, and dispositions of sentient beings differ, are the contemplative gates taught for them one or two?
Second, the text of the answer has three parts: first, a brief answer; second, an extensive answer; and finally, a concluding answer.
"Great King, the gateways for contemplating all dharmas are neither one nor two, but are immeasurable;
furthermore, all dharmas possess neither marks nor are they without marks.

This passage has two parts: first, the clarification of the gateways of contemplation, and second, the clarification of the dharmas to be contemplated. Regarding the first part, the text is easily understood: "Furthermore... [and so forth].

The first part clarifies that the phenomena under observation are neither characterized by existence, because their characteristics are not real, nor characterized by non-existence, because they are not devoid of emptiness and thus avoid the fault [of nihilism].
The second part provides a detailed response.
If a bodhisattva perceives sentient beings as seeing one or seeing two, they do not see one nor do they see two;
this "one and two" is the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya). Great King, that which is "existence" or "non-existence" is the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
Because all phenomena are subsumed within the three truths—the truth of emptiness, the truth of form, and the truth of mind—I say that all phenomena do not transcend these three truths. I...
People know and see that the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*) are empty, up to and including the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarva-dharma-śūnyatā*).

The text has three parts: first, it clarifies [the distinction] by means of the two truths; second, it shows that when a bodhisattva contemplates sentient beings, this is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*);
third, it shows that not seeing "one" or "two" is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Since the conventional is itself empty, it is said that non-duality is the ultimate truth.

Whether "existence" or "non-existence," these are the very roots of all views and are termed the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Regarding the two [truths] within the three truths, the three truths are used to reveal all phenomena.
Some say that "emptiness" is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) and "form" refers to the five sense organs, while "mind" refers to the six consciousnesses.
Now, when we speak of "all phenomena," both principle and phenomena are encompassed; as for emptiness, it extends from empty space down to... [the ultimate limit].

In Prajñā as well, there are both the ultimate and the conventional. Regarding form (*rūpa*), it ranges from substantial form (*dravya-rūpa*) up to true form (*tattva-rūpa*); these too have both ultimate and conventional aspects.

Regarding mind (*citta*), it ranges from the arising and ceasing (*utpāda-vyaya*) up to the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*); these likewise have both ultimate and conventional aspects. The inclusion of dharmas is thus vast and extensive.

The five kinds of the three truths are as explained in the *Fahua xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra). "Self, person, knowledge, and view" refers to the lower three [truths] in relation to the three [truths].

To provisionally manifest the dharmas of self, person, knowledge, and vision is called the "provisional five aggregates"; this is the provisional designation of all phenomena as "reception" (feeling), which is the "provisionality of dharmas.
Third, the conclusion.
Because the faculties and practices of sentient beings differ from category to category, there is neither a single nor a dual dharma-gate.
The section on questions and answers concludes.
The second major chapter, "Exhortation to Uphold," has two parts: first, praising the teaching; second, citing the title and exhorting its upholding. This is the first [part].
"Great King, the seven Buddhas have taught the Mahāprajñāpāramitā, and I now teach the Prajñāpāramitā;
there is no duality between them, nor is there any distinction. You and this great assembly should receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain this sutra.
The merit of doing so is immeasurable—unspeakably, unspeakably vast. Each and every Buddha teaches and transforms immeasurable, unspeakable multitudes."
Every single sentient being born attains Buddhahood; these Buddhas, in turn, teach and transform immeasurable, unspeakable numbers of sentient beings, all of whom attain Buddhahood.
These three supreme Buddhas preached the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra in eighty trillion verses.
Within a single verse, it is further divided into a thousand parts, and within one such part, the meaning of a single phrase cannot be fully expressed.
To speak of the ultimate limit, how much more so for those sentient beings who give rise to even a single thought of faith in this sutra;
they shall transcend the merits of a hundred, a thousand kalpas, and the ten stages (*bhūmi*). How much more so, then, the merit of those who receive, uphold, read, recite, explain, and expound it?

It is equal to that of all the Buddhas of the ten directions and not different. You should know that such persons are themselves Tathāgatas, and that before long they shall attain Buddhahood. At that time...

When the great assembly heard this sutra being preached, one billion people attained the patience of the three emptinesses (*trividha-śūnyatā-kṣānti*), and one hundred trillion people attained the patience of the great emptiness (*mahā-śūnyatā-kṣānti*) and the nature of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
The text is divided into five parts: first, it clarifies that the preaching is identical to that of the seven Buddhas; second, "You, the great assembly... and below, it sets forth the benefits.

This is an exhortation to uphold [the teaching]. Furthermore, the third section below clarifies that those with superior faith who can believe in this sutra achieve the three types of wisdom and thereby transcend the merits of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*). How much more so for those who receive and uphold it;

the fourth section below clarifies that they enter the first dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*) of the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya-yāna*), attain Buddhahood, and are able to transform sentient beings across a hundred Buddha-worlds. At that time, the great assembly...
The following explains the benefits of the five sciences (*pañcavidyā*).
Second, it provides the title and exhorts one to uphold it:
"Great King, this sutra is named the *Benevolent Kings’ Inquiry into the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*; you all should receive and uphold this *Prajñā*."
If this *Pāramitā-sūtra* possesses immeasurable merits, it is called the merit of protecting the nation;
it is also called the medicinal medicine for all kings, the application of which is not without great utility.
It is also the merit of protecting dwellings, and it protects the bodies of all sentient beings. This very Prajñāpāramitā is the protection of the nation, like a city with its moats and ramparts.
Just as one should protect oneself with walls, swords, spears, and shields, so too should you uphold the Prajñāpāramitā.
The text has two parts: first, the naming [of the subject], which is easily understood; second, the clarification of its function, which may be observed.
In the *Benevolent Kings’ Protection of the Nation Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Chapter Five, "The Protection of the Nation," there are four sections in the formal exposition.
