To manifest the distinct stages of practice, one cultivates the four immeasurables (*catvāry apramāṇāni*) as an antidote to afflictions such as hatred (*dveṣa*), thereby extinguishing hatred within the three realms of existence (*trai-dhātuka*).
Regarding the basis for the elimination of obstacles: according to the Sarvāstivāda school, hatred exists only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*);

however, according to the Satyasiddhi-śāstra, hatred pervades all three realms, as the "Parable" chapter of the *Saddharma-puṇḍarīka-sūtra* states that even in the higher realms there is hatred. One abides in the stage of "patience toward the middle" (*madhyama-kṣānti*).
The demarcation for the middle and lower of the three ranks corresponds to the middle grade of *anulomikī kṣānti* (conformity-acceptance).

This is because, at the time of entering the third stage among the five *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, one fulfills the *śīla-pāramitā*—which is translated as "fulfillment" (*saṃpūrṇa*) and also termed "fearless"—due to the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla*).
The sixth Dharma-preacher:
Furthermore, the practitioner of clear wisdom constantly practices the patience of signlessness (*animitta-kṣānti*) while cultivating the contemplation of the three insights (*traividya*).

Knowing that the dharmas of the three periods of time neither come nor go and have no place of abiding, their minds are quiescent and extinguished; they exhaust the delusions and afflictions of the triple world and attain the three insights.
Because they contemplate all merits, they constantly gather the immeasurable perfection of light (*prabhā-pāramitā*) throughout six *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas;
thus they enter the stage of *kalāpa*, practicing the signless (*animitta*) and upholding all dharmas.
The text has three parts. First, the initial section designates the stage: because one has attained the perfection of patience, they are called "Possessing Clear Wisdom.

From "Always by means of the signless" below, the second part distinguishes the text on contemplation, which has three sections: first, clarifying the specific knowledge of the stages, where knowing the emptiness of the three periods of time constitutes the contemplation of the three insights (*trividyā*);

second, clarifying the removal of hindrances, where "exhausting the delusions and afflictions of the three realms" refers to this; third, from "attaining the three insights" below, it clarifies the stage itself.
As for "Santuṣṭa," he always [practices] with the six *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas; "Tri-vidyā" refers to the time of entering the stages;
"Āgamata" means "crossing the limits," that is, crossing over and crossing beyond all extremes.
This is the seventh Dharma Master.

Furthermore, at that time, the Bodhisattva Er-yan Sheng-jue-da (Eternal Flame Holy Enlightenment) practiced in accordance with the patience of conforming to the Dharma (*anulomikī-dharmakṣānti*), turning back the flow of the five views, and accumulated immeasurable merit.
Abiding in the stage of *srotāpanna*, he constantly employed his supernormal powers of the divine eye, divine ear, recollection of past lives, knowledge of others' minds, and physical mastery;
in every thought-moment, he extinguished all views within the three realms. Moreover, for seven *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, he practiced the five supernatural faculties.
The *pāramitās* as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are constantly inseparable from the mind.

The text has three parts: first, the general statement; "Eryan" (爾燄) means "Mother of Wisdom" (*jñānamātṛ*), because on this stage one is able to give birth to dhyāna-wisdom, hence it is called the Mother of Wisdom.
The second part explains the specific characteristics of the stages in accordance with the practice of *anulomikī-kṣānti* (conformity-to-truth patience). This section has three sub-parts.

First, regarding the designation of the stage of abiding as "Srotāpanna" (Stream-enterer): this borrows the name of the Lesser Vehicle to refer to the Greater Vehicle. The "five views" (*pañca-dṛṣṭi*) refer to the five *ānantarya-karma* (immediate retribution).

Because one constantly employs the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) to give rise to supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) for those below the second [stage], yet has not yet perfected the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), only the five [views] are mentioned.

Regarding the phrase "in every moment," the following three [phrases] refer to the destruction of obstacles; that is to say, because this stage is assigned to the first fruit (*prathamaphala*), the five views are extinguished. Furthermore...
This refers to the distinct entry into the universal [wisdom]. Furthermore, regarding the timing of the seven lower stages of entry, the eighth is the Dharma Master.
Next, the Bodhisattva Supreme Attainment, through the patience that accords with the Path (*anulomikī-kṣānti*), contemplates *nayuta* truths within the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*).
Because he expounds the Treatise on the Path, the Treatise on Non-Buddhists, medicinal formulas, crafts, and incantations;

because he has extinguished the afflictions such as doubt within the three realms through his realization as an Omniscient One; because the mark of selfhood (*ātman*) is exhausted in him; because he knows what must be transcended at each stage (*bhūmi*), it is called the "Path of Departure" (*nairyāṇika-mārga*);

because he knows what is not to be transcended, it is called the "Obstruction to the Path"; and because he has accumulated immeasurable merit while reversing the doubts of the three realms—it is thus.
Upon entering the stage of Sakṛdāgāmin, one further accumulates practice for eight asaṃkhyeya kalpas;
because one practices all the gates of dhāraṇī, one constantly practices the contemplation of fearlessness, never departing from it in mind.

The text has three parts. First, the initial section designates the stage: because he has deeply cultivated meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), he attains supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); because he penetrates the phenomena of form and mind, he is called "Victorious" (*jina*).

Regarding the "Patience in Accordance with the Path" (*anulomikī kṣānti*), the following two sections clarify the specific practices within this stage. This section has three parts. First, it clarifies the attainment of fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*):
through the contemplation that penetrates the five characteristics—which is itself omniscient fearlessness—he extinguishes the doubts and afflictions of the three realms.

The "fearlessness regarding the exhaustion of outflows" (*āsravakṣaya-vaiśāradya*) refers to knowing that there is an exit from each stage (*bhūmi*). The phrase "and so forth" indicates the fearlessness regarding the path to the exhaustion of suffering.

The "fearlessness regarding the obstacles to the path" (*antarāyika-dharma-vaiśāradya*) refers to [knowing] that there is nothing that does not lead to an exit [from the stages]. Regarding those who oppose the three realms with doubt, two [types of] obstacles are removed.
The cultivation of immeasurable merit and the following three sections on the limits of entering the stages (*avatāra-bhūmi*) are also explained by borrowing from the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*).
The Great Re-collection of Practices enters the lower three stages of the limit of cultivation within the incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*).
Ninth is the Dharma Master.

Furthermore, constantly manifesting reality, he dwells within the stage of compliance with patience (*anulomikī kṣānti*), performing the contemplation of the Middle Way to exhaust the causes of accumulation within the three realms.
Because karma and all afflictions are thus observed as being neither existent nor non-existent—characterized by the single mark of signlessness and being non-dual—one realizes the stage of Anāgāmin.
Thereafter, for nine asaṃkhyeya kalpas, one practices the illumination of the Middle Way; thus, through the power of joy, one is born in all Buddha-lands.

The text has three parts. First, regarding the designation of the stage: because the true illumination of the Middle Way is the reality of *prajñā*, it constantly manifests as the abiding in true reality within the stage of *anulomikī-kṣānti* (conformity-patience).
Second and third, regarding the specific practice: all afflictions are the cause of accumulation (*saṃudaya*), and suffering and so forth are called the accumulation of karma;

on this stage, these are all exhausted. Because all phenomena are fundamentally empty, they are not existent; because all phenomena are established [through dependent origination], they are not non-existent.
Because neither exists as a reality, the single characteristic—the true characteristic—is likewise suchness; thus it is signless.
Furthermore, during the stage of entering the three [realms] within the nine asaṃkhyeyas, the power of delight is precisely the power of aspiration.
The tenth Dharma Master:

Furthermore, the Bodhisattva Xuanda, throughout ten *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, cultivated the patience that delights in the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), extinguishing the habitual causes and karmic fruits of the triple world.
Abiding within his final body, he fully accomplished immeasurable merits and perfected the wisdom of non-arising.
With the fivefold dharmakāya of wisdom fully perfected, they abide in the tenth bhūmi, the stage of the Arhat-Brahmā;
they constantly practice the contemplation of the three gates of emptiness, are endowed with hundreds of thousands of millions of samādhis, and extensively propagate the treasury of the Dharma.
The text has three parts. First, the title: "Mysterious and Far-Reaching" (*xuanyuan*) means "penetrating understanding.

Because one attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) at this stage and acts with effortlessness, it is called "mysteriously penetrating" (*xuanda*). "Ten asaṃkhyeyas" [of kalpas] refers to the second part:

entering the stage and extinguishing the habitual afflictions (*vāsanā-kleśa*) of the triple world. Those who dwell in the tenth stage are the thirteenth; the "Dharma Masters" below refer to the tenth Dharma Master.

"Earth" does not refer to the Bodhisattvas of the ten stages; rather, it refers to those who constantly practice within the three gates of emptiness, who distinguish the various practices through the three types of discernment, and who propagate the Buddha’s Three Dharma Treasuries by means of the contemplation of the three emptinesses.
The eleventh Dharma Master:
Furthermore, the Equally Awakened One dwells within the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), contemplating that the mind and mental objects are quiescent;

thus there is no characteristic in characteristics, no body in the body, and no cognition in cognition. He employs the mind as a vehicle throughout all directions, abiding in detachment while dwelling in non-abiding.
Abiding in the state of permanence while constantly cultivating the sphere of emptiness, one simultaneously illuminates all phenomena through the dual aspects of emptiness and permanence;

thus, one knows what is possible and what is impossible, up to the ten powers of omniscience. By means of contemplating these ten powers, one is able, in the stage of Mahāraga, to transform all lands and sentient beings, practicing the dharma of the ten powers for a thousand *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, with every thought in accord with the mind.
He constantly enters the Samādhi of Seeing the Buddha.

Regarding the three-part textual structure: first, the designation of the stage; within this stage, the simultaneous illumination of both the ultimate and conventional truths is termed "Equal Enlightenment" (Samyaksaṃbodhi), yet this is not the Equal Enlightenment of the eleventh stage.
Second, dwelling in the non-arising [of dharmas]; third, clarifying the distinctions of contemplation. Textual section one.
The contemplation of existence and non-existence has two parts: first, the correlation of the stages; second, the actual exposition of the contemplation of existence and non-existence.

Regarding the first, there are three sections: the initial detailed explanation of the text; first, clarifying that the mind is quiescent yet ever-active. "The mind is quiescent" means that every thought-moment is empty;
this clarifies the meaning of quiescence. Although it is without marks, yet there are marks; although it is without form, yet there is form. Although it is without... [text continues].

To know this while being without [discursive] knowledge is the meaning of the application of illumination; to apply the mind according to the two subsequent applications of illumination while remaining eternally quiescent is to have cultivation of emptiness within existence.
The following two lines provide a combined explanation of existence and emptiness:

"cultivating emptiness within existence" explains the aforementioned "eternal quiescence while in existence," and "while in emptiness, the myriad transformations are constant" explains the aforementioned "quiescence while constantly employing. This is because [wisdom] simultaneously illuminates all phenomena.

The three pairs of fetters are known; regarding the discernment of what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñāna*), the following two [powers] clarify the observation of the ten powers (*daśabala*).
Only the last one is explicitly explained while the remaining practices are abbreviated. Thus, one ascends to the stage of the *mahoraga*.

"Mahoraga" is translated here as "Great Attainer" (*dadeluō*) or "Dragon Elephant," and so forth. Third, the distinctions of ascending the stages: *Mahoraga* means "Great Attainer" or "Dragon Elephant."
[The section on] the duration of practice for the thousand *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, [part] three.
Twelfth, the Dharma Master.

Furthermore, regarding the supernatural transformation of the Radiance of Wisdom (*prajñā-prabhā-vikurvāṇa*): abiding in the supreme non-arising patience (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), one extinguishes the characteristics of mind and mental states, seeing with the Dharma-eye.
Through the samādhi of the emptiness of the form of all dharmas, by the power of great vows, he is constantly born in all pure lands;

for ten million asaṃkhyeya kalpas, he has accumulated the immeasurable Buddha-light samādhi and is able to manifest the spiritual powers of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of ten million Ganges Rivers;
abiding in the state of the Bhagavan, he also constantly enters the Buddha-flower samādhi.

The text has three parts. First, the designation of the stage: because the Bodhisattvas of this stage attain unimpeded wisdom (*anāvaraṇajñāna*) to transform all sentient beings and manifest various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), it is called the "Miraculous Transformation of the Light of Wisdom. Second, the explanation of the distinctions in the two modes of abiding—above and below.

This section has four parts; first, the assignment of the stages regarding the cessation of the mind and its mental characteristics. Second, the clarification of the cessation of the mind, the cessation of the intellect (*manas*), and so forth.
The cessation of the mind and mental factors is called the "dharma of the mark of cessation. The Dharma-eye sees the lower three types of clear knowledge (*vidyā*).
The Dharma-eye sees all phenomena; this specifically clarifies the three eyes. The seeing of the emptiness of form is what generally clarifies the three eyes:

the Buddha-eye is wisdom (*prajñā*). The Wisdom-eye sees the emptiness of form; the Dharma-eye sees the conventional nature of form; the Buddha-eye sees the Middle Way as the unity of emptiness and conventionality.
Non-dual yet dual, dual yet non-dual; when both are illuminated simultaneously, it is "non-dual yet dual," and when both are extinguished, it is "dual yet non-dual.
Raising the three eyes to confront the two objects of form, the single character "view" (jien) comprehensively clarifies the distinctions among the three types of vision.

Viewing form as empty is the Truth of Emptiness (*śūnyatā-satya*); viewing form as provisional is the Truth of Existence (*saṃvṛti-satya*); illuminating both simultaneously is the [Truth of the Middle Way].
Regarding the single ultimate truth (*ekārtha-paramārtha*), these three [teachings] have five aspects when categorized by their doctrinal systems: 1. **Distinct Entry into the Universal**:
Taking illusory form as existence, emptiness as the true, and that which is neither existent nor empty as the ultimate truth. 2. **Perfect Entry into the Universal**:

The three truths are the same as before, with the addition that all phenomena converge therein. 3. **Distinct Teaching**: Taking illusory existence as it is emptiness as the conventional, and its non-emptiness as the true.
Neither being nor non-being constitutes the Middle Way. Regarding the four "entering" (ju) stages, in the distinct teaching (biejiao), one adds "all dharmas enter [the truth]";
in the three truths of the perfect teaching (yuanjiao), all are likewise said to be "all dharmas enter. Question: Regarding the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, why does it speak of the Buddha-eye? Answer:

The *Lotus Sūtra* states that "opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision" refers to the initial stage of the distinct teaching (the first bhūmi) and the initial dwelling of the perfect teaching (the first vihāra), wherein the three [eyes] are manifested.

1. The primary substantial cause (*upādāna-hetu*) is the principle-mind; its activation is the Middle Way contemplation (*madhyamā-pratipad*), which opens the way to all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*).

2. The discerning cause (*vijñapti-hetu*) is the wisdom-mind; its activation is the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), which opens the way to omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). 3. The contributing cause (*pratyaya-hetu*) is the virtuous mind;

its activation is the contemplation of the provisional (*parikalpita-vipaśyanā*), which opens the way to the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*). If these are attained even at the first stage (*bhūmi*), how much more so at the ninth? This refers, however, to their partial attainment.

It is not through the attainment of full realization, but by the power of great vows, they descend into the four modes of birth in the Pure Land. "Ten *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas" refers to the third stage of entering the position.
Bhagavān—translated here as "World-Honored One"—is not the ultimate Buddha; this World-Honored One is a World-Honored One of the stage of being next in succession (*upapadya-bhūmi*).
Thirteenth: The Dharma Master. Part Four: One, Designating the Stage; Two, Clarifying the Time of Realization; Three, Discerning the Stages;
Four, Clarifying Entry into the Determinative Stage. Now, for the first [section]:
Furthermore, regarding the contemplation of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Regarding the contemplation of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas: if one opens the wondrous enlightenment, this is the stage of Equal Enlightenment (Samyagbodhi), which is still called "Bodhisattva.

Upon reaching this ground, one maintains that it is the ultimate; yet, as it is not yet the final limit, one must further observe that there is a distinct Buddha, for there remain thirty-two grades of non-obstructing wisdom.
Since the Perfect Buddha is still far off, it is called "contemplation"; in the case of the Universal Buddha, it is already present.
The forty-two categories of ignorance are even further removed from this.
Second, the clarification of the temporal period:

those who abide in the patience of cessation have, from their initial generation of the mind of awakening until now, passed through one million *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas cultivating the hundred [perfections].
By virtue of the merit accumulated over ten thousand *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, one realizes liberation from all phenomena and dwells upon the Vajra Platform.
This section has four parts; the first corresponds to the fifth stage, the Patience of Quiescent Extinction (*śānta-nirvāṇa-kṣānti*), which itself has two subdivisions: the lower and the upper.

Here, the tenth stage is the lower grade of the Patience of Quiescent Extinction. From the passage "As from the initial resolve" (*yathā cittotpādāt*) down to the end of the second sutra, it describes the duration of time.
"More or less" refers to the period from the stage of the lineage of practice (*śikṣāgotra*) up to the patience of consecration (*abhiṣeka-kṣānti*), spanning one million *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.

This involves cultivating the three types of analytical knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*) during the lower stages; "cultivating and realizing" refers to the realization of all dharmas during the fourth stage.
"Liberation from all dharmas" refers to true liberation. The "Vajra Terrace" is the Vajra Samādhi.
Section Five: Distinguishing the Stages through Three Pairs. First, the distinction between subduing and severing.
Good son, from the stage of Patience (kṣānti) up to the Samādhi of the Peak (mūrdhan), all are termed "subduing" all afflictions (*kleśa*).
However, there is no conviction that all afflictions are extinguished, nor is there the arising of the wisdom of liberation that illuminates the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
From the stage of practice up to the Peak Samādhi, the "Patience of Subjugation" (伏忍) is first elucidated;

then, from the "Faith-Understanding" (信解) downward, the severance and extinction of all afflictions is clarified, which is Great Nirvāṇa. Birth in liberation is liberation itself; the illumination of wisdom is Prajñā;
and the ultimate truth (第一義) is the stage of the Dharmakāya.
Second, faith and vision differ;
this [faith] is not called "vision," for what is called "vision" is omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).

Therefore, since time immemorial, I have always said that from the Samādhi of the Buddha’s Knowledge, Vision, and Awakening at the Summit (*buddhajñānadarśanabodhimaṇḍa-samādhi*) down to the stage of "patience in practice" (*śikṣā-kṣānti*), it is unknown and unseen.
"Seeing is non-awakening" first clarifies non-seeing; that which is called "seeing" refers to *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge), which next clarifies seeing.
Therefore, from the passage beginning "Since the distant past... onwards, it cites scriptural evidence.
Third, the distinction between the gradual and the sudden:
only the Buddha possesses sudden realization, which is not termed "faith," whereas those who subdue [the afflictions] gradually do.
Fourth, the difference between the permanent and the impermanent.
Although wisdom arises and ceases, it is capable of being without arising and without cessation. If this mind were to cease, there would be no afflictions that would not cease;

yet [wisdom] is without arising and without cessation. Being without arising means there are no afflictions that are not dispelled; being without cessation means there are no virtues that are not perfected. Thus, being without arising is the perfection of abandonment (*prahāṇa*).
Non-extinction is the virtue of wisdom.
There are five grades of equality and inequality;

entering the principle through the Vajra-samādhi that exhausts all things, one accords with the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), yet has not yet attained equality with the "unequally equal."

For example, it is like a person who ascends a great high terrace and gazes down, perceiving everything without exception; abiding in the ultimate principle through the *samādhi* of the exhaustion of phenomena is also like this.
In this passage, the dharma, the analogy, and their synthesis can be understood accordingly.
Fourth, it clarifies entering the stage of certainty:
constantly cultivating all practices to fulfill the treasury of merit and enter the stage of Bhagavat, while likewise abiding eternally in the Buddha-wisdom samādhi.
In this context, the state of the Bhagavān—whose every practice is perfected and whose wisdom is perfected—is called the "Treasury of Merit" (Guṇagañja).
This is translated here as "World-Honored One" (Shizun). Furthermore, he eternally abides in the Buddha-wisdom samādhi; this necessarily implies the sense of "should receive and cultivate.
It is said that he "eternally abides" because he also remains engaged in benefiting others in various ways.
The third section is the concluding praise:
"Good sons, all such bodhisattvas are able, within the lands of all Tathāgatas throughout the ten directions,
to transform sentient beings by correctly expounding the true meaning, receiving, upholding, reading, reciting, and penetrating the reality-mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), just as I do today."
There is no difference.

This concludes the first question-and-answer session on the necessity of receiving and upholding [this teaching], which clarifies that his manifestation of transformative power is no different from that of a Buddha.
Second, the text for exhorting the various kings to receive and uphold [it] has four parts: 1. Praising its utility to encourage its upholding; 2. Praising the name and entrusting it.

Exhorting [others] to uphold [the Dharma] consists of three explanations; the reasons for this exhortation consist of four parts; and the entrustment by name is the first. Within the first [section], there are two parts:
a brief praise and an extensive praise. Now, for the first:
the Buddha addressed King Prasenajit, saying, "After my parinirvāṇa, at the time when the Dharma is about to perish, you shall receive and uphold the Prajñāpāramitā."
The Great Perfection of Wisdom performs great Buddha-works; that all lands are established in peace and all people dwell in happiness arises entirely from this Prajñāpāramitā.
For this reason, it is entrusted to the kings, and not to the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās.
Why? Because they lack royal power. Therefore, it is not entrusted to them. You should receive and uphold it.
Reciting and explaining its meaning and principles. Section one:
Exhorting the upholding [of the teaching] by means of the cessation [of afflictions]. Section two: Clarifying the power of Prajñā.
Therefore, the entrustment follows. Section three: Explaining the reason for the entrustment; because it lacks royal power, it is not entrusted [to others].
The entrustment: "You should receive and uphold [this]" refers to the separate entrustment to Candraprabha (Moonlight) in the latter four sections.

Part Two: The Extensive Praise and Exhortation to Uphold the Text, in two parts: first, the heading on the arising of merit through the removal of obstacles; second, the analysis through question and answer. This is the first part.
"Great King, that which I have now transformed consists of ten billion Sumeru mountains and ten billion suns and moons. On each Sumeru there are four continents;
in Jambudvīpa to the south, there are sixteen great kingdoms, five hundred intermediate kingdoms, and ten thousand minor kingdoms.
Within those lands, there are seven kinds of calamities and misfortunes; for the sake of these calamities, all the kings study and recite the Prajñāpāramitā."

The seven perils of the *pāramitās* are immediately extinguished and the seven blessings are immediately produced; the myriad people are at peace and happy, and the sovereign and his ministers rejoice.
The text is intelligible.
Second, the analysis through question and answer.
What constitutes a difficulty? When the sun and moon lose their course and the seasons run contrary to their order;
when the sun rises red, or black, or two, three, four, or five suns appear together; when there is a solar eclipse and the sun is without light;

or when the solar disc appears with one, two, three, four, or five concentric halos—when such portents of transformation and anomaly occur, to read and recite this sutra is the first difficulty. Furthermore, when the twenty-eight lunar mansions lose their courses.

The Venus star, comet stars, wheel stars, ghost stars, Mars, Mercury, wind stars, sword stars, the Southern Dipper and Northern Dipper, the great stars of the Five Towns, all the stars of national rulers, the stars of the Three Dukes, and the stars of the hundred officials—each of these stars manifested various transformations and also preached this sutra;
this is the second difficulty. Furthermore, a great fire burned the nation, consuming the myriad people until they were utterly destroyed.

Or when there are fires of ghosts, fires of dragons, fires of celestial mountains, fires of mountain deities, fires of humans, fires of trees, or fires of bandits— such strange and miraculous occurrences,

one should also recite and expound this sutra as a remedy for these three great calamities. When great waters flood and submerge the populace, when the seasons are inverted, when it rains in winter and snows in summer,
when there are thunderclaps and lightning strikes in winter, or when ice, frost, hail, and red or black water rain down in the sixth month— one should likewise recite this sutra.

When water turns blue, when rain falls from the waters, when earth-mountain rains fall upon stone-mountains, when sand, gravel, and stones float down as rivers flow upstream, and when such transformations occur—reading and reciting this sutra at these times constitutes the fourth hardship.
Furthermore, when great winds blow, killing tens of thousands of people and causing the lands, mountains, rivers, and trees to perish all at once;
when untimely great winds, black winds, red winds, and blue winds arise from the heavens—[in such times, one should read and recite this sutra].
When wind and earth, wind and fire, and wind undergo such transformations, reciting and expounding this sutra shall serve as the fifth protection against calamities.

When heaven and earth, the lands and nations suffer from excessive heat and blazing fires, when the hundred grasses wither and the five grains fail to ripen due to drought, and when the land is scorched until the myriad people perish—when such transformations occur, reciting and expounding this sutra shall serve as the sixth protection against calamities. When there are bandits from the four quarters...
When enemies invade from within or without, or when fire-demons, water-demons, wind-demons, and ghost-demons arise,
causing the common people to fall into chaos and the calamity of war to break out— during such strange times, one should also recite this sutra as a remedy for the seven hardships.
First, the question regarding the loss of the regularity of the sun and moon is easily understood. Below, two answers address the seven difficulties as sevenfold.

First, the difficulty of the loss of the regularity of the sun and moon refers to the change of seasons resulting in much famine; the change of numerical proportions resulting in much warfare; and the change of physical appearances resulting in much pestilence.
Regarding the twenty-eight [constellations], the second [section] concerns the difficulty of the loss of the regularity of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*). This is extensive.

1. Fire burning the country: the disaster of fire from the three calamities below. 2. Great waters flooding and submerging [the land]: the disaster of the transformation of water from the four rains below.
3. A great wind blowing and killing the myriad people: the disaster of evil winds from the five below. 4. Heaven and earth and the state-land [suffering drought]:
the disaster of excessive heat from the six below. 5. Bandits coming from the four quarters: the disaster of evil bandits from the seven below. All are as described in the text.

[The section on] "Seeing. Second, the praise of the title, which consists of two parts: first, praising the excellence of the title; second, exhorting one to make offerings. Now, for the first [part]:
"O Great King, this Prajñāpāramitā is the heart-mind and consciousness of all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and all sentient beings."

The Spirit is the source; it is the parent of all kings. It is also called the Divine Talisman, the Ghost-Averting Pearl, the Wish-Fulfilling Jewel, the State-Protecting Pearl, the Heaven-and-Earth Mirror, and the Dragon-Treasure King Spirit.

To distinguish them: the essence of the three types of prajñā is the mind-consciousness; the father and mother of the King of Real-Phase Prajñā (dharmatā-prajñā) are the Contemplating Prajñā (pratyavekṣaṇā-prajñā), because they can give birth to the king’s wisdom and understanding; and the six subsequent names are the Scriptural Prajñā (vyañjana-prajñā).
Second, the exhortation to make offerings.
The Buddha told the Great King: "You should prepare nine-colored banners nine *zhang* long, nine-colored flowers two *zhang* high, and thousand-branch lamps five *zhang* high.
You should also provide nine jade boxes and nine jade cloths, as well as a table made of the seven precious gems, upon which you shall place the sutra."

Whenever the King travels, he constantly offers one hundred paces of ground before him; this is his constant practice. He always emits a thousand rays of light, causing the seven calamities not to arise and transgressions not to occur within a thousand *li*.
When the King stays, he constructs a pavilion of the seven precious gems, and within it, a high seat of the seven precious gems upon which the sūtra scrolls are placed.
Day by day he makes offerings, scattering flowers and burning incense, as if serving a father.

The mother serves like Śakra. The text has two parts: first, the method of making offerings is shown; second, the specific practices for walking and staying are clarified. In both the beginning and the middle, the number "nine" is mentioned;
nine signifies the suffering of sentient beings. As for the banner, it marks and reveals that one attains excellence through practice; within the nine types of suffering, it is established.
The banner of supreme liberation is adorned with flowers of nine colors, symbolizing that sentient beings undergoing the nine sufferings practice the cause of Prajñā.

The flowers of blue, yellow, red, white, and black represent the five sense-objects (*pañca-viṣaya*); the flowers of earth, water, fire, and wind represent the four great elements (*catvāri mahābhūtāni*). The two *zhang* [in height] symbolize the Two Truths;
the thousand lamps symbolize the merit of the ten wholesome actions (*daśa-kuśala-karma-patha*). Each, through the mutual support of Prajñā, gives rise to the thousand wisdoms.

The wisdom-tower is five *zhang* high, its radiance illuminating the five realms of existence. The nine jade chests symbolize the abodes of the nine sufferings; being pure, they serve as vessels for the Dharma.

The nine jade cloths symbolize that sentient beings dwelling in the abodes of the nine sufferings obtain the *prajñā*-cloth. "Level" (*an*) is a metaphor for the *prajñā* of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*);
placing the sutra upon it signifies that written words can cause the true principle to become manifest. The seven treasures... [text ends].

This indicates that those who practice the seven stages of expedient means are all "human treasures. Regarding the passage beginning with "If the king travels," the following two sections specifically clarify the offerings made during walking and standing;
first, the section on "if the king travels" clarifies the offering made while walking, and the subsequent section clarifies the offering made while standing.
Third, the explanation of the reasons for the exhortation:

"Great King, I now see clearly with my five eyes that all kings of the three periods of time have become sovereign emperors and rulers by virtue of having served five hundred Buddhas in the past; it is because they were all holy arhats that they have come to be born there."
The kingdom shall receive great benefit; however, when the king’s merit is exhausted, all the holy ones will abandon it.
When all the holy ones have departed, the seven calamities will inevitably arise.
Great King, if in future ages there are kings who uphold the Triple Gem, I shall dispatch the five Bodhisattvas of Great Power to protect their kingdoms: first, the Bodhisattva Vajraghoṣa.
1. The Bodhisattva Thousand-Jeweled Banner-Wheel Holder went to protect that land; 2. The Bodhisattva Golden Wheel Lamp Holder went to protect that land; 3.
The Bodhisattva Fearless Ten-Power Roar Holder went to protect that land, holding a vajra-pestle in his hand;
4. The Bodhisattva Thunder and Lightning Roar Holder went to protect that land, holding a single-jeweled net in his hand; 5. The Bodhisattva Immeasurable... [text continues]
The Bodhisattva Balagarjita, holding fifty sword-wheels, shall go to protect that country;
these five great beings and five thousand great deity-kings will bring great benefit within your kingdom, and you should establish their images and make offerings to them.
The text has two parts. First, the passage clarifying that the King’s merit is exhausted, which is understandable from the text.

Second, the passage clarifying the benefits for future lives, which has three sections: (1) citing the number [of benefits], which is understandable; (2) the section beginning with "Vajragarbha Bodhisattva," which is the specific explanation;
and (3) the section beginning with "These five great beings," which is the concluding explanation.
Fourth is the entrustment by name:
"Great King, I now entrust the Three Jewels to you and all the kings of the kingdoms of Kośala, Vaiśālī, Śrāvastī, Magadha, Vārāṇasī, and Kauśāmbī."
In those lands— the kingdom of Kauśāmbī, the kingdom of Kuru, the kingdom of Kaśmīra, the kingdom of Karakaṇḍa,
the kingdom of Gandhāra, the kingdom of Śāthā, the kingdom of Saṃghāṭa, the kingdom of Kanyākubja, the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra— and in all such countries as these,
they uphold the Prajñāpāramitā.
The text has three parts: first, a general clarification of the entrustment, which is easily understood; second, from "In the Kingdom of Kośala" onwards, the naming [of the recipients];
and third, from "In this way" onwards, the conclusion and exhortation. The exhortation for all kings to receive and uphold [the teaching] is hereby complete.
The third section, on the benefits for the assembly, consists of fifty-one parts. First, the benefit for the asuras:

At that time, the great assembly and the asura kings, hearing the Buddha speak of the seven terrifying things in future ages, their body hair stood on end and they cried out with loud voices, saying, "May we never be born in those realms."
The two kings’ merit increased.

At that time, the sixteen great kings entrusted the affairs of state to their younger brothers, left the household life to cultivate the Way, and contemplated the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the four colors (*catuḥ-varṇa*).

They excelled in the characteristics of the four great elements and the four colors, and practiced the characteristics of the non-appropriation of consciousness and emptiness (*vijñāna-śūnyatā-anupādāna*), entering the stages of the thirty *kṣāntis* and the first bhūmi.
The characteristics of the nine stages of the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya) constitute, O Great King, the relinquishing of the body of an ordinary person to enter the body of the sixth stage;
the relinquishing of the sevenfold retributive body to enter the eighth dharma-body; and the realization of the prajñāpāramitā of all practices.

In the first part of this section, it is explained that the eight bases of mastery (*aṣṭāv abhibhvāyatanāni*)—consisting of the four primary elements (earth, water, fire, and wind) and the four derivative colors (blue, yellow, red, and white)—are called "mastery" because they transcend craving for the four primary elements. Next, the ten totalities (*daśa kṛtsnāyatanāni*) are explained:

earth, water, fire, and wind; blue, yellow, red, and white; the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*); and the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*). These objects of focus are so vast that there is nowhere they do not pervade.
Because one enters [the first stage], the thirty *kṣāntis* (patiences) are the skillful means (*upāya*) of the first stage; they are called the "characteristics of the first stage.

The ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is precisely the first stage, for the first stage possesses the characteristics of all nine stages. As a verse in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "Just as when the first knot of a bamboo is split, the remaining knots can be quickly split;
so too, once the true wisdom (*tattvajñāna*) of the first stage is attained, the various stages will be swiftly accomplished. One abandons the ordinary body and attains [the body of] a Buddha."

At the sixth stage, one abandons the physical body; at the seventh stage, one attains the *paricchinna-bhoga-kāya* (the body of segmented retribution); and at the eighth stage, one attains the *nirmāṇa-dharma-kāya* (the body of transformed change).
Thus, the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* states: "At the seventh [stage], one abandons the birth-body and the flesh-body. This refers to the benefits of the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*).
The three heavens increase their merit.
The eighteen Brahmā heavens and the Āsura kings attain the contemplation of the Three Vehicles as being identical to the realm of non-arising. They further scatter flowers in offering:
flowers of emptiness, flowers of the dharma-nature, flowers of the sages, flowers of compliance, flowers of non-arising, flowers of the joy of the Dharma, and vajra flowers.

Contemplating the Middle Way as the causal condition, he scattered the flowers of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment upon the Buddha and the assembly of nine hundred billion great bodhisattvas.
Asuras and devas alike all benefited equally. The "empty flowers" symbolize the emptiness of persons, while the "nature-flowers" symbolize the emptiness of dharmas.

This reveals that the patience of the noble ones who have subdued [afflictions] is symbolized by the flower of the patience of faith; the patience of compliance is symbolized by the flower of compliance; the patience of non-arising is symbolized by the flower of non-arising;
the mastery of the four analytical knowledges in preaching the Dharma is the flower of the joy of the Dharma; and the lower grade of the patience of quiescence is as follows:
the Vajra-samādhi, which can sever the fetters and proclivities, is the upper grade of the patience of quiescence.
The four great assemblies offered their benefits;
all other assemblies scattered flowers of the traces of the path and its fruits, flowers of the distracted mind, flowers of the tree of emptiness, flowers of the six *pāramitās*,
and flowers of wondrous enlightenment upon the Buddha and the entire assembly.

The flower of the empty mind refers to the "mind-training" (citta-śikṣā) among the three trainings. The flower of the tree of the mind refers to the contemplation of the arising of the twelve links of dependent origination.
The flower of the six perfections refers to the practices of the ten stages (bhūmi). The flower and fruit of wondrous enlightenment refer to the practice itself.
The five benefits for bodhisattvas:
ten thousand bodhisattvas attained the Samādhi of Realizing the Sentient Beings of Future Ages, the Samādhi of Perfect Clarity, the Vajra Samādhi,
the Samādhi of the Conventional Truth, the Samādhi of the Ultimate Truth, and the Samādhi of the First Principle Truth— these three truths.
The Samādhi of All Samādhi Kings, as well as the Immeasurable Samādhi, the Seven Treasures Samādhi, the Twenty-five Existences Samādhi,
and the All-Encompassing Practice Samādhi were attained; furthermore, ten billion bodhisattvas ascended to the Vajra Pinnacle and manifested perfect enlightenment.

The explanation has two parts: first, the benefit for ten thousand [beings] is clarified and can be understood; next, from "furthermore, there are ten billion" onwards, the benefit of attaining Buddhahood is clarified.
Herein, one becomes a Buddha according to the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavyavasthāna-śāsana*). The main section on the "Part of the Correct Exposition" is hereby concluded.
The Eighth Chapter, the Third Major Section on the Dissemination, titled "Entrustment," from the *Benevolent Kings’ Sūtra of the Perfection of Wisdom for Protecting the State*.
"Entrustment" (*zhù*) refers to the act of handing over; "cumulative entrustment" (*lèi*) refers to the act of relying upon another.
Because this Dharma is handed over to kings and entrusted to them to proclaim and expound, it is called the "Chapter on Entrustment. Furthermore, if a king should encounter calamities...

Because it is difficult to rely on anything else for deliverance, it is called "entrustment" (*parindana*); furthermore, because this sutra is entrusted so that it may circulate through successive generations, it is named the "Chapter on Entrustment.

Question: Why is this not like the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, which entrusts the Dharma to the śrāvakas, or the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, which entrusts it to the bodhisattvas, but instead entrusts it to the king?
Answer: This Buddha prescribes medicine according to the illness; since the kingdom is the [illness], he entrusts it to the king.
It is entrusted [to the king] because it brings great benefit by widely proclaiming [the Dharma] during times of calamity;

furthermore, it is entrusted because the great offerings for all matters are so profound and vast that none but the power of a king could accomplish them; moreover, it is entrusted because if the king does not believe in the Dharma, he will not practice it, and since the practice of the Dharma rests with the king, it is entrusted to him.

The text of this chapter has two parts: first, the entrustment and admonition; second, the faithful observance according to the teaching. The first part further divides into two sections: first, the brief [explanation], and second, the extensive [explanation].
Herein is the first. The Buddha addressed King Prasenajit: "I admonish and charge you."
"Admonition" (jì) refers to exhortation and encouragement; "injunction" (chì) refers to instruction and command.

The two broad sections of the text are: first, clarifying the entrustment; second, clarifying the admonition and injunction. The first section is further divided into two parts: first, the time of entrustment;
second, the actual clarification of the person and method of entrustment. This is the first [part].
After my parinirvāṇa, during the periods of eighty years, eight hundred years, and eight thousand years, there will be no Buddha, no Dharma, no Saṅgha, and no faithful men or women.
Regarding the "eighty years," within one hundred years after the Buddha’s departure, five people shall maintain the teachings: first, Kāśyapa; second, Ānanda.

The three disciples of Śrīmanti saw the Buddha while he was still in the world; they successively maintained the teachings for sixty years, during which time the practice of the Dharma did not perish.
Next, Śāṇakavāsin and Upagupta—these two did not see the Buddha;

they successively maintained the teachings for forty years, after which the majestic deportment and the Dharma perished. Therefore, it is said that at this time there were no longer the Buddha’s teachings.

As for the monk’s statement that "eight hundred years" refers to the period within the years of the True Dharma (Saddharma), during which twenty masters maintained the Buddha-dharma and it was entirely the Dharma of the Sages, thus not perishing;
in the sixth century, there was the Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa, and in the seventh century, Nāgārjuna—both being the Dharma of Bodhisattvas, which likewise did not perish.
However, during the eighth century, heterodox schools flourished to the extreme; therefore, [the statement was made].
At this time, the entrustment to King Deva Bodhisattva Śabdavajra to proclaim the Dharma is fulfilled.

As for the "eight thousand years," when the Semblance Dharma (Saddharmapratirūpaka) is exhausted and it is the time of the Final Dharma (Kaliyuga), sentient beings believe in heterodoxy, and thus the Dharma perishes.
Second, the method for entrusting [the teaching] to others:
This sutra entrusts the Triple Gem to all kings and the fourfold assembly of disciples to uphold, recite, and explain its meaning,

so as to open the path of wisdom regarding emptiness for sentient beings of the three realms, cultivate the seven practices of the worthy and the ten wholesome deeds, and transform all sentient beings.

The text is divided into two parts. First, the entrustment of the Dharma, which can be understood as being for the sake of the multitudes within the three realms; second, the entrustment to specific persons. Herein, the teaching comprises three types of practice:
first, the practice of emptiness; second, the practice of the seven worthies; and third, the practice of the ten wholesome deeds. Emptiness refers to the noble practice (*ārya-caryā*);

the seven worthies refer to the seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidha-upāya*); and the ten wholesome deeds refer to the practice of ordinary beings. These proceed from the profound to the shallow.
The second admonition, consisting of seventy-one points: 1. Admonishing against the transgressions that cause the extinction of the Dharma;

2. Admonishing the destruction of the practices of the fourfold assembly; 3. Admonishing the prohibition of not relying on the Dharma; 4. Admonishing self-destruction; 5. Admonishing the employment [of improper labor]; 6. Admonishing self-reproach; 7. Admonishing erroneous faith.
Now, for the first admonition regarding the transgressions that cause the extinction of the Dharma, there are three parts: first, clarifying the extinction of the Dharma.
Next, following the analysis of the destruction of the Dharma, we conclude with the section on transgressions.

First: In the future age of the five turbidities, bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs—the fourfold assembly of disciples—as well as devas, nāgas, the eight classes of spirits, all spirit-kings, kings, ministers, crown princes, and sons of kings, relying on their own high status and nobility, shall destroy and subvert my Dharma.
The text has two parts. First, it clarifies that the time when the Dharma perishes is precisely the five turbidities (*pañca kaṣāyāḥ*):

first, the turbidity of life; second, the turbidity of the eon; third, the turbidity of afflictions; fourth, the turbidity of views; and fifth, the turbidity of sentient beings. The *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra* states:

"Sentient beings having a lifespan of ten years up to those with a lifespan of a thousand years—this variation in length constitutes the turbidity of life. Famine, pestilence, and warfare constitute the turbidity of the eon. [The latter] is manifold.

The presence of greed, hatred, and delusion is called the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*); wrong views, attachment to precepts and rituals, and attachment to views constitute the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*);

lack of filial piety, unrighteousness, and the disparagement of teachers and elders are the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*); and the bhikṣus who cause the decline and extinction of the Dharma are the turbidity of the lifespan (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*).
Second, the refutation of the faults in the doctrine of cessation (*nirodha*).
This clarifies that [the opponent] has established restrictive laws to govern my disciples— the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs— prohibiting them from leaving the household life to practice the Path,
nor permitting them to fashion images of the Buddha, stupas in the form of the Buddha, or erect official administrative offices to manage the community and maintain registers of the Saṃgha.
If a bhikṣu stands on the ground while a layperson sits on a high seat, or if a soldier or slave acts as a bhikṣu to receive the ritual for accepting special invitations;
or if bhikṣus who are acquaintances act together with a single mind of intimacy to perform a feast gathering for the sake of seeking merit— such as the practices of non-Buddhists—
all these are not my Dharma.

In this text, the prohibitions of the four orthodox practices (*catur-samyak-pratipatti*) are first clarified, followed by the establishment of the four heterodox practices (*catur-mithyā-pratipatti*).

Regarding the prohibition of the four orthodox practices: first, not permitting [non-Buddhists] to leave the household life; second, not permitting them to practice the Way; third, not permitting them to fashion images; and fourth, not permitting them to construct stupas. Regarding the establishment of the four heterodox practices:
first, establishing a central authority to control the masses; second, allowing laypeople to occupy high seats while bhikṣus stand upon the ground; and third, employing soldiers and slaves.
If a bhikṣu accepts four separate invitations,
three faults are incurred;
one should know that at such a time, the True Dharma will not long remain before it perishes.
Second, the admonition against destroying the conduct of the fourfold assembly.

Great King, it is you who have brought disorder and ruin to my Way; relying on your own power and authority, you have oppressed my four classes of disciples and the common people, so that none are free from suffering and hardship.
This is the causal condition for the destruction of the state. I shall speak of the faults and transgressions of the five turbidities for an entire kalpa.
It is not exhausted.
If a king does not practice the True Dharma, then the Buddha-way will be destroyed.
Third, the prohibitions and injunctions are not in accordance with the Dharma.

"Great King, in the final age of the Dharma, there will be bhikṣus and the fourfold assembly of disciples, while kings frequently engage in unrighteous conduct, arbitrarily committing great acts of unrighteousness against the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha, and creating various transgressions.
They will bind bhikṣus with what is neither Dharma nor Vinaya, according to the laws of prison inmates. At such a time, the extinction of the Dharma will not be long delayed."
The Four Admonitions on Self-Destruction, Part Three: First, the Initial Section; Second, the Arising of Evil and Subsequent Receiving of Retribution. Now, for the first:

"Great King, after my parinirvāṇa, in future ages, the fourfold assembly of disciples and various minor kings, crown princes, and sons of kings—who ought to be the sustainers and protectors of the Triple Gem—will instead further destroy and dismantle the Triple Gem, like the body of a lion."
The internal worms eat the lion of their own accord; this is not the case for non-Buddhists (*bāhyaka*).
The text has two parts: first the Dharma, then the simile. Now, the initial passage is clear: "Like a lion," and so forth, which clarifies the simile.
This simile is as stated in the *Padmavaktra Sūtra*, where the Buddha told Ānanda: "For example, when a lion reaches the end of its life and dies..."
Whether in the air, on land, in water, or on dry ground, no sentient beings dare to eat their flesh;
yet the insects born upon the body of a lion devour the lion’s own flesh. Ānanda, within my Buddha-dharma, it is not others who cause destruction;
it is that bhikṣu who destroys my dharma of three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas. That sutra merely uses this as a metaphor for those who have left the household life.
This sutra applies as a general metaphor for both the monastic and the lay.

Second, the arising of evil leads to much destruction of my Buddha-dharma, resulting in great transgressions; the true teaching declines and thins out, and the people lack correct practice, gradually [falling into ruin].
They detest that their lifespans have decreased to a mere hundred years;
they face the three retributions;
people destroy the Buddha-dharma; there are no more filial sons; the six types of kinship are in disharmony; celestial deities do not grant protection; and pestilence and malevolent spirits prevail.

If one has recently committed offenses and encountered calamities and portents, with misfortunes following one after another in all directions, and dies to enter the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals—if one is reborn as a human, one will become a soldier or a slave;
such karmic retribution is like a shadow or an echo, like characters written by someone at night that remain visible even after the fire is extinguished.
The karmic retribution within the three realms is likewise thus.
In the text, the correspondence between the Dharma and the analogy can be seen. The "six relations" refer to parents, siblings, and spouses. There are three analogies:

the first two illustrate retribution in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavipāka*), while the last one illustrates retribution in the next life (*upapadyavipāka*) and subsequent lives (*aparaparyāyavipāka*).
The Five Prohibitions Regarding Service:
Great King, in future ages, if all kings, crown princes, sons of kings, or the fourfold assembly of disciples should arbitrarily impose written precepts upon the disciples of the Buddha—
such as the laws for laypeople or the laws for soldiers and slaves— if my disciples encounter such [treatment]...
When the bhikṣuṇīs are required to register their names with the government officials and are no longer my disciples at all— being instead like soldiers or slaves—

and when the Dharma establishes official administrators to govern the Sangha and manage the monastic registers, with both senior and junior *sengtong* (monastic heads) binding one another like prisoners in a jail,
such being the law for soldiers and slaves, then at that time, the Buddha-dharma will not endure long.
The sixth admonition regarding self-reproach:

"Great King, in future ages, various minor kings and disciples of the fourfold assembly who commit such sins and create the causes and conditions for the destruction of their kingdoms shall themselves undergo the retribution;
it is not the fault of the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Sangha."
Seventh, the admonition against erroneous faith:
In future ages, when this sutra— the vessel of the seven Buddhas’ Dharma and the path constantly traversed by the Buddhas of the ten directions—
is being circulated, many evil bhikṣus who greedily seek fame and profit will speak of themselves before kings, crown princes, and sons of kings.

The causes and conditions for destroying the Buddha-dharma and the causes and conditions for destroying the nation are as follows: when a king does not distinguish between right and wrong but listens to such words, he arbitrarily establishes laws and regulations that do not rely on the Buddha's precepts;
this constitutes the cause and condition for destroying the Buddha and destroying the nation. At such a time, the True Dharma will not endure for long.
In this passage there are four parts: first, it demonstrates that the good does not destroy the true teaching, saying:
"The stream opens the path of the Dharma of emptiness" and "it is a vessel capable of containing merit and wisdom. Second, from "Various evil bhikṣus... onwards, it demonstrates evil.
Third, from "That king did not distinguish... onwards, it shows erroneous faith. Fourth, from "This is the destruction of the Buddha's [teaching]... onwards, it demonstrates the transgression.
Section Two: The Great Assembly Upholds the Text. This section has two parts: first, the act of upholding; second, the practice thereof. Now, for the first:
At that time, the sixteen great kings, having heard the Buddha’s seven admonitions concerning future events, wept with tears streaming down, their voices shaking the trichiliocosm.
The sun, moon, five planets, and twenty-eight lunar mansions lost their radiance and ceased to appear at that moment. Then the kings...
Each of them, with a sincere heart, received and upheld the Buddha’s words: "The fourfold assembly of disciples who have left the home life shall act in accordance with the Buddha's teachings.
At that time, the great multitude—the eighteen Brahma Kings and the various devaputras of the six heavens of desire—exclaimed:
"At such a time as this, the world is empty and void; it is an age without a Buddha."
The text has two parts: first, expressing grief; second, lamenting. The first part has two sections: first, the actual expression of grief (beginning with "At that time, the various kings...");
second, the reception and upholding [of the teaching]. The second part, beginning with "Then the great assembly...", is the lamentation over this time of grief.

Second, the Practice of Devotion. At that time, from among the immeasurable great assembly— consisting of ten billion bodhisattvas such as Maitreya and Siṃhacandra, ten billion Śāriputras and Subhūtis,
five hundred billion deities of the eighteen Brahma heavens and the six heavens of the desire realm, and those of the three realms and six paths of existence— [all were present].
Upon hearing the Buddha’s discourse on the causes and conditions for protecting the Buddha and the causes and conditions for protecting the nation, King Asura was filled with immeasurable joy;
he prostrated before the Buddha and received and upheld the Prajñāpāramitā.
The five sections of the text are as follows: first, listing the great assembly who heard what the Buddha taught;
second, clarifying that upon hearing the meaning of the Buddha’s Dharma, they experienced immeasurable joy; third, explaining their state of joy; fourth, their prostration before the Buddha;
and fifth, their upholding and practice of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Commentary on the Benevolent Kings’ Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra for Protecting the State, Scroll Lower (End).
